Dear Reader,

Recently, a new branch of a bank was built on my route to work. Because I was driving past it twice a day, I got to see how it was built, brick-by-brick. First the ground was leveled, and then the foundation poured. From there, the whole building was framed and then gradually filled in with brick and plaster. At some point, pre-roof, the vault was lifted in, disappearing into the building before I could even see it.

While building a secure bank branch and setting up security in your SAP HANA system are wildly different processes, there are some lessons to be drawn. A new SAP HANA system is good chance to start your security practices fresh, leveling on the ground beneath you. Layers of security in the form of privileges, authorizations, certificates, and other measures are the best way to put up walls and vaults between those who should have access, and those who shouldn’t.

What did you think about SAP HANA 2.0 Security Guide? Your comments and suggestions are the most useful tools to help us make our books the best they can be. Please feel free to contact me and share any praise or criticism you may have.

Thank you for purchasing a book from SAP PRESS!

Preface

SAP HANA powers SAP applications and hosts data from a variety of sources, functionalities that are often critical to an organization’s operations. Failure to properly secure an SAP HANA environment often can lead to system instability and hurt data integrity; therefore, SAP HANA security must be given the proper attention and scrutiny.

Purpose

This book was written with the goal of educating readers about securing SAP HANA. We’ll focus on key aspects of the SAP HANA security model, including user provisioning, role creation, privilege assignment, encryption, auditing, and authentication. We’ll also discuss the tools you can use to create and maintain an SAP HANA security model. Such information is critical for SAP HANA security architects to implement security models for their organizations. This information is also necessary for organizations to protect the data hosted within SAP HANA and to maintain the reliability of systems that rely on SAP HANA.

Who Should Read This Book?

This book will help security teams, SAP Basis teams, security consultants, and anyone looking for a comprehensive guide to implementing an SAP HANA security model.

We recommend the following prerequisites for readers of this book:

  • General knowledge of the SAP HANA cockpit

  • General knowledge of SQL

  • Experience working in areas of database administration

  • Experience working with database objects such as tables, views, and stored procedures

Each chapter is structured to offer background and theory for specific security-related concepts. Many chapters conclude with a case study—centering on the fictitious E-Corporation—for a “real-world” application of the topics covered in the book. Our goal is to provide you with technical knowledge and a unique perspective on how security has been implemented in the field based on real customer engagements.

Structure of This Book

The book is structured into 18 chapters. The Introduction and Chapter 1 through Chapter 4 introduce SAP HANA, SAP HANA security, the SAP HANA cockpit, privileges, and database objects. Chapter 4, Chapter 5, and Chapter 6 introduce users and roles. Chapter 7 through Chapter 11 discuss the various privilege types within SAP HANA. The remaining chapters discuss SAP HANA authentication, encryption, lifecycle management, audit policies, security troubleshooting, and general recommendations for securing your SAP HANA environment.

Introduction

Representing the next evolution of data management for many organizations, SAP HANA also powers critical applications for managing your organization. Thus, SAP HANA can be a valuable asset in many organizations. Because of its importance, SAP HANA must be secured. In the Introduction, we’ll provide an overview of SAP HANA’s hardware and software layers. We’ll introduce the basic concepts of SAP HANA security and list several reasons why securing your SAP HANA environment is important.

Chapter 1: Managing Security with the SAP HANA Cockpit

This chapter introduces the SAP HANA cockpit, a key tool for managing SAP HANA security. We’ll start with an overview of the architecture of the SAP HANA cockpit. We’ll explain how you can navigate the SAP HANA cockpit. We’ll also provide a detailed workflow to help identify key security management areas within the SAP HANA cockpit, including all security-related functionalities, the SAP HANA database explorer, and the SQL console.

Chapter 2: Introduction to SAP HANA Privileges

This chapter introduces the key privilege types available within SAP HANA. We’ll provide a summary of each privilege type, including system, object, analytic, package, and application privileges. We’ll also discuss how SAP HANA validates the assignment of privileges for users and roles.

Chapter 3: Catalog Objects

This chapter explains the role catalog objects play within an SAP HANA system. We’ll review the process for creating both standard schemas and repository-based schemas. We’ll also review how you can create other standard schema- and repository-based catalog objects. You’ll need to understand the nature of catalog objects because they relate to object privileges and the overall SAP HANA security model architecture.

Chapter 4: User Accounts

Authentication and authorization center on user accounts. Every individual user and every application that interacts with SAP HANA requires a user account. This chapter will provide detailed information on types of user accounts, on how to create user accounts, and how privileges are granted or revoked from user accounts. We’ll also discuss how roles are granted to user accounts. At the end, we’ll provide a case study to review a programmatic approach to provisioning users from external sources.

Chapter 5: Database Roles

When granting privileges, you should always avoid granting them directly to users, which can lead to significant inconsistencies within a security model. As an alternative, you can grant privileges to roles, which can then be granted to one or more users, thus providing consistency. In this chapter, we’ll explore multiple options for creating roles. We’ll also discuss the different ways that privileges can be granted or revoked from roles and how roles can be nested to simplify the management of the security model.

Chapter 6: Repository Roles

In addition to creating standard database roles, you can also define roles within the SAP HANA development repository. Using repository-based roles can overcome many issues associated with standard database roles. In this chapter, we’ll discuss why you should use repository-based roles. We’ll also review the syntax needed to define repository roles within design-time scripts. As an alternative to defining scripts, we’ll also review how you can use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor graphical user interface (GUI) to create repository-based roles. We’ll also discuss how repository-based roles are granted to existing users and roles. In the end, we’ll walk through a case study in which we’ll discuss common roles implemented at E-Corporation.

Chapter 7: System Privileges

System privileges govern your ability to perform specific actions within an SAP HANA system. These actions are typically related to administrative and development roles. In this chapter, we’ll explore the system privileges available within SAP HANA. We’ll demonstrate how system privileges are granted using SQL statements, the SAP HANA cockpit, and the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager as well as within repository-based roles. We’ll close this chapter with a case study outlining several commonly used administrative roles and their required system privileges.

Chapter 8: Object Privileges

Object privileges play an important role in the development of any SAP HANA security model since they define the types of SQL script actions a user can perform on a catalog object. SAP HANA hosts multiple types of catalog objects. In this chapter, we’ll look closely at object privileges. We’ll demonstrate how you to grant object privileges to users or roles using SQL statements or the SAP HANA cockpit as well as within repository-based roles. We’ll close the chapter with a case study reviewing the workflow used by E-Corporation to add object privileges to a few existing repository-based roles.

Chapter 9: Package Privileges

SAP HANA is a development platform in addition to a data management solution. To facilitate application development, application code storage, security, and application lifecycle management, SAP HANA provides a repository organized into packages. To secure a repository at the package level, you must implement package privileges. In this chapter, we’ll start by discussing the SAP HANA development repository. We’ll then review the various privileges that can be granted for packages and how they’re granted to grantees. Finally, we’ll walk through a case study in which E-Corporation identifies and resolves the gaps in their existing package hierarchy and package privilege design.

Chapter 10: Analytic Privileges

Analytic privileges are used to grant or restrict access to data hosted within the SAP HANA system. In this chapter, we’ll provide an overview of analytic privileges. We’ll discuss the differences between static analytic privileges and dynamic analytic privileges and discuss how classic XML-based analytic privileges are being replaced with newer SQL-based analytic privileges. We’ll demonstrate how to manage and create static and dynamic privileges and review the process for troubleshooting a grantee’s effective analytic privileges. Finally, we’ll discuss the processes available to grant analytic privileges.

Chapter 11: Application Privileges

SAP HANA is an application development platform in which web-based applications are both developed and hosted. At times, these applications also need their own security models, which are called application privileges. In this chapter, we’ll provide an overview of application privileges within SAP HANA, how you can create them, and how they’re granted to roles using a variety of options. We’ll also review the Privileges on Users option and show you how to use it for granting the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege to another grantee.

Chapter 12: Authentication

For authorization mechanisms to work properly, the SAP HANA system must first properly identify each user. To identify users, SAP HANA supports several authentication mechanisms. In this chapter, we’ll walk through the details of SAP HANA’s internal basic authentication system and its configurable password policy settings. We’ll also discuss the various external providers supported for seamless authentication with the SAP HANA system. Finally, we’ll walk through the process by which E-Corporation defines a stored procedure to add a Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) identity to an existing user account within SAP HANA.

Chapter 13: Certificate Management and Encryption

In addition to authorization and authentication, you’ll also need encryption to protect your SAP HANA system. In this chapter, we’ll review Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) certificate management within SAP HANA. We’ll also discuss the options available for encrypting communication between client applications and the SAP HANA server. Finally, we’ll discuss the necessary steps for encrypting SAP HANA data and log volumes.

Chapter 14: Security Lifecycle Management

Since SAP HANA is a development platform, security administrators will discover that security-related development artifacts can be transported easily between different SAP HANA instances. In this chapter, we’ll outline the best practices and options available to use this transportation mechanism. We’ll start by discussing how you can maintain a consistent security model. We’ll then review the necessary steps for defining a delivery unit containing security-related artifacts. Then, we’ll review how you can access the SAP HANA application lifecycle management tool. Finally, we’ll discuss additional features within SAP HANA application lifecycle management that can benefit the lifecycle management of security artifacts.

Chapter 15: Auditing

Auditing allows organizations to configure rules that record important activities conducted within the SAP HANA system. In this chapter, we’ll discuss why you need auditing within SAP HANA. We’ll also discuss the required steps for enabling auditing and for defining policies to record critical activities. Finally, we’ll walk through a case study in which you’ll create auditing rules to track important changes within E-Corporation’s SAP HANA landscape.

Chapter 16: Security Tracing and Troubleshooting

In the real world, most security models are quite complex. SAP HANA offers security trace options and system views to help administrators manage their security models. This chapter outlines the required steps for enabling security-related authorization traces and describe how you can review trace file results. In addition, we’ll review various system views that provide details about the rights effectively granted to individual users. We’ll close the chapter with a case study in which E-Corporation queries system views to troubleshoot authorization issues within its environment.

Chapter 17: Security Recommendations

Knowing how to configure and implement security within SAP HANA is vital, and guidelines based on established best practices can help. This chapter provides several recommendations for securing an SAP HANA system based on the principles learned throughout this book. We’ll discuss recommendations related to password authentication, encryption, high-level privileges, the SYSTEM account, escalation vulnerabilities, appliance handover, and audit policies.

Chapter 18: SAP HANA XSA Security

SAP has enhanced the application server included within the SAP HANA platform with SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA). With this enhancement, a new layer of security and a new methodology for securing application components was introduced. In this chapter, we’ll take a closer look at the security structure of the SAP HANA XSA platform. We’ll start with an overview of the SAP HANA XSA platform. We’ll then discuss SAP HANA XSA users, role collections, organizations, and spaces and show you how they are administered and secured. We’ll briefly discuss SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, including why it is needed and how you can secure access to the application. Finally, we’ll review the SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI) container’s architecture, how runtime security works within the HDI container, how HDI container roles work, and how security administrators can manage runtime access to objects outside of an HDI container.

Introduction

SAP HANA represents the next evolution of data management for many organizations. As a valuable asset, data must be secured.

Most organizations see their data as an asset: Data helps conduct business, identify trends, manage operations, and anticipate change. Over the decades, the volume of data produced by computer systems has increased substantially. As data volumes have increased, so has the need for computer systems powerful enough to process that data. For many organizations, SAP HANA is a powerful and important tool for managing and processing large volumes of data.

SAP HANA hosts data and operates applications critical to an organization. If data is lost or applications aren’t available, an organization can suffer substantial financial loss. Therefore, security is one of many important aspects required to ensure the integrity of the data and the applications that rely on SAP HANA.

Throughout this book, we’ll walk you through the key concepts of the SAP HANA security model, at its core comprised of users, roles, and privileges. You must also take steps to secure its data using encryption, authentication, and operating system controls. You must also understand the various tools available for managing security while also tracking changes for auditing. Before we dive into the security model, let’s first look at an overview of SAP HANA.

Overview of SAP HANA

Some consider SAP HANA just another database, but SAP HANA offers much more than its database services. SAP HANA is a next-generation data appliance that can play many roles throughout an organization. To be more precise, SAP HANA can facilitate many solutions, including solutions in which SAP HANA manages data for an application and solutions in which SAP HANA manages data and analytics. The first step in understanding SAP HANA security is to understand its architecture. Thus, we must first examine both the software layers and hardware layers of SAP HANA.

Software Layers and Features

At its core, SAP HANA acts as a database. However, SAP HANA is also an application development environment, with layers that facilitate multidimensional models. SAP HANA offers a predictive analytics engine and even an online transaction processes (OLTP) engine. Let’s not forget that SAP HANA can also act as an unstructured data processor, a full-text search engine, a data federation engine, and a data integration tool. Because of these capabilities, securing an SAP HANA system requires a knowledge of components well beyond standard relational database management system (RDBMS) objects and their security.

At a high level, Figure 1 shows the software features and layers of the SAP HANA appliance. These layers allow SAP HANA to facilitate more than just standard database processing. Security within SAP HANA must address each of these layers.

Figure 1    High-Level Overview of the SAP HANA Software Appliance Layers

The SAP HANA in-memory database layer contains multiple query processing engines, such as the calculation engine, the online analytical processes (OLAP) engine, the row engine, and the join engine. This layer also contains the row store tables, columnar store tables, and the new SAP HANA smart data access logical database tables. Engines have also been designed to manage text processing and text searches.

The SAP HANA software appliance layer, which includes the SAP HANA in-memory database layer, also includes the SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS) engine (XS engine) to enable SAP HANA’s use as a development platform. Some features are embedded, such as the Predictive Analytics Library (PAL), the Business Function Library (BFL), planning engines, rules engines, and geospatial engines. SAP HANA supports the real-time replication of data using replication agents and data integration using SAP HANA smart data integration. SAP HANA also offers a more robust and sophisticated SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA) application server, which supports more complex coding languages and application process isolation. In total, these layers build upon each other to form the SAP HANA appliance. Because SAP HANA is a robust data and application platform, securing this data and application appliance can be a challenging endeavor.

Hardware Layers and Features

Understanding SAP HANA’s hardware components is also fundamentally important for understanding what SAP HANA is and how it is secured. With SAP HANA, data is stored in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), in Intel Optane DC persistent memory, and within the central processing unit (CPU) cache. As a result, SAP HANA software can deliver exceptional performance because data is stored close to the CPU. Traditional databases store and access data on disk drives that are architecturally further away from the CPU and, for a variety of technical reasons, slower in accessing data.

Each server is also configured with multiple CPU sockets, each with multiple CPU cores. Multiple CPU sockets and cores allow the software to process multiple requests concurrently. For example, when data is stored in a column store, the software can reduce the processing of each column of data into one or more parallel requests. Because multiple CPU cores are available, each request can be processed by one or more CPU cores in parallel. The net result is more data is processed at the same time for an individual query.

Because DRAM is volatile or erased when the server loses power, the data stored in DRAM must be backed up to nonvolatile storage layers both automatically and periodically. The SAP HANA appliance manages these periodic snapshots of memory to disk and persistent memory automatically. The SAP HANA in-memory database stores data in two primary persistent locations: First, a mirror image of the in-memory data is routinely synchronized and stored in the /hana/data file path. For systems with persistent memory, non-delta data storage can also be placed in a persistent memory pool and in the /hana/data path simultaneously. Second, all transactions are recorded within the redo logs. SAP HANA is compliant with the principles of atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID). ACID compliance guarantees that each database transaction is reliable, even if the server loses power. SAP HANA’s redo logs facilitate ACID compliance, and redo logs are stored in the default /hana/log path. Security administrators must understand this process because these locations must also be encrypted.

The amount of RAM supported on a single SAP HANA appliance is finite, and organizations often need to store more data in-memory than is supported on a single host. To overcome this limitation, SAP HANA can be scaled out to run on multiple servers that act as a single instance, acting as a single appliance when scaled over multiple nodes while also serving as a single point of access for users. When distributed on multiple nodes, the core software engines are active on each node and are used to manage the distributed data in memory.

In a multinode or scale-out SAP HANA appliance, all nodes share a single logical persistent storage layer. As a result, the in-memory data of each node is written to the same shared persistent storage layer during regular in-memory data snapshots and backups. Figure 2 shows the SAP HANA appliance running as a single instance distributed over multiple nodes.

Each SAP HANA node communicates over dedicated redundant network links. From a security standpoint, the communications between each SAP node must be secured. In addition, the data stored in the persistent layers might also need to be encrypted. Fortunately, because the SAP HANA scale-out cluster acts as a single instance, users, roles, and privileges are centrally managed for all server nodes.

SAP HANA Hardware Selection

A variety of server hardware vendors provide certified, prebuilt systems for running SAP HANA. Each hardware vendor must undergo strenuous certification processes to ensure that its hardware platform meets or exceeds the standards set by SAP. A certified SAP HANA 2.0 appliance should only be run on the following CPU modes:

  • Haswell v3 Intel E7-8880 v3, E7-8890 v3, or E7-8880L v3

  • Broadwell v4 Intel E7-8880 v4, E7-8890 v4, or E7-8894 v4

  • Skylake SP Intel Xeon Platinum 8176, 8176M, 8180, or 8180M

  • Cascade Lake SP Intel Xeon Platinum 8276 or 8280

For a complete listing of certified servers by vendor, refer to the SAP Certified Appliance Hardware for SAP HANA Directory, available at http://s-prs.co/v498226.

In addition to using certified, prebuilt SAP HANA systems, you can design your own certified systems using the Tailored Datacenter Integration (TDI) program. This program allows you to use your own internal network infrastructure and storage infrastructure to build a fully supported SAP HANA system. However, you can only use servers or compute nodes listed in the SAP Certified Appliance Hardware for SAP HANA directory. For more information, refer to http://www.saphana.com/docs/DOC-4380.

Figure 2    SAP HANA Scale-Out Appliance with One or More Nodes

SAP HANA Versions

When we refer to “SAP HANA” in this book, we’re talking about the security features and functionalities in SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 01 or higher. In many cases, the same functionality will apply to SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 12, but in general, we won’t systematically indicate differences between SAP HANA 1.0 and SAP HANA 2.0.

SAP HANA Architecture

At a high level, Figure 3 shows the basic service architecture of SAP HANA, including the standard connectivity or communications protocols. The SAP HANA system is comprised of several core services, such as the name server, the preprocessor server, the compile server, the script server, the index server, the XS engine, and the XSA engine. Each service provides one or more of the many features available within the SAP HANA platform. Interservice communications are secured automatically within SAP HANA. The index server is predominantly responsible for the core security model elements, such as users, roles, and privilege verification. The index server is also responsible for the core RDBMS catalog objects and their security. Both the XS engine and the XSA engine also have security that extends through to the index server.

Figure 3    SAP HANA Services and Connectivity Overview

To better understand the functions of each SAP HANA service, let’s review the responsibilities of each service within the platform and how each service relates to security.

Index Server

The core service of the platform is the index server, responsible for all database, data storage, and data processing tasks. When stored in-memory, data resides within the index server process. This data includes data stored in row or columnar store tables. When a SQL or Multidimensional Expression (MDX) query is executed by a business intelligence application, the index server processes the query and returns the results. The index servicer is responsible for queries executed in the OLAP engine, the calculation engine, the join engine, and the row engine, making it the most important service in the platform.

The index server manages many objects within the security model, such as users, roles, authentication, audits, catalog objects, and development repositories, and thus is responsible for most of the security within SAP HANA.

XS Engine

The XS engine acts as a web application server and manages and processes application code deployed to the SAP HANA platform. Applications like the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor reside in the XS engine. Developers can also create custom applications using JavaScript and HTML5 and operate these applications in the XS engine.

The XS engine hosts many applications for managing security within SAP HANA and also provides applications to help you with the lifecycle management of SAP HANA. However, SAP has indicated that, in the long term, the XS engine and its application development will be replaced with the SAP HANA XSA platform. As of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, the XS engine, the _SYS_REPO repository, and some SAP HANA XS applications are still available and usable.

XSA Engine

Introduced in SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 11, the XSA engine is a robust web application server that you can use to manage and process application code. However, its overall architecture is quite different from the XS engine. Applications like the SAP HANA cockpit and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA are hosted within this service. The XSA engine can be installed with your SAP HANA instance or on SAP HANA, express edition, where it can run as a standalone application server. Each SAP HANA XSA application is assigned a child process and a TCP/IP connectivity port. Thus, an individual application can crash without crashing the entire SAP HANA XS runtime. SAP HANA XSA also supports advanced programing languages, which enables you to create more sophisticated applications.

You can also use applications like the SAP HANA cockpit and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to manage many aspects of the SAP HANA security model.

Name Server

The name server is responsible for managing the topology of the SAP HANA architecture. With an SAP HANA scale out, the name server tracks which services are active and where data tables reside in the cluster.

The name server configuration file contains the configuration of the global password policy, which defines how SAP HANA manages password authentication throughout a scale-out landscape.

Preprocessor Server

The preprocessor server helps the index server process text-based searches. This server includes features such as sentiment analysis, text analysis, full-text search, and fuzzy search of both structured and unstructured text. This service does not play a major role in securing SAP HANA.

Compile Server

The compile server is responsible for helping the index server compile L language-based procedures. This server was removed from the index server in SAP HANA SPS 06 to prevent compiling tasks from crashing the index server. However, the exact reason why the compile server was isolated from the index server have never been officially published by SAP. This service does not play a major role in securing SAP HANA.

Script Server

The script server is responsible for helping SAP HANA process operations that require the Application Function Library (AFL), which includes the BFL and the PAL. Developers or applications using SAP HANA for predictive modeling will use this service. This service does not play a major role in securing SAP HANA.

Outside of its core services, several external applications can also access SAP HANA. Figure 3 shows a few common clients and their communication protocols. The communications between these clients and the core SAP HANA server is particularly important in the realm of security. SAP HANA supports secure communication with all client applications. SAP HANA Studio, the SAP HANA cockpit, and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA can use Open Database Connectivity (ODBC), Java Database Connectivity (JDBC), or Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to communicate with the SAP HANA system. Each of these communication paths supports strong encryption. Many business intelligence applications also support ODBC and JDBC connectivity. For applications hosted in the XS engine, SAP HANA supports secure communication over HTTP or secure HTTPS.

Now that you have a basic understanding of the architecture of SAP HANA, in the next section, we’ll provide a basic introduction to SAP HANA security.

Introduction to SAP HANA Security

At its core, SAP HANA security consists of users, roles, and privileges. User accounts are created and assigned one or more roles, and roles are created and assigned one or more privileges. The combination of roles and privileges determines what a user account is authorized to do within the SAP HANA platform. Figure 4 shows a high-level overview of the relationships among users, roles, and privileges.

Figure 4    Overview of Users, Roles, and Privileges

Privileges are categorized into system, package, application, analytic, and object categories. Each category controls a specific area within the SAP HANA architecture. However, a user account can’t interact with the SAP HANA system until the account is authenticated. Typically, a password is provided for authentication, but SAP HANA also supports several third-party authentication mechanisms.

Outside of the core areas of users, roles, and privileges, security administrators must also focus on encryption, audit policies, user provisioning, lifecycle management, and security model troubleshooting. Throughout this book, we’ll introduce these key concepts and immerse you in the knowledge necessary for mastering the SAP HANA security model.

Importance of Securing Your SAP HANA System

As mentioned in the Overview of SAP HANA section, SAP HANA often hosts critical data for the organization. SAP HANA also often operates applications that are vital to the organization. Databases like SAP HANA often contain master sources of data, such as customer, product, and financial data; sales orders; and bills of materials (BOMs). If the integrity of these systems are compromised, your organizations could suffer substantial financial loss or lose competitive advantage.

Therefore, your organization must implement a proper security model within its SAP HANA systems. Of equal importance is for an organization to invest in training and resources for managing the security model and accessing the system. SAP HANA can only be secure when its administrators and users can adhere to all aspects of the security model.

Four key reasons that your organization needs to secure its SAP HANA systems include the following:

  • Organizations should provide privacy to protect data that is stored and accessed within the SAP HANA system. This protection includes the use of encryption to secure both in-memory data and data on disk as well as encryption to secure the communication of data between a client and the SAP HANA server. Authorization and authentication also play an important role in maintaining the privacy of data. In general, only authorized individuals should be granted access to your organization’s data.

  • Organizations must ensure the integrity of the data hosted within the SAP HANA system. When financial transactions are recorded, these records should be protected from unauthorized changes. Data integrity is protected by allowing only authorized individuals to make changes to the data and through auditing, encryption, and strong password authentication policies.

  • Organizations must also ensure the availability of the SAP HANA system. Security is an important component in maintaining a system’s availability. Both authorized and unauthorized users can lead to poor database availability. A security model can govern access among trusted users, those that have been explicitly granted privileges within the database. However, organizations must ensure that user access is limited to only their areas of responsibility. You must also ensure that users are well trained for their level of access. Unauthorized users are users outside your organization that are not explicitly granted privileges within the SAP HANA system. These users often gain access through unscrupulous or unauthorized means and intend to steal data or disrupt the operations of your database. The security model can both govern authorized access and prevent unauthorized access.

  • When collecting sensitive data from customers, organizations must protect that data. Organizations that fail to protect customer data often have their reputations tarnished. If customers can’t trust your organization with their sensitive data, they might choose to conduct business with your competitors. Your organization could also be subject to major fines if sensitive customer data isn’t secured.

Thus, your organization should prioritize, emphasize, and scrutinize its SAP HANA security models for several reasons. Throughout this book, we’ll teach you how to implement a security model, identify risky privileges, and follow best practices when possible.

Summary

We’re now ready to embark on our journey through the SAP HANA security model, starting with an overview of the SAP HANA cockpit, an important tool for managing many SAP HANA security artifacts.

1    Managing Security with the SAP HANA Cockpit

In this chapter, we’ll introduce you to the SAP HANA cockpit and many of the workflows necessary for managing security settings and security models.

Since its inception, most of the SAP HANA security model has been developed and maintained using SAP HANA Studio, a client tool installed on an SAP HANA developer or administrator workstation. However, in November 2016, SAP announced and released SAP HANA 2.0, including a new administration tool called the SAP HANA cockpit.

The SAP HANA cockpit provides monitoring, configuration, performance optimization, security, platform lifecycle management, and other administration capabilities. Unlike SAP HANA Studio, the SAP HANA cockpit does not provide application or content development tools. These tools have been migrated to SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, another independent, web-based development tool in the SAP HANA 2.0 portfolio.

The SAP HANA cockpit is a standalone, web-based HTML5 application server, not a desktop-based client tool. It operates in SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA) and also requires an SAP HANA 2.0, express edition, database or an SAP HANA 2.0 tenant database to operate. The architecture of the SAP HANA cockpit is designed to centralize and simplify the management and administration of SAP HANA throughout an IT landscape. Given its importance in the realm of SAP HANA security, the goal of this chapter is to introduce you to the various security workflows and security options that you can manage in the SAP HANA cockpit. However, this chapter is not intended as a comprehensive guide to using the SAP HANA cockpit.

Other Web-Based Administration Tools

As of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, some aspect of the security model can still be managed with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. This tool is hosted in the legacy SAP HANA extended application services, classic model (SAP HANA XS) engine (XS engine).

References to the SAP HANA cockpit will be prominent throughout this book, so you’ll require a basic understanding of it and its security-related interfaces. In this chapter, we’ll provide an overview of the SAP HANA cockpit, introducing its architecture, basic navigation steps, and specific security management interfaces. We’ll also introduce the SAP HANA database explorer and the SQL console, in which security-related SQL commands are executed, and we’ll outline the key user interfaces you’ll use to administer security-related items, including the graphical interfaces for user and role administration. We’ll also discuss other interfaces used to manage data encryption, authentication, and database security.

1.1    What Is the SAP HANA Cockpit?

In this section, we’ll provide an overview of the architecture of the SAP HANA cockpit, show you how to access it the first time, review the SAP HANA cockpit manager, and walk you through the steps required for registering SAP HANA databases within the SAP HANA cockpit.

1.1.1    SAP HANA Cockpit Architecture

Architecturally, the SAP HANA cockpit is an SAP HANA XSA multi-target application (MTA) that requires an SAP HANA database to operate. SAP provides several deployment options, as shown in Figure 1.1.

As shown in Figure 1.1, you can deploy the SAP HANA cockpit on a supported standalone server using SAP HANA, express edition. The SAP HANA cockpit can also be installed alongside your existing SAP HANA instance or within an existing instance by using separate tenant databases sharing the same instance. In all cases, the software must be deployed to a supported Linux operating system (OS). Be sure you size your hardware properly based on the deployment option you choose.

Both a standalone installation and an installation as a separate instance require the use of SAP HANA, express edition. Fortunately, the installation media for the SAP HANA cockpit includes every required component and deploys the entire architecture for you. The installation media can also deploy the SAP HANA cockpit to an existing SAP HANA database, SAP HANA XSA application, and a dedicated tenant if you choose that option.

Figure 1.1    Deployment Options for the SAP HANA Cockpit

More Information about Installing and Upgrading the SAP HANA Cockpit

For more information concerning installation, the architecture of the SAP HANA cockpit, and upgrade options, refer to the SAP HANA Installation and Update Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498200.

1.1.2    Getting Started with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Before you can begin managing security within SAP HANA, you must first learn how to access the SAP HANA cockpit, create SAP HANA cockpit users, and register SAP HANA systems. In some cases, you’ll also need to create resource groups to limit users from seeing registered resources or SAP HANA database connections when accessing the SAP HANA cockpit. In this section, we’ll walk you through the high-level process of determining your SAP HANA cockpit URLs, accessing the SAP HANA cockpit manager, creating SAP HANA cockpit users, creating resource groups, and finally registering SAP HANA databases. Note that this chapter is not intended to serve as a comprehensive guide to the SAP HANA cockpit. Rather, the goal in this chapter is to discuss high-level functionalities that are necessary when using the SAP HANA cockpit to manage parts of the SAP HANA security model.

Important URLs for SAP HANA Cockpit

Once you’ve installed the SAP HANA cockpit, you can query SAP HANA XSA via the SAP HANA XSA command line to list the installed applications and their URLs and ports. When deploying the SAP HANA cockpit from the provided media, several SAP HANA XSA applications are installed. The SAP HANA cockpit application is called cockpit-web-app as of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04. If you need to find the exact URL, use the SAP HANA XSA command line to list the installed application. Let’s walk through that process:

  1. The SAP HANA XSA command line is included with your SAP HANA cockpit installation. The SAP HANA XSA command line is executed from the OS shell. To use the SAP HANA XSA command line, log on to your SAP HANA cockpit server via Secure Shell (SSH) as the <sid>adm user. By default, the SAP System Identification (SID) of the SAP HANA cockpit is H4C. Therefore, you would log on to Linux as the h4cadm user.

  2. You can run SAP HANA XSA command line commands from any directory. To start the process, run the following command to log on to SAP HANA XSA:

    • xs login

  3. Log on with your SAP HANA cockpit admin user, typically the COCKPIT_ADMIN user.

  4. Enter the application programming interface (API) endpoint URL, typically https:<cockpit-host-name>:39630.

  5. By default, you should log on with the HANACockpit organization and SAP space set. If you’re not in this space, run the following commands to enter the correct organization and space:

    • xs org HANACockpit

    • xs space SAP

  6. Execute the following command to list the cockpit-web-app application URL and port:

    • xs a | grep cockpit-web-app

  7. On the right of the output, look for the URL and port. In most cases, this URL will run on port 51028 and will match the following pattern:

    • https://<cockpit-host-name>:51028

  8. You’ll also need the URL for the SAP HANA cockpit manager application. Run the following command to list the URL and port of this application:

    • xs a | grep cockpit-admin-web-app

  9. On the right of the output, look for the URL and port. In most cases, this URL will run on port 51030 and will match the following pattern:

    • https://<cockpit-host-name>:51030

  10. Enter the URL, including the port, for the SAP HANA cockpit application to access the logon page. For example, enter “https://hanacockpit.ecorp.com:51028/.” You can log on using your COCKPIT_ADMIN user or the user provided by the SAP HANA cockpit administrator.

The SAP HANA cockpit Home page will provide several links and tiles that will navigate you to various management options when clicked, as shown in Figure 1.2. For example, you can click the Resource Directory tile to view registered SAP HANA systems. You can also click the Manage Cockpit tile, to access the SAP HANA cockpit manager.

Figure 1.2    SAP HANA Cockpit Homepage

Now, let’s look at the SAP HANA cockpit manager in more detail. Before you can navigate further in the SAP HANA cockpit, you must register SAP HANA systems and establish SAP HANA cockpit users and SAP HANA cockpit groups.

SAP HANA Cockpit Manager

By default, you can access the SAP HANA cockpit manager using the following URL pattern:

  • https://<cockpit-host-name>:51030

However, the application might be deployed to a different port in your environment. As mentioned earlier, use the xs a command from the SAP HANA XSA command line to list applications, URLs, and ports. The SAP HANA cockpit manager application name is cockpit-admin-web-app.

Enter the URL and log on using your provided credentials. The COCKPIT_ADMIN user can be utilized your first time accessing the manager. The Cockpit Manager homepage is divided into a list of menu options on the left and configuration pages in the pane on the right, as shown in Figure 1.3.

Figure 1.3    SAP HANA Cockpit Manager Homepage

The following bullet list will outline how each of the items in the Categories menu is used in the administration of the SAP HANA cockpit:

  • Registered Resources
    Use this menu option to add or import SAP HANA database connection information. SAP HANA databases must be registered within the SAP HANA cockpit manager before they can be available in the SAP HANA cockpit.

  • Resource Groups
    Use this menu option to create and manage resource groups, which are organizational and security objects that you’ll use to group one or more registered SAP HANA databases into. SAP HANA cockpit users are assigned to one or more groups. For standard SAP HANA cockpit users, you can use groups to limit the registered systems they see in the SAP HANA cockpit. However, users granted the Administrators or Resource Administrators role will see all resource regardless of their assigned groups.

  • Cockpit Users
    Use this menu option to create and manage SAP HANA cockpit users.

  • Cockpit Settings
    Use this menu option to manage SAP HANA cockpit-specific settings.

  • Active Sessions
    Use this menu option to view and terminate active sessions within the SAP HANA cockpit.

  • XSA Logs
    Use this menu option to view SAP HANA XSA application logs. SAP HANA cockpit users must be SAP HANA XSA organization managers to use this functionality. You can grant this access to SAP HANA cockpit administrators using the SAP HANA XSA command line interface by running this command: xs set-org-role COCKPIT_ADMIN HANACockpit OrgManager.

Let’s look at the process for creating users and granting them SAP HANA cockpit roles.

Creating SAP HANA Cockpit Users

Everyone that needs to interact with the SAP HANA cockpit will need a user account to log on and access resources. SAP HANA cockpit users are effectively SAP HANA XSA users, which are also effectively SAP HANA database users. You can create these users at each layer mentioned, but a best practice would be to create them from the SAP HANA cockpit manager to avoid any setup issues.

SAP HANA cockpit user credentials only apply to the SAP HANA cockpit application and its supporting SAP HANA database. These credentials do not provide access to the registered SAP HANA databases. A user will need credentials for each registered database in addition to their SAP HANA cockpit user credentials. Note also that the password policy for an SAP HANA cockpit user follows the password policy configured in the SAP HANA, express edition SYSTEMDB or SAP HANA tenant database that supports the application. Administrators should consider registering this SAP HANA, express edition, database or tenant database within the SAP HANA cockpit to manage these and other database settings.

To create an SAP HANA cockpit user, click the Cockpit Users menu option from the homepage. A new window will appear with existing users listed on the left and details about a selected user on the right, as shown in Figure 1.4.

Figure 1.4    Cockpit Users Interface in the SAP HANA Cockpit Manager

Click the Create User button, located at the bottom of the user list, to create a new user. To edit an existing user, select a user in the list and then click the Edit button located on the bottom right of the user’s details. Now, let’s look at the process of creating a user and describe the various roles that you can grant to users.

When you click the Create User button, a three-step process wizard will appear. On the first page, 1. User Information, using the provided fields, enter the User Name, Password, Confirm Password, and Email for the new user, as shown in Figure 1.5.

Click the Step 2 button to continue. On the 2. Cockpit Roles page, select the checkboxes for the roles you want to grant the user. Click the Step 3 button to continue. On the 3. Resource Groups section page, click the Add Groups button to open the Add User to Existing Group popup window. In this popup window, select the checkboxes for the groups you want to assign to the user. Click OK to close the popup window and then click Create User one last time to finalize the process.

Figure 1.5    Creating Users in the SAP HANA Cockpit Manager

Now, let’s look at the various roles that can be granted to users. Note that roles are not cumulative, meaning that one role does not build upon another. Instead, each role is explicit, and each role only provides access to one area directly. Users will need all roles granted to have full access to the SAP HANA cockpit and SAP HANA cockpit manager.

The following list outlines each role and provides additional information about the permissions each role grants a user:

  • Cockpit Administrator Role
    This role only provides administration access to SAP HANA cockpit settings. This role is not a master role and only provides access to change settings; no other access is included.

  • Cockpit Resource Administrator Role
    This role will grant a user access to register SAP HANA databases, create resource groups, and manage resource group assignments. Users with this role will have access to all registered resources regardless of their assigned SAP HANA cockpit group.

  • Cockpit User Administrator Role
    This role will grant a user the ability to create and manage other users in the SAP HANA cockpit manager and the underlying SAP HANA cockpit database. At the database level, this role grants the ROLE ADMIN and USER ADMIN system privileges. At the SAP HANA cockpit manager application level, this role grants similar access.

  • Cockpit User Role
    This standard role is required for a user to access the SAP HANA cockpit. A user must have this role to access the SAP HANA cockpit homepage. Two additional options for this role will grant a standard SAP HANA cockpit user limited but additional privileges. Let’s look at these options in more detail:

    • Register resources through the Cockpit Manager
      This subrole option grants the user limited access to the SAP HANA cockpit manager to create and register SAP HANA server resources. Resources will be created without groups, and access is limited only to members of the Cockpit Resource Administrator role and to itself.

    • System configuration template administrator role
      This subrole allows the user access to the SAP HANA cockpit Configuration Templates tile. Configuration templates contain SAP HANA database .ini file settings and can be stored and applied to SAP HANA databases.

  • Cockpit Troubleshooting Role
    This role grants a user access to view the SAP HANA XSA logs area of the SAP HANA cockpit manager. Users must be an SAP HANA XSA organization manager to use this functionality. You can grant this access to the SAP HANA cockpit admin using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit graphical user interface (GUI) or using the SAP HANA XSA command line by running the following command: xs set-org-role COCKPIT_ADMIN HANACockpit OrgManager.

In the next section, we’ll explore SAP HANA cockpit groups in more detail and show you how to create groups in the SAP HANA cockpit manager.

Creating SAP HANA Cockpit Resource Groups

SAP HANA cockpit uses resource groups to organize and secure registered SAP HANA databases. SAP HANA cockpit users can be assigned to one or more groups. For standard SAP HANA cockpit users, you can use groups to limit the registered systems they see in the SAP HANA cockpit. However, if users are granted the Administrators or Resource Administrators role, they will see all resource groups regardless of their assigned groups.

Resource groups are created using the SAP HANA cockpit manager. From the SAP HANA cockpit manager homepage, click the Resource Groups menu option to access the resource group management interface. The interface is organized into two panes. On the left is a list of existing resource groups within the Resource Groups pane. On the right is the Resource Group Details pane, as shown in Figure 1.6. When you click on a resource group on the left, its registered resources or SAP HANA databases will appear on the right.

Figure 1.6    SAP HANA Cockpit Manager Resource Group Management Interface

To create a group, locate the Create Group button at the bottom of the resource group list. Click the button to launch the three-step Create Group wizard. In the first step, 1. General information, enter the resource Group name and Description in the provided fields. Click the Step 2 button to continue. In the second step, 2. Resource, assign existing registered SAP HANA systems to the group. Click the Step 3 button to continue. In the third step, 3. Cockpit Users, assign one or more user to the group. Click the Create Group button to finish the wizard.

You can alter an existing group by selecting a group on the right side of the SAP HANA cockpit manager, toggling between the Resource and Cockpit Users tabs found above the resource or users listed in the left in the Resource Group Details pane. You can also use this interface to delete or remove registered resource or users from the resource groups.

Users assigned to a group will now see the corresponding registered resource when they log on to the SAP HANA cockpit. In the next section, we’ll explore the purpose of registered resources and how you’ll use the SAP HANA cockpit manager to register them.

Registering SAP HANA Databases and Tenants

Before you can interact with an SAP HANA system, you must first add or configure a connection to the SAP HANA system and store this connection within the SAP HANA cockpit.

To register resources or SAP HANA databases, click the Registered Resources button located on the SAP HANA cockpit manager homepage to access the registered resources management interface. This interface is organized into two panes. On the left is a list of existing registered resources or SAP HANA servers within the Registered Resources pane. On the right is the Resource Details pane, as shown in Figure 1.7. When you click on a resource group on the left, details about the registered resources or SAP HANA databases will appear on the right.

Figure 1.7    SAP HANA Databases or Registered Resources within the SAP HANA Cockpit Manager

Click the Register Resource button to launch the five-step Register Resources wizard. In the first step, 1. Resource, provide the connection details for your SAP HANA database. Click the Step 2 button to continue. In the second step, 2. Connection, select the desired communication encryption options when connecting to the SAP HANA database. Click the Step 3 button to continue. In the third step, 3. Technical User, enter the credentials that will be used to gather runtime and health information from the database. This step also provides an additional option for creating a technical user within the target database. Click the Step 4 button to continue. In the fourth step, 4. Resource Groups, assign the registration to one or more existing resource groups. Click the Step 5 button to continue. In the fifth step, 5. Contact, enter the contact information for the administrator of the database. Click the Review button to view a summary of the registration. If the information looks correct, click the Register button to activate the connection.

A basic understanding of the SAP HANA cockpit manager will be required when creating SAP HANA cockpit users and when managing access to the overall SAP HANA cockpit functionality. In this section, we provided a high-level overview of the components and steps necessary to set up access to the SAP HANA cockpit and SAP HANA cockpit manager. In the next section, we’ll provide a few tips on navigating the SAP HANA cockpit Home page, connecting to a registered database, and locating security-specific options on the System Overview page.

1.1.3    Navigating SAP HANA Cockpit

Navigating the SAP HANA cockpit requires a basic understanding of the interface layout and the workflow used to connect to a registered database and then interact with security and administration tools on the System Overview interface. We discussed how to obtain the SAP HANA cockpit URL in Section 1.1.2 and how to set up user access to the SAP HANA cockpit. Once you’ve logged onto the SAP HANA cockpit, you’ll start with the SAP HANA cockpit Home page.

Figure 1.8 shows an example layout of the SAP HANA cockpit Home page. The tabs near the top of the interface (Monitor Landscape, Manage Landscape, and SAP One Support) will each navigate you to a different section and tile set on the homepage. Let’s look at each of these tabs in more detail.

The first tab and tile set is the Monitor Landscape tab. Under this tab, you can view the entire resource directory by clicking the Resource Directory tile. You can also see registered systems organized into Production, Development, and Test resource groups based on the database’s configured profile. When installing SAP HANA, the installer will establish the intended use of the system, and that information is used by the SAP HANA cockpit to automatically organize registered systems into the Production, Development, and Test resource groups. Any resource groups assigned to your user account will also display as tiles in this section. Finally, the Administration Help tile enables you to navigate to documentation relevant to administering the SAP HANA cockpit.

Figure 1.8    SAP HANA Cockpit Homepage

To navigate to an SAP HANA database, locate the connection based on the tile groups found on your homepage. In most cases, you’ll find a system in one or more of the tile groupings. Each tile is not exclusive to a registered SAP HANA system. For example, to see all registered systems that your account has access to, click the Resource Directory tile to see a complete list. Within the resource directory, you can use the filter bar to locate a specific SAP HANA database. This feature makes locating a specific SAP HANA database easy even in large landscapes that might have several registered systems.

Once you’ve located a registered SAP HANA database, click the resource name, typically following the format <database tenant>@<SID>. For example, if the tenant database is H4E, and the SID of the database is HDB, the registered name would be H4E@HDB. Figure 1.9 shows a list of registered SAP HANA systems and the filter bar. Once you’ve located your target system, click the system name to access that system’s System Overview page.

Figure 1.9    List of SAP HANA Systems within the SAP HANA Cockpit Resource Directory

The System Overview page is also divided into tiles and sections. A smaller filter bar exists at the top of the page. You can use this filter bar to limit the administration tiles that are displayed. In the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose Security to limit the interface to tiles that contain SAP HANA security functions.

Figure 1.10 shows an example of the tile layout and the various options available for managing security. The tiles in the security area are the Data Encryption, Auditing, Authentication, Security Related Links, User & Role Management, and Anonymization Report tiles.

In the next section, we’ll explore each of these tiles in more detail. For now, understanding how to access a registered resource, how to access the System Overview page, and how to filter for security-related areas or tiles are the most important processes for you to understand.

Figure 1.10    Security-Related Tiles and Configuration Options within the SAP HANA Cockpit When Connected to a Registered System

1.2    Security Areas in SAP HANA Cockpit

Up to this point in the chapter, we’ve discussed the architecture of the SAP HANA cockpit, including deployment options. We’ve explored the SAP HANA cockpit manager and described the high-level steps required to set up users, resource groups, and registered systems. Finally, we provided high-level information about how you can access a registered system in the SAP HANA cockpit and then access a registered system’s System Overview page. On the System Overview page, you can filter the various options available using the Filter by Area dropdown list. For the purposes of managing security, we’ll find most options in this area.

The security area provides tiles and links to the Data Encryption, Auditing, Authentication, Security Related Links, User & Role Management, and Anonymization Report areas. In the next section, we’ll provide a high-level overview of each area and describe how you’ll use these areas to manage an SAP HANA security model.

1.2.1    User & Role Management Area

The User & Role Management area provides several links, such as the Manage Users, Assign roles to users, Assign privileges to users, Manage roles, Manage user groups, and View database object dependencies links, as shown in Figure 1.11.

Figure 1.11    The User & Role Management Tile in SAP HANA Cockpit

The following list outlines what each link in this tile is used for. In subsequent chapters, we’ll demonstrate these items in more detail. However, in this chapter, we’ll only provide a basic overview of each link. Let’s briefly look at each link:

  • Manage users
    You’ll use this link to create, edit, and delete database users. You can only configure user account settings in this link. For example, you can configure the user’s authentication mode, password, third-party authentication settings, and custom user properties in this area. You cannot use this area to grant roles or privileges to users. Instead, you’ll use the Assign role to users and Assign privilege to users links for those activities. We’ll discuss these options in more detail in Chapter 4.

  • Assign role to users
    You’ll use this link to grant or revoke a role from a user account. We’ll discuss this link in more detail within Chapter 5.

  • Assign privilege to users
    You’ll use this link to grant or revoke individual privileges to a user. We’ll discuss this link in more detail in Chapter 4 and from Chapter 6 through Chapter 11.

  • Manage roles
    You’ll use this link to view and manage standard database runtime roles, for example, granting additional roles, system privileges, and object privileges to a role. You’ll also use this link to create and delete roles. We’ll discuss this link in more detail in Chapter 5.

  • Manage user group
    You’ll use this link to create and edit user groups. User groups help organize users into groups. You can configure user groups so that only specific users can manage the other user accounts within the group. You can also establish a unique password policy for each user group.

  • View database object dependencies
    You’ll use this link to review the authorization dependencies of a given catalog objects, an important step that security administrators must perform before deleting database objects and for determining which users have access to a database object.

In the next section, we’ll explore the Data Encryption tile and its links.

1.2.2    Data Encryption

You’ll use the Data Encryption tile and its links to manage data encryption options for data at rest. The tile itself contains slider buttons where you can quickly enable or disable (ON or OFF) Data Volume Encryption, Redo Log Encryption, and Backup Encryption, as shown in Figure 1.12.

Figure 1.12    Data Encryption Tile and Links in SAP HANA Cockpit

In addition to using the sliders, each item can be clicked, including the tile’s title, to navigate to additional options for each item in the Data Encryption configuration interface. We’ll discuss this interface and these options in more detail in Chapter 13. You should now have a basic understanding of how to access the Data Encryption tile and of the options it offers for managing an SAP HANA security model. In the next section, we’ll explore the Authentication tile and links.

1.2.3    Authentication

You’ll use the Authentication tile and its links to manage password policies, single sign-on (SSO), and the SYSTEM user’s password. The links in this tile (Password Policy, Single Sign-On, and SYSTEM User Password) can be clicked to manage each specific area, as shown in Figure 1.13.

Figure 1.13    Authentication Tile and Links in SAP HANA Cockpit

In Chapter 12, we’ll discuss these link options in more detail. You should now have a basic understanding of how to access the Authentication tile and the options available when managing an SAP HANA security model. In the next section, we’ll explore the Security Related Links tile and its links.

1.2.4    Security Related Links

You’ll use the Security Related Links tile and its links to manage several security-related items SAP HANA database, as shown in Figure 1.14.

Figure 1.14    Security Related Links Tile and Links in SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s explore the purpose and intended use of each link in more detail:

  • Manage certificates
    You’ll use this link to access in-database certificates. As we’ll discuss further in Chapter 13, you’ll use this interface to import and delete certificates.

  • Manage certificate collections
    You’ll use this link to manage certificate collections. A certificate collection is a physical or logical store that holds a certificate and defines its purpose. As we’ll discuss further in Chapter 13, you’ll use this interface to manage certificate collections stored within the database.

  • View network security information
    You’ll use this link to access a page that provides general information concerning the status of communication encryption, the Transport Layer Security (TLS)/Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) settings and types, and internal communication encryption. This information is read-only, and no settings can be changed within this interface.

  • Manage SAML identity providers
    You’ll use this link to manage third-party Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication providers and to import and delete SAML certificates critical to this mechanism. As we’ll discuss further in Chapter 12, SAML can provide SSO capabilities to the SAP HANA database and web application interfaces.

  • Manage JWT identity providers
    You’ll use this link to manage JSON Web Token (JWT) providers supported for SSO within the SAP HANA system. JWT is an open standard (RFC 7519) that outlines a means for communicating security information between two parties using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) objects. SAP HANA has limited support for this functionality, as we’ll discuss further in Chapter 12.

  • Security checklist
    You’ll use this link to access SAP’s checklist for comparing current SAP HANA security settings to recommendations from SAP. This checklist provides real-time reports, warnings, and information related to securing your SAP HANA system. The interface only provides warnings and does not recommend specific actions. See Chapter 17 for ways to mitigate the risk associated with some of the warnings found in the checklist.

  • Security administration help
    You’ll use this link to open the SAP HANA Administration with SAP HANA Cockpit Guide hosted on the SAP HANA cockpit web application server. This guide provides detailed information on administering the SAP HANA cockpit. This link will take you directly to the “Security Administration” section of the guide.

  • SAP HANA security website
    You’ll use this link to open the SAP HANA security product page at www.sap.com. On this page, you’ll find links to pertinent security help documents, white papers, and case studies.

You should now have a basic understanding of how to access the Security Related Links tile and the options it offers when managing an SAP HANA Security model. In the next section, we’ll explore the Anonymization Report tile and its links.

1.2.5    Anonymization Report

Starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, you can define SQL views for anonymizing data when the data is queried based on a variety of parameters and methods. Views protected with the functionality are called anonymization views. You can use Anonymization Report tile and link to access the View Available Anonymization Views link navigating you to the Anonymization Report interface. On the Anonymization Report interface, you’ll see a list of catalog views where this feature is enabled. You can click on each listed view to view read-only information about the Anonymization Parameters and method that have been applied to the view.

Note that you can apply this feature to a view using SQL statements or when developing a calculation view with SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. You cannot create these views using the SAP HANA cockpit at this time.

You should now have a basic understanding of how to access the Anonymization Report tile and the options it offers when managing an SAP HANA security model. In the next section, we’ll explore the Auditing tile and its links.

1.2.6    Auditing

The Auditing tile and its links can be used to access audit settings and to configure audit policies within the SAP HANA database. Audit polices, as discussed further in Chapter 15, are used to track specific actions within the SAP HANA database. All the links in this tile can be clicked, including the Auditing header, which navigates you to the Auditing configuration interface, as shown in Figure 1.15.

Figure 1.15    Auditing Tile and Links in SAP HANA Cockpit

The Status link; the Audit Trail Target link; the Enabled Audit Policies link, which includes a summary of the enabled polices; and the Disabled Audit Policies link, which also includes a summary, can be clicked to take you directly to the corresponding setting in the Auditing configuration interface. At the bottom of the tiles is Turn on Auditing link, which will enable the auditing mechanism.

You should now have a basic understanding of how to access the Auditing configuration interface using the Auditing tile and the links options it provides. We’ve concluded our high-level overview of the tiles and links that the SAP HANA cockpit provides for managing security. Subsequent chapters will provide additional information on how to use each tile and their links to manage your SAP HANA security mode.

In the next section, we’ll explore the SAP HANA database explorer and the SQL console, both important tool sets within the SAP HANA cockpit. As you’ll discover, you’ll need to use these tools to explore the database and to execute SQL statements, all of which are necessary to manage an SAP HANA security model.

1.3    SAP HANA Database Explorer and SQL Console

The SAP HANA cockpit provides the SAP HANA database explorer so you can connect to an SAP HANA database and work with catalog objects at runtime. From the SAP HANA cockpit homepage, click the Browse Database Objects tile to access the SAP HANA database explorer, as shown in Figure 1.16. You can also access the SQL console directly from this page by clicking the Execute SQL tile.

Figure 1.16    Browse Database Objects and Execute SQL Tiles

Alternatively, you can access the SQL console when connected to a registered SAP HANA database. On the System Overview page, as shown in Figure 1.17, you’ll see two links on the top right: Open SQL Console and Manage Databases.

Figure 1.17    Open SQL Console Link Used to Access the SQL Console from the SAP HANA Cockpit System Overview Page

Click the Open SQL Console link to navigate directly to the SAP HANA database explorer, connect to the registered system, and launch the SQL console in a single step. Technically, this link also takes you to the SAP HANA database explorer in addition to opening the SQL console.

Within the SAP HANA database explorer interface, you can add connections by clicking the plus icon (+) in the pane below the SAP HANA Database Explorer heading. You have several Database Types available to choose from: SAP HANA database, SAP HANA database (Multitenant), or Cockpit Resource. Select the Cockpit Resource option to connect to an SAP HANA database using the SAP HANA cockpit registration information. To connect to classic SAP HANA database objects, select the SAP HANA database or SAP HANA database (Multitenant) options and enter the connection information for the desired database.

For each connection, you’ll be provided with a graphical list of various catalog object types, as shown in Figure 1.18. For example, if you’re searching for a table, click the table option under Catalog and then use the schema selection bar and search bar in the pane below to locate a table by name within the selected schema. Once you locate an object in the list, double-click that object to reveal its metadata or right-click the object to open a popup window containing options for interacting with the selected object.

As you further look below the Catalog folder in the connected database, you’ll see a Host Diagnostic Files folder. Expand the subfolders below this node until you locate the folders named after each SAP HANA database service. For example, the Name Server and Index Server folders will appear. Within each of these folders, you’ll find various .trc files (trace files) specific to the service’s folder. Double-click the file to open and view its contents in a tab to the right of the SAP HANA database explorer interface. Security administrators often need to view these files when troubleshooting security configurations or when users are unable to access content.

Figure 1.18    SAP HANA Database Explorer Found in the SAP HANA Cockpit

You should now have a basic understanding of the SAP HANA database explorer within the SAP HANA cockpit.

More Information on the SAP HANA Database Explorer

For more information on the SAP HANA database explorer, refer to the SAP HANA Database Explorer Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498201.

Once you’ve established a connection to the database, you can access the SQL console where you can execute SQL statements. To launch the SQL console, select an existing database connection from the list found in the SAP HANA database explorer. Click the icon with the word SQL located to the top right of the data list, as shown in Figure 1.19. A new tab will appear to the right with the label SQL console and possibly a number.

Within this tab is the SQL console. Enter the desired SQL then click the run icon (green play button). You can also press the (F8) button to run the SQL command. The results of the SQL statement will appear below the entered statement, as shown in Figure 1.19.

Figure 1.19    Accessing and Using the SQL Console within the SAP HANA Cockpit

You should now have a basic understanding of the steps necessary to access the SAP HANA database explorer and the SQL console. As security administrators, you’ll use the SQL console to execute security specific statements. The SAP HANA database explorer is useful when you need to locate a catalog object in the database and view its metadata. You’ll also use the SAP HANA database explorer to access .trc files that can contain security-specific trace information.

1.4    Summary

This chapter introduced you to the SAP HANA cockpit. We also provided the basic information you’ll need to manage access to the SAP HANA cockpit and the various applications, tiles, and links allowing you to manage an SAP HANA database’s security model. In subsequent chapters, we’ll provide additional information and examples of how you can use the SAP HANA cockpit to manage specific aspects of the SAP HANA security model.

2    Introduction to SAP HANA Privileges

In this chapter, we’ll introduce you to SAP HANA privileges and define several related key terms. Privileges are a major component of SAP HANA security because they control what operations a user can conduct.

Users can interact with SAP HANA in a variety of different ways. In the past, users would use SAP HANA Studio to develop content and administer the system. With SAP HANA 2.0, you’ll probably use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to develop content. You’ll also use the SAP HANA cockpit to administer the system. Other users might interact with business intelligence tools and query the data hosted in SAP HANA. In other cases, SAP NetWeaver uses the SAP HANA database to help operate applications like SAP Business Warehouse (SAP BW) and SAP S/4HANA. In all cases, database user accounts are required to interact with SAP HANA. These user accounts are often assigned to individual people. However, you can also set up dedicated service accounts to allow an application to delegate access for multiple users to the SAP HANA system. To govern these interactions, user accounts must be assigned a variety of privileges.

When a user account interacts with SAP HANA, that user can only perform operations and actions that have been granted via privileges. Granting privileges is the process whereby a grantor assigns privileges to another user account. For a grantor to grant an individual privilege, the grantor must be granted that privilege and must also have been assigned the WITH GRANT OPTION or Grantable to Others option, an additional right that allows the grantor the ability to grant the same privilege to another user. If you’re using SQL to grant privileges, you’ll use the WITH GRANT OPTION syntax. If you’re using the graphical user interface (GUI) in the SAP HANA cockpit, you’ll see a slider button labeled Grantable to Others.

When you first set up an SAP HANA system, the first user account available will be the SYSTEM account. The user name of that account is just SYSTEM. By default, the SYSTEM account can create users and grant privileges to other user accounts for all the default system objects, privileges, and roles.

The first time you interact with SAP HANA, you’ll most likely log on using the SYSTEM user account. If you’re following best practices, you’ll then create new user accounts, set up a new security model, and assign that security model to new dedicated user accounts. Most organizations will then disable access to the SYSTEM account so that they can properly audit activities by individual users.

By definition, the various operations and actions you perform in SAP HANA are organized into objects called privileges. Throughout this chapter, we’ll introduce you to the five major categories of privileges available in SAP HANA, and we’ll also describe how privileges are properly granted to roles and users and how the system validates a user’s access. In subsequent chapters, we’ll take a much deeper dive into individual privileges and outline what each privilege authorizes; however, the goal of this chapter is to provide an overview of privileges.

2.1    Privileges within SAP HANA

The five major categories of privileges available in SAP HANA are system, object, analytic, package, and application. Each category contains individual privileges that can be granted to either users or roles. In the following sections, we’ll look at each category in turn.

2.1.1    System Privileges

System privileges are designed to govern various system activities that a user can perform. They are predominantly used to govern administrative actives within the SAP HANA database. However, some system privileges specifically govern developer activities related to the SAP HANA development repository and development content.
