Sometimes, you can manipulate runtime security for a repository object, but these settings will be lost when the system reboots.

When a role is created in the SAP HANA development repository, that role is owned by the system user _SYS_REPO. These roles are repository roles. You can’t use the standard GRANT and REVOKE SQL syntax to assign repository roles to a standard role; instead, you must use a specific stored procedure to grant repository roles to standard roles and use a different stored procedure to revoke repository roles from standard roles.

The first stored procedure is stored in the _SYS_REPO schema and is named GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE. To use this procedure, the security administrator must have the EXECUTE object privilege on the stored procedure. The procedure has two input parameters: The first input parameter requires the name of one repository role and doesn’t support entering multiple repository roles; the second input parameter requires the name of an existing standard role. The following SQL statement uses variables for the repository role name standard role parameters:

CALL 
"_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE"('<REPOSITORY_ROLE_NAME>', '<STANDARD_ROLE>');

The following example demonstrates the execution of the procedure with sample parameters:

CALL 
_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE"('sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer',
'TEST_ROLE');

The second stored procedure is stored in the _SYS_REPO schema and is named REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE. To use this procedure, the security administrator must have the EXECUTE object privilege for the stored procedure. The procedure has two input parameters: The first input parameter requires the name of one repository role and doesn’t support entering multiple repository roles; the second input parameter requires the name of a standard role. The following SQL statement uses variables for the repository role name and standard role parameters:

CALL 
"_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE"('<REPOSITORY_ROLE_NAME>', '<ROLE_NAME>');

The following statement demonstrates the execution of the procedure with sample parameters:

CALL "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE"('sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer','TEST_ROLE');

5.4.2    Granting and Revoking Roles with the SAP HANA Cockpit

As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit GUI action called Manage Roles to grant a standard role to another standard role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Manage Roles area, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen and locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Click the Manage Roles link in the User & Role Management tile. This action will launch the Manage Roles window where you’ll see a list of roles on the left and selected roles properties on the right. The role list provides a search filter bar at the top of the list that you can use to filter the list of roles. Select a role to reveal its assigned privileges in the Role Details pane to the right.

Let’s review the workflows necessary to grant and revoke roles to an existing role. The first tab in the Role Details window is named roles. Use this tab to list, grant, or revoke additional roles to an existing role. This process is how you nest one role into another role to simplify your security model.

Roles listed in this interface are those that are already granted to the role. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant a role, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface just to the right of the search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Save, Cancel, Add, and Remove will appear. Click the Add button to open the Select Roles popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of roles with checkboxes to their left. Use the search bar to filter the list. Then, scroll through the list and select the checkboxes beside the roles you want to nest. With one or more roles selected, click the OK button to add the desired items to the role. Your selected roles should now appear in the Roles section, as shown in Figure 5.12.

Figure 5.12    List of Selected Roles

To assign the Grantable to Others privilege, locate a role in the list. To the right, move the slider button to Yes to allow the user to grant the same role to another user or role. Repeat this process for each role in the list. Once you’ve added all the desired roles to the list, click the Save button to grant the roles.

Repository Roles in the SAP HANA Cockpit

Based on our testing, you can grant a repository role to another role using the SAP HANA cockpit. However, we couldn’t revoke that role in the same way. Therefore, in our experience, the SAP HANA cockpit does not fully support repository-based roles. When working with repository-based roles, use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager.

To revoke a role, start by clicking the Edit button again, then select the checkbox beside each role in the list, and click the Remove button to revoke the role. Repeat the process for each role you want to revoke. Once you’ve removed all the desired roles, click the Save button. The removed roles will be revoked, and the role object will be updated.

During the process of adding or removing roles, you can use the Cancel button to discard any unsaved changes. Clicking the Cancel button will deactivate the Save, Add, Cancel, and Remove buttons and return you to a read-only list of currently granted roles.

5.4.3    Granting and Revoking Roles with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

As mentioned earlier, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface to create users, create roles, or manage security. In summary, you can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager by updating the following two URLs to match the details of your environment:

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right side of the window. Expand Roles to reveal a list of roles. Double-click a role to open the management interface for the given role. With the selected role management window open, you can begin granting and revoking roles using the Granted Roles tab.

To grant or revoke role within the selected role, locate the Granted Roles tab. To add a role, click the plus sign (+) to open the Find Role popup window. You can use the search box to filter the list. Select one or more roles from the list and click OK to continue. Your selected roles will now be listed in the Granted Roles tab. To assign the Grantable to Other Users and Roles, select the role and select the checkbox in the Details for area to the right of each selected role as needed.

To revoke a role, select the role from the list and click the red X. To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S). Alternatively, click the save icon (floppy disk) at the top left to save and activate the role. Look for activation errors just below the Granted Roles tab in the section with a dark background. Errors will be listed in red text. White text will indicate that the change was successful.

5.5    Mapping LDAP Groups to Roles

Starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 03, Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)-based users can now be provisioned within SAP HANA, and their LDAP-managed passwords can be used for authentication. In addition to authentication, starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 00, you can also map SAP HANA database roles to LDAP groups to simplify authorization. Effectively, SAP HANA will look up a user’s group memberships in the LDAP directory. If the LDAP group is mapped to an SAP HANA role, the user will be granted the SAP HANA database role and its privileges. This check is performed each time a user is authenticated. Before you can use this functionality, you’ll need to set up and configure an LDAP provider within the SAP HANA system. We’ll discuss this setup in more detail in Chapter 12. In this section, we’ll review the process for mapping LDAP groups to roles using both SQL statements and the SAP HANA cockpit.

5.5.1    Mapping Roles with SQL

You can use SQL to create an SAP HANA database role and map that role to an LDAP group in a single step. You can also modify an existing role and add an LDAP group. (Note that you can’t map an LDAP group to a repository role at this time.) Let’s first review the SQL required to create a role and map it to an LDAP group in a single step. The following SQL statement will create the SAP HANA role ECORP_SECURITY_ADMINS and map it to the LDAP group HANA Security Team:

CREATE ROLE ECORP_SECURITY_ADMINS LDAP GROUP 'CN=HANA_SECURITY_TEAM,CN=Users,DC=ecorp,DC=com';

To modify an existing role and add map and LDAP group, you would run the following SQL statement to add the LDAP group HANA Security Team to the SAP HANA role ECORP_SECURITY_ADMINS:

ALTER ROLE ECORP_SECURITY_ADMINS ADD LDAP GROUP 'CN=HANA_SECURITY_TEAM,CN=Users,DC=ecorp,DC=com';

To remove the LDAP group mapping from a role, run the following SQL statement:

ALTER ROLE ECORP_SECURITY_ADMINS DROP LDAP GROUP 'CN=HANA_SECURITY_TEAM,CN=Users,DC=ecorp,DC=com';

In the next section, we’ll review the process for mapping LDAP groups to SAP HANA roles using the SAP HANA cockpit.

5.5.2    Mapping Roles with the SAP HANA Cockpit

As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit GUI action called Manage Roles to map an LDAP group to a role. This interface allows you to both add or remove LDAP groups from a standard role. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Manage Roles area, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen and locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Click the Manage Roles link in the User & Role Management tile. This action will launch the Manage Roles window where you’ll see a list of roles on the left and selected roles properties on the right. The role list provides a search filter bar located at the top of the list that you can use to filter the list of roles. Select a role to reveal its assigned privileges in the Role Details pane to the right.

In the Role Details pane, locate the Edit button to the right of the role name, as shown in Figure 5.13. The role edit pane will appear allowing you to modify basic information for the role such as its Comments, Schema, and LDAP Groups.

Figure 5.13    Locating the Edit Button to Configure the Role’s Mapped LDPA Group

In the LDAP Groups section, you’ll see the option to enable LDAP group mappings titled Assign LDAP Groups. Change the radio button option to Yes to enable additional LDAP group mapping options. In the LDAP Group Name field, click the Add LDAP Groups button and then type the name of the LDAP group using the LDAP naming convention, as shown in Figure 5.14.

Figure 5.14    Configuring LDAP Group Mappings Using the SAP HANA Cockpit

Click the Save button to enable the LDAP group mapping. To remove the mapping, click the remove icon (X in a circle) to the right of the listed LDAP group and save to remove the mapping.

You now understand how you can use SQL and the SAP HANA cockpit to manage LDAP group mappings to roles.

5.6    Summary

The process of creating and managing roles can be accomplished using SQL statements, the SAP HANA cockpit, or the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager hosted in the XS engine. You can also use all three interfaces to grant and revoke both privileges and roles with some limitations with the SAP HANA cockpit and repository-based roles. In the next chapter, we’ll will explore repository-based roles, which are an alternative to standard roles and which in most cases provide advantages over standard roles.

6    Repository Roles

In this chapter, we’ll provide a complete overview of repository roles, including the processes used to create, maintain, and grant privileges to repository roles.

Roles are objects that aid in the creation of a security model. The bulk of the security model development process involves defining roles, assigning privileges to roles, and assigning roles to user accounts. However, SAP HANA offers a unique type of role called a repository role, which we’ll explore throughout this chapter. We’ll start by defining repository roles and discussing their importance, then we’ll review the options for creating and managing repository roles. As with standard roles, we’ll also review the process for granting and revoking privileges and roles to repository roles. Because of the importance of repository roles, we’ll outline a basic example of the structure of a repository role. Finally, we’ll demonstrate the process for creating a basic security model with repository roles.

6.1    What Are Repository Roles?

In Chapter 5, we discussed standard roles and the process used to create them. If you have experience creating roles in other relational database management systems (RDBMSs), creating standard SAP HANA roles will seem quite similar. During the process, you’ll issue statements to generate a runtime version of the role, meaning that the object only exists in an active state within the RDBMS. Once the standard role is created, that role is instantly available for use.

Once a role is created, you’ll issue a series of GRANT statements to assign privileges to the role. To remove privileges from the role, you’ll issue REVOKE statements. As each individual command is issued, the runtime version of the role is immediately updated. With this process, you won’t be able to easily roll back changes or promote changes seamlessly to upstream SAP HANA environments. For example, if you make a change in a development environment, you’ll need to make the same change in a test environment and possibly a production environment by issuing the same commands. This process historically has been cumbersome to manage, a problem that often required third-party software to remedy. Without software to help, the SQL scripts issued to create, alter, grant, or revoke roles would all need to be manually retained and executed sequentially in each upstream environment.

Repository-based roles can overcome many of the limitations attributed to standard database roles. Repository roles are defined and saved in the SAP HANA development repository or package hierarchy. These roles can be defined using an SAP HANA-specific script language or using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. In either case, you can save a design-time version of the role within a development artifact, meaning that the role and its granted privileges can exist as a separate object, independent of the runtime version. Once the design-time version of the role is activated, a matching runtime version is created in the SAP HANA RDBMS. This feature of SAP HANA allows you to implement change management, rollback, and transportation of roles between environments.

In addition to these benefits, repository roles also help simplify the management of your SAP HANA security model. To illustrate these benefits, let’s first discuss the importance of the _SYS_REPO system account. We’ll then discuss how repository roles can help you avoid issues related to the grantor of privileges and roles. Finally, we’ll outline the overall benefits of using repository roles.

6.1.1    User Account _SYS_REPO and Repository Roles

As mentioned earlier, when you use the SAP HANA development repository to define repository-based objects and roles, the runtime versions of these objects will be owned or granted by the _SYS_REPO system account. You must understand the importance of this ownership arrangement, which has a profound impact on how you establish security models in SAP HANA.

Recall that catalog objects created using the SQL CREATE statement will be owned by the user issuing the statement. The owner therefore must grant privileges to other users or roles if those users/roles require access to the owner’s catalog objects. The owner must also grant privileges to security administrators if these administrators are expected to facilitate access to the owner’s objects. This step is required because of the how standard catalog security in RDBMSs operates in a multiple user account environment. By design, no single user is automatically granted privileges to objects owned by other users without some form of action by the owner or security administrator.

Although this methodology enhances security, a nearly unmanageable security model may result in practice. Object owners must work closely with security administrators and follow strict procedures to maintain a security model. Security administrators must rely on each other to revoke any roles they granted because only the grantor can revoke a granted role. This requirement, among other requirements, makes the security management of standard catalog roles and objects quite difficult without an external software system delegating, managing, controlling, and tracking the process.

To simplify this mechanism within SAP HANA, you would need to logically devise a system in which a single user owns all objects and that same user grants all privileges. This user should also be set up in such a way that the user can never be deleted from the system. Ideally, this special user would delegate the actions of the developers to prevent their accounts from owing objects. This user would also delegate the actions of security administrators to prevent their accounts from being listed as the grantors of privileges.

Creating this logical system seems an unlikely solution in a multiple user environment. Luckily, SAP HANA has already incorporated this solution into the SAP HANA development repository. The _SYS_REPO system user, in this case, becomes both the owner of all repository objects and the grantor of all privileges defined within a repository role. With SAP HANA, you have a single system user account managing security processes while avoiding most of the pitfalls of security management in a multiple-user RDBMS environment.

If you follow the repository-based model when creating objects, developers only need the ability to create repository objects, and security administrators only need the ability to create repository roles and grant them to others. You’ll thus also be able to segregate these actions within the system because the repository-based model offers a way to delineate between users that can define roles and users that can grant roles to others.

In contrast, when you use standard roles and catalog objects, the definer and grantor of roles must have the ROLE ADMIN system privilege. This privilege should only be granted sparingly and only to security administrators. Not having a clear delineation also forces security administrators to define all roles and work closely with the developers while doing so. This dependency often proves to be inefficient and prone to error.

The _SYS_REPO account therefore is important to the structure of your security model. You should strive for a security model that ensures that this account owns all catalog objects and grants privileges to repository roles.

6.1.2    Grantors and Privileges

When you issue a GRANT <PRIVILEGE> SQL statement using a standard user account, that user account becomes the grantor of the privilege. The grantor is an important function within a security model. When a privilege is granted to a role or user, only the grantor can revoke the privilege. If you have multiple security administrators operating within an SAP HANA environment, this limitation on who can revoke privileges can be difficult to manage.

For example, if one security administrator grants a privilege to a role, only that administrator can revoke the privilege. If that security administrator is not available one day and the privilege must be revoked, no other user account in the system can revoke that privilege. This situation can be problematic and also introduces risk because key individuals must be always present to manage changes to the security model.

Some organizations will try to solve this problem by creating a dedicated account that’s shared by multiple administrators. However, doing so isn’t recommended because sharing an account reduces your ability to properly audit an individual’s activities when shared accounts are used. In other words, someone can make an important change that affects the security of the system without any record being made of the actual person that performed the change.

When you use repository roles, you don’t need to be concerned with these issues. With repository roles, privileges are always granted using the _SYS_REPO system account. You also don’t need to worry about multiple users managing security. A repository role can be updated by anyone with access to the package where the role resides in the SAP HANA repository. Each time a repository role is activated, the privileges within that role are granted with _SYS_REPO as the grantor. If a privilege is removed from the repository role definition, the privilege will be revoked from the runtime version of the repository role. Because _SYS_REPO is the original grantor, full access to revoke the privilege is always available.

Another important requirement for grantors entails the privileges the grantor needs before it can grant privileges. An account can serve as the grantor if two prerequisites are met. First, the grantor must have been granted the privilege with WITH GRANT OPTION. Second, the grantor must own the object. If the grantor doesn’t own the object, the owner must first grant the security administrator the necessary privileges. As mentioned earlier, this arrangement makes the management of a security model based on standard catalog objects and standard roles difficult.

If you use repository objects, again, you won’t encounter this issue. All repository objects will be owned by _SYS_REPO. If you reference repository objects in a repository role, _SYS_REPO will already be the owner and the natural grantor of the privileges. Now, let’s look at how repository roles can help with the grantor of roles.

6.1.3    Grantors and Roles

Just as the security manager account can grant individual privileges, it can also grant existing standard roles to other users or roles. However, before a security account can grant a standard role, the account must meet one of two prerequisites:

  • The user must be directly or indirectly granted the role, and the WITH ADMIN OPTION must be set for the granted role.

  • The user must have the system privilege ROLE ADMIN. This system privilege allows the assignee to grant or revoke any existing standard role to another user or role.

The ROLE ADMIN privilege allows the security administrator to both create and grant roles, which might not be an issue for some organizations. However, if your organization requires the segregation of duties, preventing the creator from also being the grantor of the role will be difficult. Some organizations will insist that the model allow one group to create the roles and another group to be responsible for assigning those roles.

Repository roles are granted using the "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE" stored procedure and are revoked using the "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE" stored procedure. Repository roles themselves are created within the SAP HANA package hierarchy, and design-time objects can be secured independently from these stored procedures. Therefore, organizations that require a segregation of duties have a solution: The creation of repository roles can be isolated from the privileges required to grant repository roles. Now, let’s summarize the benefits of using repository roles.

6.1.4    Why Use Repository Roles?

SAP has announced that the SAP HANA extended application services, classic model engine (XS engine) and _SYS_REPO-owned objects will be removed from the platform in the future. However, as of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, in our opinion, no viable alternative exists for managing a comprehensive security model, and repository-based roles work perfectly fine if you continue to develop content in the SAP HANA XS _SYS_REPO repository. However, if you’re developing content in the new SAP HANA extended application services, advanced model (SAP HANA XSA) platform, you’ll have no choice but to adopt some of the new security principles of SAP HANA XSA, even if numerous gaps in securing such objects based on best practices still exist.

Overall, repository roles can help your organization achieve a security model in the following ways:

  • As mentioned earlier, the definition of the repository role is stored in the SAP HANA development repository in the form of a text-based script. Therefore, the repository role definition can be managed independently of the runtime version of the repository role.

  • Repository roles can be transported from one SAP HANA system to another using SAP HANA application lifecycle management or using the delivery unit export and import process.

  • When a user is copied in SAP HANA Studio, all the user’s repository roles are also copied to the target user account.

  • Because they’re development artifacts, the standard SAP HANA version management process applies. Each activated version is maintained in the SAP HANA database and repository, allowing each version to be retrieved and activated as needed.

  • Repository roles are granted and revoked using special stored procedures, which make defining accounts used by security administrators easier. Security administrators only need EXECUTE access to the stored procedures that grant repository roles or revoke them from others. They won’t require the ROLE ADMIN system privilege, which could grant them too many rights in the system, nor do they need first to be granted a role and the additional WITH ADMIN OPTION privilege before gaining the ability to grant roles to others.

  • Users only require access to the SAP HANA package repository to define a repository role and its privileges. They don’t require the ROLE ADMIN system privilege, which could grant them too many rights in the system. Although these users can define the repository role, they can’t grant the role to others without EXECUTE access to the special stored procedures mentioned in the previous bullet point. As a result, you can separate the granting and revoking processes from the repository role definition process. Developers can define repository roles and privileges for their applications without needing the ability to grant roles and privileges to other users.

  • If standard database objects are used in the system, the object’s owner only needs to grant privileges using WITH ADMIN OPTION or WITH GRANT OPTION to the _SYS_REPO user account. Without repository roles, the owner would need to grant privileges to existing security administration users or roles each time an object is created.

  • If repository-based objects are used in the system, the _SYS_REPO account will already own the objects and therefore can grant privileges to them without any further actions by the developer. For this reason, among others, we highly recommend that developers use repository-based objects rather than catalog objects in their solutions.

Additional Comparison of Repository Roles to Standard Roles

SAP provides an additional matrix to compare the differences between standard catalog roles, design-time repository-based roles, and design-time SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI) roles in the SAP HANA Security Guide for SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, available at http://s-prs.co/v498205.

Within the document, look for the “Catalog Roles and Design-Time Roles Compared” section.

Given the benefits of using repository roles, using them as the basis for a security model is a worthwhile idea. Based on our firsthand experience, a system based on repository objects and repository roles is considerably more manageable than one based on standard roles and catalog objects. With their importance established, let’s now look at how repository roles are created, how you grant privileges to them, and how repository roles assigned to other users or roles.

6.2    Managing Repository Roles with Design-Time Scripts

In broad terms, as of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, you can create repository roles in two ways: First, you can define repository roles in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor text editor as hand-coded scripts. The scripting language is unique to SAP HANA but is similar to JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) scripting. To avoid hand-coding scripts, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor offers a graphical user interface (GUI) that is similar to the role creation user interface (UI) found in SAP HANA Studio. Most beginners will find using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor GUI much easier because learning a scripting language is not required.

6.2.1    Creating a Repository Package

Before you can create a package, let’s review the information necessary to access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, a tool where you can create and manage packages. You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following two URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

  • http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor

In the last example, replace <sap_hana_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor

  • https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor

To use the editor, the user account first will need to be granted one of the roles listed in Table 6.1. Users only need one of these two roles to access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor.

Role Name

Summary

sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper

Within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench, users will only be able to access the editor. The editor provides interfaces to create a variety of repository objects, including repository-based roles.

sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer

This role grants a higher level of privileges for users that need full access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. This role grants access to the editor, catalog, and security interfaces and is considered the parent of the sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper role.

Table 6.1    Roles Required to Use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

Additional Privileges

Note that the roles in Table 6.1 simply allow the granted user access to the interface. The user will also need access to the package in which the repository roles are stored. To grant repository roles to other users and roles, the user will need EXECUTE access to the system stored procedure named "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE". To revoke repository roles, the user will need EXECUTE access to the "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE" stored procedure.

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, expand the Content node on the right side of the window. Expand Packages to reveal a list of packages defined in the system.

Before you create a repository role, you must define a unique repository package in which to store repository roles. The package should be structured in such a way that it can be completely isolated using package privileges. Only administrators assigned the responsibility of creating repository roles should have any level of access to the package. We typically recommend that a first-level package named Security be created. Within that package, a subpackage named Roles should be created to host your repository roles. Figure 6.1 shows one way to set up a package hierarchy for security-related objects such as repository roles.

Figure 6.1    SAP HANA Package Hierarchy for Security-Related Objects

We highly recommend using this methodology because only security role creators should access to these objects. If a standard developer were to accidently gain edit access to this package, the developer could update the design-time repository role, activate changes, and elevate its own privileges. Therefore, placing this package at the root level is less risky through preventing the accidental inheritance of package privileges. Ideally, this package will contain the base repository roles used to establish roles and privileges in the SAP HANA system. Now, let’s look at the process used to create a repository role.

6.2.2    Creating Repository Roles within a Package

As mentioned earlier, packages are used to store repository roles. To create a new repository role in the Security.Roles package, shown in Figure 6.1, right-click the Roles package and choose New • File. Name the file ExampleRole.hdbrole, as shown in Figure 6.2. The extension .hdbrole is mandatory, and you should name the role file with the same name you expect to give the role.

Figure 6.2    Naming Your .hdbrole File

By default, a new tab will appear to the right. The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench will default the object to the repository role GUI editor interface. However, for illustration, we want to review the role file script’s text. To view the text, you’ll need to save the file, close the tab, and reopen the file with the text editor. Once the file is saved, right-click the ExampleRole.hdbrole file and choose Open With • Text Editor. Figure 6.3 shows the right-click menu used to open the Examplerole.hdbrole file with the text editor.

Figure 6.3    Opening the ExampleRole.hdbrole File with the Text Editor

6.2.3    Defining the Role Name Tag

Because we used the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor to create the role, this portion of the syntax was completed during the creation process. However, the syntax of a repository role begins with the word role followed by the fully qualified repository role name. A fully qualified role name is prefixed with the complete package hierarchy name, followed by two colons and the role name. The role name here in this script be exactly the same as the .hdbrole file name prefix. The following script represents the basic syntax of a repository role. Replace the items in angle brackets (<>) with objects unique to your environment:

role <package.subpackage>::<repository role name> {    
}

For example, let’s assume that you need to create a role named ExampleRole that will be stored in the Security.Roles package. The following script would be the starting point for defining that repository role:

role Security.Roles::ExampleRole {    
}

6.2.4    Extending Roles

Between the name of the role and the first opening bracket, you can optionally add existing roles that will extend the new repository role. Thus, the privileges within the referenced roles will be granted to your new repository role, in addition to any privileges you explicitly define after the brackets. Listing 6.1 shows you how to include existing roles by adding extends role, followed by a comma-separated list of existing, fully qualified repository role names.

role Security.Roles::ExampleRole extends role     
sap.hana.xs.formLogin.profile::ProfileOwner,
sap.hana.xs.selfService.user.roles::USSExecutor {
}

Listing 6.1    Repository Role Script with Multiple Extended Roles

6.2.5    Assigning Privileges

Each privilege is granted or assigned to a role using a special syntax. The privileges will be specified within the opening and closing curly brackets ({}). The script shown in Listing 6.2 will grant schema privileges for the StagingMart and SalesMart schemas in addition to granting the CATALOG READ system privilege, an analytic privilege, and a package privilege.

role Security.Roles::ExampleRole extends role   
 sap.hana.xs.formLogin.profile::ProfileOwner,
 sap.hana.xs.selfService.user.roles::USSExecutor {

  -- Begin Schema Privileges  
  catalog schema "StagingMart": SELECT, EXECUTE;
  catalog schema "SalesMart": SELECT, EXECUTE;

  -- Begin System Privileges
  system privilege: CATALOG READ;

  -- Begin Analytic Privileges
  catalog analytic privilege : "_SYS_BI_CP_ALL";

  // Begin Package Privileges
  package .REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT: REPO.READ; 
}

Listing 6.2    Repository Role Script Granting Different Privilege Types

Each privilege line must end with a semicolon. To place comments in the script, start the comment line with two consecutive dashes or slashes (-- or //). Comments are optional, but they should be included to communicate important information about the script as a whole or about each script line. Again, the individual privileges must be confined within the opening and closing curly brackets. As shown in Listing 6.2, you can define different types of privileges within the same script. In most cases, each privilege type will require a slightly different syntax.

6.2.6    Save and Activate

Once the script is complete, you’ll need to save and activate the script. To save the script, click the save icon (floppy disk) or press (Ctrl)+(S). Saving also activates the file in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. However, if any error arises when saving the file, look for the status pane just below the text editor. The status area has a dark background by default. If there are any errors, look for them with red text. Messages in white text typically indicate a successful save action.

6.2.7    Runtime Repository Roles

When a repository role is activated, a runtime version of the role will be created within the SAP HANA catalog. The name of the runtime role will be constructed using a combination of the package hierarchy and repository role name. Each element will be separated by two colons, as shown in the following examples:

  • <package.subpackage>::<repository role name>

  • Security.Roles::ExampleRole

The role will be visible within the standard roles list found in the security manager of SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. Now, let’s take a moment to look at how you can define privileges for each object and privilege type.

6.3    Granting and Revoking Privileges in Design-Time Scripts

When developing repository roles with design-time scripts, you’ll find that the syntax varies based on the object type or the privilege type. Figure 6.4 shows an example of a complete repository role script within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench’s text editor tab. For demonstration purposes, this role grants a variety of privileges to various design-time and runtime object types.

Figure 6.4    Example Repository Role Script

When using repository-based scripts, note that the _SYS_REPO system user either must own the catalog objects or must have been granted the same privileges using either WITH ADMIN OPTION or WITH GRANT OPTION. If _SYS_REPO doesn’t meet these requirements, the repository role will fail to activate. In this section, we’ll explore the syntax for granting privileges using design-time repository role scripts.

6.3.1    System Privileges

When defining system privileges in design-time repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with system privilege:. After the colon, provide a comma-separated list of system privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. If you don’t want to include a comma-separated list, you can explicitly list each privilege on its own line, ensuring that each line begins with system privilege:.

The following snippets of code show the definition of system privileges within a repository role script. The first line includes two privileges, and the remaining two lines include only a single system privilege each:

system privilege: AGENT ADMIN, AUDIT ADMIN;    
system privilege: AUDIT OPERATOR;    
system privilege: CREATE REMOTE SOURCE;

Notice how you can reuse the system privilege: expression multiple times within the script. You can also consolidate all these instances into a single line in which each privilege is separated from the next with a comma. Note that the _SYS_REPO account has been granted all system privileges by default and can grant also all system privileges to other users or roles by default.

6.3.2    Schema Privileges

Schema privileges can be granted in two ways. First, you can grant schema privileges to any runtime catalog schemas active in the system. In this instance, you can reference a schema regardless of the method used to create it. Schema privileges can also be granted to design-time schema objects. In this instance, you can only reference schemas created within the repository.

Runtime Schemas

When defining runtime catalog schema privileges within design-time repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with catalog schema. Following this term, include the name of the schema followed by a colon. You can also include a comma-separated list of schemas if you want them all to share the same privileges. After the colon, include a comma-separated list of schema privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line.

The following snippets of code show the definition of catalog schema privileges within a repository role script. The first line grants EXECUTE and SELECT on the _SYS_BIC schema. The second line grants several privileges for the MySchema schema. The third line shows the use of multiple schemas in the same line:

catalog schema "_SYS_BIC": EXECUTE, SELECT;    
catalog schema "MySchema": CREATE ANY, DROP, ALTER, UPDATE;    
catalog schema "_SYS_REPO", "_SYS_BIC": SELECT;

Note also that the _SYS_REPO system account must have full privileges for the listed schemas or must own the schemas before such privileges can be activated within the definition of a repository role.

Design-Time Schemas

In addition to referencing runtime catalog objects, you can also reference design-time schemas. Referencing a design-time schema is only possible if the schema itself is a repository object. In most cases, we recommend that you reference the design-time version of a schema because creating a dependency chain that can be identified can be useful during lifecycle management. The privileges will be granted on the runtime version of the object once all referenced objects are activated.

When defining repository schema privileges, you must start each line with schema. This term is only applicable for design-time schema objects. Following this term, include the name of the repository schema file. The name of the file will need to include the package hierarchy and a colon preceding the file name. You can specify multiple schema files in the list as well. The following example includes the fully qualified name of a design-time schema object:

Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema

After the schema file name, include a colon, then a comma-separated list of schema privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. Listing 6.3 shows two complete lines that grant the listed schema privileges. The first line references a single schema file, and the second references multiple schema files within the same line.

schema Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema: SELECT, EXECUTE;
schema 
  Security.Schemas:SalesMart.hdbschema,
  Security.Schemas:MySchema.hdbschema: 
  SELECT;

Listing 6.3    Repository Role Script Granting Schema Privileges

In summary, you’ll use different syntaxes to program runtime schema objects and design-time schema objects.

6.3.3    Object Privileges

Object privileges can be granted in two ways. First, you can grant object privileges to any runtime catalog object, which works for both standard catalog objects and activated repository objects. Object privileges can also be granted to design-time objects listed in the repository. In this instance, you can only reference objects created within the repository. The privileges assigned to the design-time object will also be granted to the runtime version of the same object.

Runtime Objects

When defining runtime object privileges in repository role scripts, you must start each line with catalog sql object. Following this term, include the fully qualified name of the catalog object, followed by a colon. You can also specify a comma-separated list of catalog objects if you want them to all have the same privileges. After the colon, include a comma-separated list of object privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. Note that the _SYS_REPO system account must have full privileges for the object or own it before such privileges can be included within the definition of a repository role.

Listing 6.4 shows the definition of catalog object privileges within a repository role script. The first line references a single catalog object. The second line references two different catalog objects, each granted the listed privilege.

catalog sql object "MySchema"."TestTableTwo": SELECT, ALTER, DROP;
catalog sql object 
  "MySchema"."DIM_CUSTOMER", "MySchema"."DIM_PRODUCT": 
  SELECT, DELETE, ALTER;

Listing 6.4    Repository Role Script Granting Runtime Catalog Object Privileges

We recommend that you only reference catalog objects that exist exclusively in runtime when using this syntax—that is, objects created using the SQL CREATE statement. Instead, you should use the design-time syntax for any repository-based catalog objects.

Design-Time Objects

In addition to referencing runtime catalog objects, you can also reference design-time catalog objects. Referencing design-time objects is only possible if the object itself is a repository object. In most cases, we recommend that you reference the design-time version of an object because creating a dependency chain that can be identified can be useful during lifecycle management.

To reference design-time repository objects, you’ll need to use a different syntax. The syntax must start each line with sql object. In effect, you’re just removing the term catalog from the statement used when referencing runtime objects. Following this term, include the package and object name of the design-time object. You’ll separate the package name and object name with two colons. Unlike schemas, you don’t need to include the file extension in the fully qualified name. For example, to reference repository table STG_CUSTOMER stored in the e-corp.sales.table package, you’d use the following repository table syntax:

e-corp.sales.tables::STG_CUSTOMERS

Note that the package name and object name are separated by two colons. You can also specify multiple repository objects within a comma-separated list. After the name of the repository object, you’ll need to include another colon. After the final colon, include a comma-separated list of object privileges. At the end of the list, include a semicolon to finish the line. Listing 6.5 shows two lines of code referencing design-time object privileges within a repository role script.

sql object Security.Tables::adusers: SELECT, ALTER, DROP;

sql object 
 e-corp.tables::STG_CUSTOMERS, e-corp.tables::STG_PRODUCTS,
 e-corp.tables::STG_EMPLOYEE: 
SELECT, ALTER, DROP, DELETE;

Listing 6.5    Repository Role Script Granting Design-Time Catalog Object Privileges

6.3.4    Structured Privileges

As of SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, structured privileges can only be defined as standard catalog objects. No documented repository artifacts can produce a structured privilege other than an analytic privilege. As you’ll recall, an analytic privilege is a type of structured privilege that regulates access to SAP HANA information views. In generic terms, structured privileges extend beyond information views and can also provide restrictions to standard catalog views. Therefore, we only need to discuss the syntax required to include catalog-structured privileges within a repository role.

When defining runtime structured privileges within repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with catalog analytic privilege. Following this term, include a colon and the structured privilege name, wrapped in double quotes for avoiding potential case-sensitivity issues. Include a semicolon to finish the line, such as in the following:

catalog analytic privilege : "MyStructuredPriv";

Note that a catalog-structured privilege will be owned by the account that created it. Repository roles are activated when the system account _SYS_REPO is the grantor of privileges. Therefore, the owner of the structured privilege will need to grant _SYS_REPO the structured privilege and include WITH GRANT OPTION. The following example SQL statement grants the structured privilege "MyStructuredPriv" to the _SYS_REPO user and includes the WITH GRANT OPTION:

GRANT STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE "MyStructuredPriv" TO "_SYS_REPO" WITH GRANT 
OPTION;

This statement must be executed by the user that owns the structured privilege or by a user that was previously granted full access to the structured privilege.

6.3.5    Remote Source Privileges

In SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, remote source catalog object privileges can’t be specified within SAP HANA repository roles. We couldn’t find any documentation from SAP that provides an example, nor were we able to configure such privileges using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. To all appearances, remote source privileges aren’t supported.

If you’re using SAP HANA smart data access or SAP HANA smart data integration and you need to develop a security model that includes remote source privileges, we have the following recommendations:

  • You can configure repository role privileges for individual remote source virtual tables that are published in a schema. This arrangement helps limit access to the individual remote source tables without the need for a workaround.

  • Create one or more standard roles using a technical user account and assign the remote source privileges. Grant the roles and privileges to the _SYS_REPO system account and include the WITH GRANT OPTION or WITH ADMIN OPTION.

  • Extend the standard catalog roles within a standard repository role.

  • Preserve all SQL statements in a repository text object, which is the only way to store SQL code in the repository. You’ll likely need to use this SQL code in upstream SAP HANA environments governed by proper lifecycle management. Remember that these repository roles won’t activate until the catalog roles have been created.

6.3.6    Analytic Privileges

When defining analytic privileges within repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with analytic privilege. Following this term, include a colon. After the colon, include the fully qualified name of the analytic privilege file. The file name must include the package hierarchy name, analytic privilege name, and .analytic privilege extension. The package hierarchy name and analytic privilege name will be separated by a single colon. At the end of the statement, include a semicolon to finish the line. Because all analytic privileges are owned by _SYS_REPO, you won’t need to grant _SYS_REPO privileges to these analytic privilege objects, as shown in the following example:

analytic privilege: <package.name> : <analytic privilege name>   
<.analyticprivilege> ;

The following example grants the ap_sales_reporting_region analytic privilege, stored in the e-corp.sales.security package. Remember that repository package and object names are case-sensitive:

analytic privilege:     
  e-corp.security:ap_sales_reporting_region.analyticprivilege;

In a final example, you’ll grant the _SYS_BI_CP_ALL system analytic privilege. This special catalog analytic privilege, when granted, gives full access to all information views defined within the repository:

catalog analytic privilege : "_SYS_BI_CP_ALL";

6.3.7    Application Privileges

When defining application privileges within repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with application privilege. Following this term, include a colon. After the colon, include the name of the application privilege. The application privilege name must include the package hierarchy name, two colons, and the name of the application privilege. For case-sensitivity purposes, the name must be wrapped in double quotes. At the end of the statement, include a semicolon to finish the line.

The following example is a single line used to grant application privileges within a repository-based role:

application privilege: "sap.hana.security.base::DataService";

6.3.8    Package Privileges

When defining package privileges within repository-based roles scripts, you must start each line with package. Following this term, include the name of the package hierarchy node. After the package name, include a single colon, then a comma-separated list of package privileges. At the end of the statement, include a semicolon to finish the line.

The following example is a single line used to grant package privileges within a repository-based role:

Package e-corp.sales: REPO.READ, REPO.ACTIVATE_NATIVE_OBJECTS, REPO.MAINTAIN_NATIVE_PACKAGES, REPO.EDIT_IMPORTED_OBJECTS;

To grant root package privileges, use the system package value of .REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT to represent privileges that will be applied to all packages. The following example shows the syntax needed to grant root package privileges:

package .REPO_PACKAGE_ROOT: REPO.READ;

6.4    Managing Repository Roles with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the SAP HANA XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to manage and create repository roles. In the previous section, we used this interface to create, view, and modify a repository role’s script text. The interface looks similar to the standard role management interface found in SAP HANA Studio, but the role objects created in this interface are profoundly different. This graphical editor creates repository-based roles.

Most users will find using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor GUI easier when creating repository roles. The interface eliminates the need to memorize the exact syntax for each object type. You can also search for objects within the catalog or repository. In the following sections, we’ll first look at accessing the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench and navigating its basic functionality. We’ll then review the specific processes required to grant system privileges, object privileges, analytic privileges, package privileges, and application privileges.

6.4.1    Accessing and Navigating the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench using the instructions found in Section 6.2.1. Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, expand the Content node on the right side of the window. Expand Packages to reveal a list of packages defined in the system. As stated before, repository roles must be stored in a package that only security administrators can access. You’ll typically create a top-level package named Security to host such objects.

To create a repository role, right-click the package in which you want to store the role, then choose New • Role, as shown in Figure 6.5.

Figure 6.5    Navigating the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor and Creating a Repository Role

A small window named New Role will appear. Enter the desired name of the role and click Create. A new tabbed window will appear in the large pane on the right. The tab label should match the provided name of the repository role. The new window will contain a series of subtabs: Granted Roles, System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Package Privileges, and Application Privileges.

In relation to repository-based roles, you can perform three main tasks within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. You can create a new role, edit an existing role, or manage privileges assigned to an existing repository role.

We already discussed the process for creating a repository role in Section 6.2, so now let’s discuss the process for deleting a repository-based role within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor. First, locate the role to be deleted in the package hierarchy. Right-click the role and choose Delete. A Confirmation Needed window will appear. Choose OK to delete the repository role.

To edit an existing repository role within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, first locate the role to be edited within the package hierarchy. Click the role to open the role editor GUI. Alternatively, right-click the role and choose Open With • Role Editor to edit the role using the GUI. You can also choose Open With • Text Editor if you want to edit the role’s script, as discussed earlier in Section 6.2.1.

If you opened the repository role with the role editor, you can now add or remove privileges from the role. Let’s now take a closer look at the process required to grant each type of privilege.

6.4.2    System Privileges

Click the System Privileges tab to reveal the interface where you can add or remove system privileges. To add a system privilege, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select System Privilege popup window will appear, as shown in Figure 6.6. A search box will appear in this window; enter a portion of the system privilege name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired system privilege. Select one or more privileges within the list. Hold down (Ctrl) while clicking to select multiple items. The selected items will be highlighted in light blue. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

Figure 6.6    Selecting and Assigning System Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The selected privilege will now appear in the System Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 6.7.

Figure 6.7    Selected System Privileges

To remove an assigned system privilege, select one from the list, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list to remove the privilege. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of system privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks) at the top left.

If any issues arise when saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text in the console window just below the opened Repository Roles tab. The console window has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text, and error messages will appear in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

6.4.3    Object Privileges

Click the Object Privileges tab to reveal the interface where you can add or remove object privileges. To add an object, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select Object Privilege popup window will appear, as shown in Figure 6.8. The search box is divided into two broad types of objects. The top two radio buttons allow you to toggle between design-time or runtime objects. When searching for design-time objects, choose the Design-time radio button. When searching for runtime objects, choose the Run-time radio button.

Figure 6.8    Selecting and Assigning Object Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

Below the radio buttons, filter options are available for limiting the results to a specific object type. Use the Select Object Type dropdown list to choose the specific object type you want to limit the search results. The default option is All, meaning that all objects types are considered. For example, if you want to limit the search results to just tables, choose Table from the dropdown list, and only table objects will appear in the results.

Just below the dropdown list, a search box will appear. In the text box, enter a portion of the object name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired object by name. Select one or more objects within the list. Hold down the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

The selected objects will now appear in the Object Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 6.9.

Figure 6.9    Selected Runtime and Design-Time Objects

With the objects listed, you’ll now need to assign the various object privileges to each selected object. To specify the privileges for an individual object, click the object to select it in the list. To the right of the selected object, a series of privileges and corresponding checkboxes will appear, as shown on the right in Figure 6.9.

Select the checkbox beside each privilege to assign the selected privilege to the selected object. Repeat the process for all objects. To remove the privilege, simply deselect the checkbox beside the privilege you want to remove.

To remove an assigned object and all its privileges, select an object from the list, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list to remove it. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of objects and established their privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks).

If any issues arise saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window just below the opened Repository Roles tab. The console window has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

6.4.4    Analytic Privileges

Click the Analytic Privileges tab to reveal the interface where you can add or remove analytic privileges. To add an analytic privilege, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select Analytic Privilege popup window will appear, as shown in Figure 6.10.

Figure 6.10    Selecting and Assigning Analytic Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The search box is divided into two broad types of analytic privileges. The top two radio buttons allow you toggle between design-time and runtime objects. When searching for design-time analytic privileges, choose the Design-time radio button. When searching for runtime analytic privileges, choose the Run-time radio button. Note that the runtime list also includes generic structured privileges.

A search box will appear in this window; enter a portion of the analytic privilege’s name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired analytic privileges by name. Select one or more analytic privileges within the list, holding down the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

The selected analytic privileges will now appear in the Analytic Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 6.11.

Figure 6.11    Selected Runtime and Design-Time Analytic Privileges

To remove an assigned analytic privilege, select the privilege from the list, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list to remove it. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of analytic privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks).

If any issues arise saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window, which has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

6.4.5    Package Privileges

Click the Package Privileges tab to reveal the interface where you can add or remove package privileges. To add a package, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select Package popup window will appear, as shown in Figure 6.12.

Within the window, a search box will appear. In the text box, enter a portion of the package name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired package by its complete hierarchical name. Select one or more objects within the list, using the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

Figure 6.12    Selecting and Assigning Package Privileges in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The selected packages will now appear in the Package Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 6.13.

Figure 6.13    Selected Packages and Their Privileges

With the objects listed, you’ll now need to assign the various package privileges to each selected package. To specify the privileges for an individual package, select and highlight the package within the list on the left side. To the right of the selected package, a series of privileges and corresponding checkboxes will appear, as shown on the right in Figure 6.13.

Select the checkbox beside each privilege to assign the selected privilege to the selected package. Repeat the process for all packages. To remove a privilege, simply deselect the checkbox beside the privilege you want to remove.

To remove an assigned package and all its privileges, select an object from the list on the left, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of packages and established their privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks).

If any issues arise when saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window, which has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

6.4.6    Application Privileges

Click the Application Privileges tab to reveal the interface where you can add or remove application privileges. To add an application privilege, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select Application Privilege popup window will appear, as shown in Figure 6.14.

A search box will appear in this window; enter a portion of the application privilege’s name to narrow the results. Alternatively, you can scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired application privileges by name. Select one or more application privileges within the list, using the (Ctrl) key while clicking to select multiple items. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

The selected application privileges will now appear in the Application Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 6.15.

To remove an assigned application privilege, select the privilege from the list and click the large minus sign (–) above the list. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Figure 6.15    Selected Application Privileges

Once you’ve configured the desired list of application privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks). If any issues arise saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window, which has a dark background and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

6.5    Granting Repository Roles to Users

Unlike standard roles, repository roles require a slightly different process when assigning them to existing users or roles. Standard roles rely on specific GRANT SQL syntax. For example, GRANT <SOME PRIVILEGE> TO <GRANTEE> must be executed to assign a standard role. Repository roles are different. Since they’re owned by the _SYS_REPO system account, repository roles can only be granted by that account. Since you cannot log on as this system account, you’ll need an alternative method to impersonate _SYS_REPO for granting actions.

To accommodate this need, SAP HANA provides special stored procedures to either grant or revoke the assignment of repository roles to other users or roles. You can call these stored procedures directly using the SQL console. These stored procedures also can be automatically invoked using either SAP HANA Studio or the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager. Let’s look at how to grant and revoke repository roles using each of the three available methods.

6.5.1    Granting and Revoking Repository Roles with Stored Procedures

Repository roles are granted using the GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE stored procedure in the SYS_REPO schema. For a security administrator to use the stored procedure, he must have EXECUTE rights on the procedures.

The stored procedure requires that you specify two input parameters for proper execution. The first parameter requires the name of an active repository role, and the second requires the name of a grantee. The grantee can be either a user or a role. Use the following syntax:

GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE"('<Repository Name Name>','Grantee Name')

For example, to grant the Security.Roles::consumer repository role to the user account G3457543, you would execute the stored procedure in the SQL console as follows:

CALL "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE"
('Security.Roles::consumer','G3457543');

To revoke a repository role, you’ll need to use another stored procedure found in the _SYS_REPO schema, named REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE. For a security administrator to use the procedure, they must have been granted EXECUTE rights on the procedures. This stored procedure has the same two input parameters as the previous example. For example, to revoke the repository role Security.Roles::consumer from the user account G3457543, you would execute the stored procedure in the SQL console as follows:

CALL "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE"
('Security.Roles::consumer','G3457543');

The grant procedure is set up to execute the role granting actions as if the system account _SYS_REPO were executing the code. This arrangement ensures that the grantor is not the user account executing the procedure. Therefore, you don’t need to worry about protecting the grantor of the role. The revoke procedure performs a similar function. When executed, the procedure impersonates the _SYS_REPO user, and the role is easily revoked because _SYS_REPO was the grantor.

6.5.2    Granting and Revoking Repository Roles with SAP HANA Cockpit

At this time, the SAP HANA cockpit does not properly support the granting of repository-based roles, and therefore, we do not recommend using this interface when granting repository-based roles. As an alternative, you can use the SQL syntax in the SAP HANA cockpit SQL console to grant and revoke repository roles.

6.5.3    Granting and Revoking Repository Roles with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

As mentioned in Chapter 5, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the SAP HANA XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, and manage security.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager by updating the following two URLs to match the details of your environment:

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right side of the window. Expand Users to reveal a list of users. Click a user to open the management interface for the given user account. With the selected user management window open, you can begin granting and revoking repository roles using the Granted Roles tab. Figure 6.16 shows an example of the Granted Roles tab with existing repository role granted.

Figure 6.16    Granting Repository-Based Roles with the SAP HANA Web-Based Workbench Security Interface

Notice that, in the GUI under Granted Roles, the grantor for repository roles is _SYS_REPO. Effectively, the GUI is executing the correct stored procedures when granting or revoking repository roles.

To revoke the repository role, select the role in the Granted Roles list. Click the red X button to revoke the role. Save your changes to activate the action at runtime.

To help demonstrate the concept of repository roles further, let’s review a case study where we examine how E-Corporation used repository roles to create a security model.

6.6    Case Study: Creating Basic Repository Roles

E-Corporation has recently implemented an analytic solution within the SAP HANA platform. The company has provisioned tables; loaded data with an extract, transform, and load (ETL) tool; and created a series of SAP HANA information views. The user community will primarily interact with the SAP HANA information views, which will be secured with an analytic privilege that limits data access by region. Each user will have her own logon to the SAP HANA system to accommodate the data security requirements. However, users will primarily access the data via SAP BusinessObjects Business Intelligence (BI). The SAP BusinessObjects BI system has been configured to support single sign-on (SSO) for the SAP HANA platform with Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication.

In addition to the privileges needed to secure access to the information views, the security model must support power user access, developer access, and security administrator access.

E-Corporation has contacted its lead SAP HANA security consultant and requested help in defining a security model to accommodate its security requirements. The consultant has determined that a series of repository roles will need to be defined. Let’s look further at the consultant’s decision-making process and the four repository roles recommended for this project.

6.6.1    Consumer Repository Role

The first repository role will provide a base level of access to SAP HANA information views. The name of the repository role will be consumer. This role will grant SELECT and EXECUTE access to the _SYS_BI schema, which is required because additional metadata is published to this schema. The role will also grant SELECT access to the design-time calculation view e-corp.sales.models::SCV_CUSTOMER_SALES. Users will need to have SELECT access, at a minimum, to query the information views and metadata in the _SYS_BIC schema. When you reference the design-time calculation view in the repository role, the system will automatically grant access to its corresponding column view in the _SYS_BIC schema. An analytic privilege will also be granted. The analytic privileges will limit the consumer’s access to a series of information views and will dynamically filter the results of the views so that each user will be limited to one or more sales regions based on his predetermined security profile.

Data consumers also need access to the SAP HANA Info Access service hosted in the SAP HANA XS platform. To use this service, these users are granted the role sap.bc.ina.service.v2.userRole::INA_USER. In addition, some consumers need the ability to change their passwords using a web interface hosted in the SAP HANA XS platform. The role sap.hana.xs.formLogin.profile::ProfileOwner must be granted to allow consumers access to this utility.

Figure 6.17 shows the configuration of the consumer repository role script, which in our example, contains two catalog schema privileges and one analytic privilege.

Figure 6.17    Consumer Repository Role Script

6.6.2    Power User Repository Role

In addition to the standard users at E-Corporation, a small group of power users require unique permissions. These users need access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench to query information views and tables for debugging purposes. They’ll also need to access the SAP HANA packages to view the design-time versions of the SAP HANA information views. Therefore, they’ll need basic access to the SAP HANA repository. To accommodate this requirement, the security consultant recommends that an additional repository role named poweruser be created.

Figure 6.18    Poweruser Repository Role Script

The poweruser repository role will be an extension of the consumer repository role, which means that power users will inherit all the privileges assigned to the consumer repository role. The poweruser repository role will grant access to the REPOSITORY_REST stored procedure, which is required to access the package hierarchy within SAP HANA. It will also grant SELECT access to the schemas housing the data used by the SAP HANA information views. Finally, it will grant REPO.READ access to the e-corp package, which will allow a power user the ability to view the configuration of each information view within the repository.

Figure 6.18 shows the configuration of the poweruser repository role script, which contains all the privileges necessary to accommodate the security requirements.

6.6.3    Developer Repository Role

The developers at E-Corporation will require access to SAP HANA and the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. These users will be responsible for creating the development artifacts used by the analytic solution. At a high level, developers require the following privileges and accesses:

  • Developers will require at least the privileges assigned to the consumer and power user repository roles.

  • Developers need the ability to fully manage the staging and data mart schemas. They’ll also be responsible for creating and managing the tables used by the solution.

  • Developers will require access to the SAP HANA repository, system views, SAP HANA application lifecycle management, delivery units, analytic privileges, and import and export interfaces.

  • Developers will require access to all data when querying SAP HANA information views.

  • Developers will require full access to the e-corp package and its child packages.

  • Developers will require read access to all packages and development artifacts.

  • Developers will require access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

To accommodate these requirements, a repository role named developer will be created. Figure 6.19 shows the repository role script designed to accommodate E‐Corporation’s requirements for developers.

Let’s look at how the developer repository role script shown in Figure 6.19 fulfills the requirements:

  • By including three existing roles within the extends role section of the script, two requirements are achieved. Developers will gain all the privileges of the consumer and poweruser roles and will gain access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench.

  • The two schema privilege lines grant the role full access to the staging and data mart schemas using their design-time reference.
