Privileges listed in this interface are have already been granted to the user or role. If the list is blank, nothing is currently granted. To grant an application privilege, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Save, Cancel, Add, and Remove will appear. Click the Add button to open the Select application Privileges popup window. Within this window, you’ll see a search bar and a list of application privileges with check boxes to their left. Use the search bar to filter the list based on the entered text. Then, scroll through the list and select the checkbox beside the application privilege you want to grant. With one or more application privileges selected, click the OK button to add the desired items to the user. Your selected application privileges should now appear in the Application Privileges section.

To revoke an application privilege, start by clicking the Edit button again, then select the checkbox beside each system privilege in the list, and click the Remove button to revoke the privileges. Repeat the process for each application privilege you want to revoke. Once you’ve removed all the desired application privileges, click the Save button. The removed privileges will be revoked, and the grantee will be updated.

During the process of adding or removing privileges, click the Cancel button to discard any unsaved changes. Clicking the Cancel button will deactivate the Add, Cancel, and Remove buttons and return you to a read-only list of currently granted application privileges.

11.3.3    Granting Application Privileges with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Security Manager

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to create users, create roles, or manage security for standard roles. This interface provides a web-based alternative to SAP HANA Studio and also serves as an alternative to issues GRANT and REVOKE statement with SQL.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

  • http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

In the last example, replace <sap_hana_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the right. Expand Roles to reveal a list of standard roles defined in the system. Double-click a role to open the management interface for the given role. With the selected role management window open, you can begin granting and revoking privileges.

Note

To perform the same action for an individual user account, expand the Users node and double-click the desired user account.

Recall that we recommend you use repository-based roles to support an SAP HANA security model. However, in this section, we’ll simply highlight the basic workflow if you choose to manage security with standard roles or directly on individual user accounts.

With the GUI management interface open for a given grantee, you can add an application privilege as follows. Click the Application Privileges tab. Click the plus sign (+) button to add and search for the desired analytic privilege. The Find Application Privileges window appears allowing you to search for a specific application privilege. Select the desired application privileges and click OK to add them to the list.

To save your changes, press (Ctrl)+(S) or click the disk icon at the top left to save and activate the privilege. To revoke an application privilege, select it in the list and click the red X. Once again, save the changes to make them active within the database system.

If any activation issues arise, warning messages will appear in the status pane at the bottom of the user management window. The status pane has a dark background color. Error messages will appear in red text. Errors are only generated when you attempt activation or save changes.

11.3.4    Granting Application Privileges within Repository Roles

As mentioned earlier, basing a security model on repository-based roles is best. Because of their benefits, we’ll review the process of granting application privileges within repository-based roles. To assign application privileges to a repository-based role, you can either modify or develop repository roles within design-time scripts, or you can use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor to create and modify repository-based roles.

SQL Syntax in Design-Time Scripts

In Chapter 6, we introduced you to repository roles and outlined the workflows required to create and manage repository roles. In this section, we’ll again review the syntax necessary to assign application privileges to design-time repository-based role scripts. If you require more information about this process, refer to Chapter 6.

When defining application privileges within repository-based role scripts, you must start each line with application privilege. Following this term, include a colon, then include the name of the application privilege. The application privilege name must include the package hierarchy name, two colons, and the name of the application privilege. For case-sensitivity purposes, the name must be enclosed in double quotes. At the end of the statement, include a semicolon to finish the line.

The following example shows a single line used to grant application privileges within a repository-based role:

application privilege: "sap.hana.security.base::DataService";

Granting and Revoking with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface that you can use to build and test development artifacts. From a security perspective, you can use this interface to create and manage repository-based roles. This interface offers all the advantages of repository-based roles without the need to define the repository roles using scripts and the SAP HANA domain-specific language. However, you can use this same interface to either edit the role via a GUI or open the role file in the text editor.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. The following URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

  • http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/editor

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor

In the last example, replace <sap_hana_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/editor

  • https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/editor

To use the editor, the user account first will need to be granted one of the roles listed in Table 11.1. Users only need one of the two roles to access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor.

Role Name

Summary

sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper

Within the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench, users will only be able to access the editor. The editor provides interfaces to create a variety of repository objects, including repository-based roles.

sap.hana.ide.roles::Developer

This role grants a higher level of privileges for users that need full access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench. This role grants access to the editor, catalog, and security interfaces and is considered the parent to the sap.hana.ide.roles::EditorDeveloper role.

Table 11.1    Roles Required to Use the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Editor

Additional Privileges Needed to Use the Editor

Note that the roles listed in Table 11.1 simply allow the granted user access to the interface. Users will also need access to the package in which the repository roles are stored. To grant repository roles to other users and roles, users will need EXECUTE access to the system stored procedure named "_SYS_REPO"."GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE". To revoke repository roles, they’ll need EXECUTE access to the "_SYS_REPO"."REVOKE_ACTIVATED_ROLE" stored procedure.

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, expand the Content node on the right, then expand Packages to reveal a list of packages defined in the system. As mentioned earlier, repository roles must be stored in a package that only security administrators can access. You would typically create a top-level package named Security to host such objects.

To create a new repository role, right-click the package in which you want to store the role and choose New • Role, as shown in Figure 11.2.

Figure 11.2    Navigating the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench
and a Creating Repository Role

A small window named New Role will appear. Enter the desired name of the role and click Create. A new tabbed window will appear in the large right-hand pane. The tab label should match the provided name of the repository role. The new window will contain a series of subtabs: Granted Roles, System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Package Privileges, and Application Privileges. Like in SAP HANA Studio, each tab allows a developer to define specific privileges.

Click the Application Privileges tab to open the interface where you can add or remove application privileges. To add an application privilege, click the large plus sign (+) button on the subtab header. The Select Application Privilege window will appear, as shown in Figure 11.3.

Figure 11.3    Selecting and Assigning Application Privileges in the SAP HANA
Web-Based Development Workbench

A search box will appear in this window; enter a portion of the application privilege’s name to narrow the results or scroll through the unfiltered list to locate the desired application privileges by name. Select one or more application privileges within the list, holding down (Ctrl) while clicking to select multiple items. The selected items will be highlighted in light blue. Click the OK button at the bottom of the window to finalize the selection.

The selected application privileges will now appear in the Application Privileges tab, as shown in Figure 11.4.

Figure 11.4    Selected Application Privileges

To remove an assigned application privilege, select it from the list, then click the large minus sign (–) above the list to remove it. Items in the list must be deleted one at a time.

Once you’ve configured the desired list of application privileges, click the save all icon (three floppy disks) at the top left.

If any issues arise when saving and activating the repository role, messages will appear in red text within the console window just below the opened repository roles tab. The console window has a dark background color and is located at the bottom of the opened tab. Affirmative messages will appear in white text and error messages in red text.

To close the open repository role tab, click the small X to the right of the tab.

11.4    Privileges on Users

Unrelated to application privileges, an additional option named Privileges on Users can be used to grant the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege but has a limited scope of usage within SAP HANA. Privileges on Users allows a user to grant a grantee debug access to the user’s own session. This privilege only offers the ability to assign the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege and is limited to the grantor’s account.

For example, the user account SYSTEM can log on to a SQL console and grant to the user account ADMIN_MIKE the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege but only for the user SYSTEM. In fact, GUI interfaces for this functionality will only allow you to specify SYSTEM account under the User column. This privilege grants ADMIN_MIKE debug SQLScript code rights within the SYSTEM account’s session. SYSTEM is also the only user that can grant this privilege to ADMIN_MIKE.

In the following sections, we’ll review two options for granting privileges on users using the SAP HANA cockpit and using SQL statements.

11.4.1    Granting Privileges on Users with the SAP HANA Cockpit

Let’s review the workflows necessary to grant and revoke privileges on users with the SAP HANA cockpit. As an alternative to using SQL statements, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit GUI action called Assign Privileges or Manage Roles. Each interface allows you to both grant and revoke privileges on users. Most users will find using the SAP HANA cockpit easier than memorizing and entering in SQL statements.

To access the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles area, start at the SAP HANA cockpit Home screen and locate an SAP HANA system in the Resource Directory. Connect to the desired tenant database or SYSTEMDB, which will take you to the System Overview window. Using the Filter by Area dropdown list, choose the option Security. Locate the Assign Privileges or Manage Roles in the User & Role Management tile.

Figure 11.5 shows the Assign Privileges interface within the SAP HANA cockpit Assign Privileges for the TEST_01 user account. In the window, you’ll see several tabs for the various privilege categories starting with the System Privileges, Object Privileges, Analytic Privileges, Application Privileges, Package Privileges, and Privileges on Users tabs. You’ll find a similar interface when working with roles. However, the Role Details GUI has an additional link called Roles where you can grant existing roles to the selected role.

The sixth tab in the Assign Privileges window is named Privileges on Users. Use this tab to configure privileges on users.

If already configured, the interface will list the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege with the grantor that assigned this privilege. If the list is blank, nothing is currently configured. To grant attach debugger, click the Edit button located on the far-right side of the interface near the Search field. Once you click the Edit button, new buttons labeled Save, Cancel, Add, and Remove will appear. Click the Add button to add ATTACH DEBUGGER to the grantee. Notice that the grantor will always be the account used to authenticate with the SAP HANA system. The Attach Debugger assignment should now appear in the list. Note that nothing else can be configured here. Only the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege can be assigned, and the grantor is automatically determined as the account used to access the system via the SAP HANA cockpit. Once you’ve configured this option, click the Save button to grant the privileges.

Figure 11.5    Managing Privileges Assigned to User Accounts in the SAP HANA Cockpit

To revoke the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege, start by clicking the Edit button. Highlight the Attach Debugger assignment line then click the Remove button to revoke the privilege. Once you’ve removed the item, click the Save button. The removed privileges will be revoked, and the user object will be updated.

During the process of adding or removing privileges, you can click the Cancel button to discard any unsaved changes. Clicking the Cancel button will deactivate the Add, Cancel, and Remove buttons and return you to the prior, read-only state.

11.4.2    Granting Privileges on Users with SQL

In addition to using the SAP HANA cockpit, a grantor can execute the following SQL code to grant the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege to another grantee:

GRANT ATTACH DEBUGGER TO <GRANTEE>;

Replace the <GRANTEE> variable with the name of a grantee within your environment. When executed, the grantee will be granted access to debug the grantor’s session.

11.5    Summary

Application privileges define custom levels of access to applications developed in the XS engine. Once activated, these privileges can be granted to users or roles within the SAP HANA system. The Privileges on Users tab in SAP HANA GUI interfaces is used to grant the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege to another grantee. You can also use SQL to grant the ATTACH DEBUGGER privilege.

12    Authentication

Authentication is key in validating a user’s access to the SAP HANA system. In this chapter, we’ll discuss how SAP HANA supports external authentication providers in addition to its basic internal authentication mechanism.

Most of the chapters in this book have spent a great deal of time discussing authorization, a process in which the SAP HANA system determines if a user is allowed to perform specific actions within the platform. To define allowable actions in SAP HANA, you’ll effectively grant privileges to a user to define the individual actions a user account is authorized to perform. However, for the authorization mechanism to work properly, the SAP HANA system must first properly identify each user. The process of identifying a user is called authentication. SAP HANA supports several different types of authentication mechanisms, including both internal basic authentication, Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) authentication, and external authentication systems supporting single sign-on (SSO).

SAP HANA’s internal basic authentication systems work through password authentication, meaning that SAP HANA will challenge users to supply both their user name and password—or, user credentials—as a form of identification. Like most authentication systems, SAP HANA assumes that the account owner is the only individual with knowledge of these credentials and therefore can prove his identity. Once an account is verified through password authentication, SAP HANA will conduct authorization checks based on the user’s granted privileges or roles.

Starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 03, SAP HANA also supports LDAP authentication. With LDAP authentication, SAP HANA will delegate the process of validating credentials to an external system. Most organizations support one or more LDAP-based directory and authentication system. The most common being Microsoft’s Active Directory.

SAP HANA can also leverage many external authentication systems to support SSO, which allows a user’s credentials to be challenged once by a master system and then passed to subsequent systems without the need to supply the credentials again. In the case of SAP HANA, you can configure the system to support the following external provider options: Kerberos, Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), JSON Web Tokens (JWT), SAP logon tickets, SAP assertion tickets, and X.509 client certificates. By default, all user accounts support SAP HANA’s internal basic authentication mechanism. LDAP authentication is also supported, but SAP HANA will not allow an account to support both LDAP authentication and internal basic authentication at the same time. However, both internal and LDAP users can be configured to support one or more additional external authentication providers for the purposes of SSO.

When configuring a user account for external authentication, you must first activate the external provider and then specify mapping data. SAP HANA uses this mapping data to validate an SAP HANA user account’s external identity. Thus, a dedicated SAP HANA user account is required for every internal or external user of the system. For example, you can’t use SAML SSO authentication between SAP HANA and another system unless a user account exists in SAP HANA, with its SAML identity enabled and configured. Therefore, every authenticating user must be a provisioned user for all authentication scenarios.

To better understand the authentication providers supported by SAP HANA, this chapter will walk you through the internal basic authentication system and its configurable settings in detail. We’ll also discuss LDAP authentication and its setup. Finally, we’ll discuss the various external providers supported for SSO to the SAP HANA system.

12.1    SAP HANA Internal Authentication Mechanism

SAP HANA provides an internal basic authentication mechanism, in the form of an internal user account and password system. The internal password authentication mechanism must be secured in two ways: First, you’ll need to identify the methods you’ll use to transmit these passwords to the SAP HANA system and implement encryption to prevent others from intercepting these passwords. Second, you’ll need to establish policies related to a user’s password. The password should be sufficiently complex and changed periodically. Let’s look at how to use both encryption and password policies to protect the internal SAP HANA authentication mechanism.

12.1.1    Protecting SAP HANA Passwords with Encryption

When a client application communicates with SAP HANA and when password authentication is used to authenticate the user, you’ll often need to use encryption to prevent unauthorized individuals from intercepting the password. By default, many client applications don’t use encryption when communicating with SAP HANA. However, SAP HANA supports communication encryption with the Open Database Connectivity (ODBC), Java Database Connectivity (JDBC), and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) protocols.

You can use ODBC, JDBC, HTTP, or HTTPS client connection protocols depending on your mode of connection. Tools like SAP HANA Studio will use JDBC to communicate user-provided authentication credentials to the SAP HANA system. Business intelligence tools often use ODBC and JDBC as well. Users accessing applications in the SAP HANA extended application services, classic mode (SAP HANA XS) engine (XS engine) will likely use HTTP or HTTPS to communicate authentication credentials to the SAP HANA system.

JDBC and ODBC client credentials can be transmitted in an encrypted format to help protect them from unauthorized access. Applications hosted in the XS engine can be accessed using the HTTPS protocol. The HTTP protocol isn’t encrypted; using HTTPS will provide the necessary encryption. In general, HTTP access shouldn’t be used for SSO or form-based authentication because HTTP isn’t secure. Form-based authentication, in which users enter their user name and password in a form, is used by web-based applications to collect credentials for authentication. Most XS engine applications support form-based authentication by default. Many external authentication systems also rely on the HTTP protocol when communicating SSO credentials. In all cases, SAP HANA should be configured to use HTTP with SSL or HTTPS for encrypted communications over the HTTP protocol. We’ll discuss how encryption is enabled and managed in Chapter 13; for now, note that you need encryption in addition to strong password policies to properly protect SAP HANA’s internal authentication mechanism.

12.1.2    Configuring the Internal Authentication Password Policy

Password policy security settings within SAP HANA can be configured using a few different methods: First, you can issue ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION SQL commands to update security settings stored in the SAP HANA INI configuration files. Second, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit’s database administration Manage System Configuration options to directly update the individual INI settings. Third, the SAP HANA cockpit also provides a graphical user interface (GUI) for authentication with password policy that provides easy access to security settings within SAP HANA. Fourth, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit’s manage user groups GUI to establish a unique policy for each custom user group. Finally, the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager provides an interface where you can manage legacy settings.

These password policy security settings, specific to SAP HANA internal authentication, allow for changes to password policies. Two main configuration files affect the password policy. If the SAP HANA system is set up as a single container system, the indexserver.ini file will be used for password policy settings. This configuration file contains settings specific to the SAP HANA index server process. Settings can be entered for an index server process on a specific server node or for all index servers in the cluster. To accommodate all servers in a cluster, the system layer should be used. To accommodate a specific host, the host layer should be used. If the SAP HANA system is set up as a multicontainer system, the nameserver.ini file will be used to manage the policy for the system database.

In this section, we’ll review password policy settings in SAP HANA and demonstrate step-by-step how you can configure password policy settings using SQL statements, the SAP HANA cockpit, and the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager.

SAP HANA offers security administrators several options to manipulate the behavior of its internal basic authentication mechanism. The specific settings allow you to either strengthen password policy standards or relax them as needed. Let’s look at these settings, listed by their technical names, in more detail.

minimal_password_length

The minimal_password_length setting governs the minimum allowed length for passwords. The system supports a length between 6 and 64 characters. When creating user accounts or changing passwords, the specified password must comply with the configured minimum password length. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Minimum Password Length.

password_layout

The password_layout setting governs the minimum supported complexity of the password. The setting value is based on the entered expression pattern. To define the pattern, you can choose one or more of the following character expressions:

  • Lowercase letters from a to z

  • Uppercase letters from A to Z

  • Numerical digits from 0 to 9

  • Most special characters found on the keyboard

To define the minimum complexity expression, choose values from each of the supported characters. Characters can be entered in any order, but keep in mind that repeated characters do change how the pattern is evaluated. For example, if the minimum password complexity requires the use of at least one uppercase letter, two lowercase letters, and three numbers, you could specify the expression Abc123, 156Cxf, or Fa103c. For special characters, you’ll use an underscore (_) in the pattern. If the complexity requires at least one uppercase letter, one number, and one special character, you could specify the expression G3_. Again, the specific letter, digit, or character order used isn’t important but the use of multiple characters of the same type is. The system looks at the pattern specified to determine the minimum complexity. To disable the minimum complexity requirement, specify an empty string value as the expression. However, it’s advisable that the default expression pattern of Aa1 be specified at a minimum. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Required Character Types.

Using Special Characters in Passwords

Although using special characters in passwords is an excellent way to increase password complexity, users might have trouble authenticating with SAP HANA from some clients. When a password contains a special character, SAP HANA requires that the special character be sent to the system enclosed in double quotes (e.g., "_"). If the client fails to comply with this requirement, the user might not be able to authenticate. As a result, we highly recommend checking that all required client interfaces authenticate users with special characters in their passwords before special characters are mandated in all passwords.

force_first_password_change

The force_first_password_change setting mandates whether a user must change his initial password before the first attempt to authenticate with the system. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Password Change Required on First Logon.

When set to true, the user must change the password established by the administrator before he can completely log on to the system. When set to false, the user can log on using the password created by the administrator. Note that, at some point in the future, the user might be forced to change his password based on other password policy settings.

On a per-user basis, you can issue the following SQL statement to require a password change before the next authentication attempt:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> FORCE PASSWORD CHANGE

You can also create or alter user accounts on a per-user basis and disable this policy. The following SQL statements disable the policy on a per-user account basis:

CREATE USER <USER_NAME> PASSWORD "!niti@LPass" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE
ALTER USER <USER_NAME> PASSWORD "!niti@LPass" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE

When issuing the ALTER statement, you must specify a password, or the statement won’t execute. Depending on the configuration of the password reuse policy, a new password might be required when issuing ALTER statements.

last_used_passwords

The last_used_passwords setting governs the minimum number of times that a password must be changed before the same password can be used again. This setting forces users to choose a password not used in the last x number of passwords each time they change it or each time they’re required to change it. The default value is five previous passwords. If the value of 0 is specified, a password can be reused at any time. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Number of Last Used Passwords That Cannot Be Reused.

maximum_invalid_connect_attempts

The maximum_invalid_connect_attempts setting specifies the minimum number of failed logon attempts for a given account before the system locks the account to prevent further access. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Number of Allowed Failed Logon Attempts.

A minimum value of 1 is required for this setting, and no maximum value is specified in the documentation. The system defaults to six invalid logon attempts before an account is locked. Once an account is locked, the user account can’t authenticate with the system. The user must wait until the system unlocks the account after a configured duration or until the administrator manually unlocks the account. The system won’t unlock the account if the lock indefinitely policy setting is set to true in the configuration settings. Only administrators can unlock an account when the lock indefinitely policy is enabled.

Administrators can issue the following SQL statement to unlock a user account:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> RESET CONNECT ATTEMPTS;

To list accounts that have invalid connection attempts exceeding the configured invalid connection attempt policy, execute the SQL code shown in Listing 12.1.

SELECT 
X.USER_NAME, 
X.INVALID_CONNECT_ATTEMPTS,
(CASE WHEN X.INVALID_CONNECT_ATTEMPTS >= X.PASSPOL 
THEN 'Locked' ELSE 'OK' END) AS ACCOUNT_STATUS
FROM
    (
SELECT USER_NAME, INVALID_CONNECT_ATTEMPTS,
(SELECT TOP 1 "VALUE" FROM "SYS"."M_PASSWORD_POLICY" 
WHERE PROPERTY = 'maximum_invalid_connect_attempts') 
AS PASSPOL
FROM "SYS"."USERS"
    ) X
WHERE X.INVALID_CONNECT_ATTEMPTS >= X.PASSPOL

Listing 12.1    SQL Code to List Account Status for Users in an SAP HANA System

The number of active consecutive failed connection attempts will be reset each time a user logs on successfully. However, the system records the number of historical failed attempts issued before each successful logon. The following SQL statement will query the system view containing the failed connection attempt history preceding each successful connection attempt’s timestamp:

SELECT * FROM SYS.INVALID_CONNECT_ATTEMPTS

To remove all historical data related to failed connection attempts, issue the following SQL statement per user:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> DROP CONNECT ATTEMPTS;

password_lock_time

The password_lock_time setting specifies the amount of time in minutes the system will wait before it unlocks accounts that have exceeded the maximum number of failed logon attempts. Most GUIs refer to this setting as User Lock Time.

The default is 1,440 minutes or 1 day. If a value of 0 is specified, the account will be unlocked immediately, and the maximum_invalid_connect_attempts setting will effectively be disabled.

To lock an account indefinitely, enter a value of -1 in the file settings or choose the Lock User Indefinitely option found in some SAP HANA GUIs.

minimum_password_lifetime

The minimum_password_lifetime setting, or Minimum Password Lifetime in most GUIs, dictates the minimum number of days that must elapse before a user can change his/her own password. The default value is one day, and a value of 0 disables this setting. This setting is designed to prevent users from changing their passwords repeatedly to circumvent the password reuse policy. A default value of one day will discourage consecutive password changes for most users given the required delay. The value should be increased if users aren’t discouraged by the default value.

maximum_password_lifetime

The maximum_password_lifetime setting, or Maximum Password Lifetime in most GUIs, governs the age of passwords in days. The default value is 182 days and a minimum value of 1 is supported. When the password lifetime is exceeded, a user will be forced to change her password before she can successfully authenticate with the system. Passwords should be changed periodically to protect from intentional decryption and to reduce the likelihood of the password being compromised.

On a per-user basis, issue the following SQL statement to disable the password lifetime policy:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> DISABLE PASSWORD LIFETIME;

To reenable the policy, issue the following SQL statement:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE PASSWORD LIFETIME;

maximum_unused_initial_password_lifetime

The maximum_unused_initial_password_lifetime setting determines the validity of passwords established by the administrator in days. When an account is created or a password generated by an administrator, this setting will determine how long the password remains viable before it expires and the account is disabled. The system default value is seven days, and a minimum value of one day is supported. After the duration of the configured value, a user’s account will be disabled until the administrator resets the password. Note that this value was misspelled in versions of SAP HANA prior to SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 12. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Lifetime of Initial Password.

maximum_unused_productive_password_lifetime

The maximum_unused_productive_password_lifetime setting specifies the number of days before an inactive user account is disabled. Inactive user accounts are those that haven’t authenticated with the system for some time. The default value is 365 days, and a minimum value of one day is supported. Administrators must reset the account password once the user account expires. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Maximum Duration of User Inactivity.

password_expire_warning_time

The password_expire_warning_time setting specifies how long in days before the expiration of a password the system will notify a user. The notification is transmitted during any ODBC or JDBC successful authentication or connection attempt. The connecting application is responsible for sending this message through to the user. If a value of 0 is specified, password expiration notifications are disabled. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Notification of Password Expiration.

password_lock_for_system_user

When configured with the default value of true, the password_lock_for_system_user setting will prevent the SYSTEM user account from being locked out, even if multiple consecutive invalid passwords are issued. This setting supersedes the password_lock_time and maximum_invalid_connect_attempts settings. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Exempt SYSTEM User from Locking.

detailed_error_on_connect

The detailed_error_on_connect setting determines the amount of failed logon information provided during authentication attempts. Most GUIs refer to this setting as Detailed Error Information on Failed Logon. The default value is false, which means that the generic Authentication Failed message is returned regardless of the failure reason. When true, a more specific message, such as Invalid User or Password, User Is Locked, Connect Try Is Outside Validity Period, or User Is Deactivated is returned. Using the default value of false is best because this value makes it more difficult for hackers to gain unauthorized access to the SAP HANA system.

12.1.3    Managing Password Policy Settings with SQL

Using SQL commands, you can directly set the value for each of the settings listed in Section 12.3.1. The syntax is based on the ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION commands. You’ll need the INIFILE ADMIN system privilege to modify these settings using SQL. The following generic SQL statement demonstrates the required syntax to manipulate password policy settings within SAP HANA:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('<ini file name>', '<layer>') 
   SET ('password policy', '<Setting Name>') = '<value>' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

The <ini file name> variable should be replaced with the name of the configuration file. For a single-container system, use indexserver.ini. For a multiple container system, use nameserver.ini. The <layer> variable should be replaced with SYSTEM or HOST. Use SYSTEM to apply the setting to all configuration files in the cluster. Use HOST to apply the setting to a specific host. The <Setting Name> variable must contain a setting listed in Section 12.3.1. The <value> field should be replaced with a supported value for the given setting. Specify WITH RECONFIGURE to apply the setting instantly. If this setting isn’t specified, the configured value won’t take effect until the next reboot.

The following example SQL statement will configure the password_layout password policy setting with a value of Aa1:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('nameserver.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('password policy', 'password_layout') = 'Aa1' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

To revert a setting to its default value, use the UNSET option within the command. The following example will revert the password_layout setting to its default value:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('nameserver.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   UNSET ('password policy', 'password_layout');

You can use the same syntax to unset all the password policy settings listed in Section 12.3.1; simply update the variables to match your environment. Remember to specify the correct INI settings file and layer specific to your environment. Now, let’s review how to change the settings using SAP HANA GUIs.

12.1.4    Managing Password Policy Settings in GUIs

SAP HANA offers GUIs in which password policy settings can be configured. The SAP HANA cockpit provides the Manage System Configuration GUI and also the Password Policy link in the Authentication section of the System Overview page. The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager also provides an interface to configure the password policy. Let’s look at these four options in more detail.

SAP HANA Cockpit: Manage System Configuration GUI

Instead of using SQL commands to update the security policy settings, you can use the Manage System Configuration options in the SAP HANA cockpit found under Database Administration. Click on Manage System Configuration to launch the System Configuration GUI.

The System Configuration GUI lists any default or custom defined configuration settings for SAP HANA. Just below the Parameters tab, you’ll see a search bar and a series of dropdown lists, as shown in Figure 12.1 for reference. Note that you’ll need the INIFILE ADMIN system privilege to view or modify these settings.

Figure 12.1    SAP HANA Cockpit System Configuration GUI

You can use the search bar to search for a specific parameter name. In addition, you can use the Configuration File dropdown list to filter the list to a specific configuration file. Individual parameters are organized into sections of associated parameters. You can use the Section dropdown list to filter to a specific section. If the SAP HANA system has multiple servers (scale-out), you can use the Host section to filter the list for a given server node or host. Finally, you can use the Database dropdown list to filter the list to settings specific to a given tenant database.

Once a parameter is located, you can use the Override Value link, located on the far-right side of the parameter, to change the current value or, in some cases, the default value. Figure 12.2 shows an example of the GUI where we’ve searched for the term “password” and chosen the indexserver.ini option in the Configuration File dropdown list. The results show the section [ ]password_policy and a list of parameters that can be changed. To change an individual parameter configuration value, click the Override Value option on the far right, which will launch a configuration window for the associated parameter.

Figure 12.2    Viewing Password Policy Settings of the indexserver.ini Configuration File Using the SAP HANA Cockpit GUI

Figure 12.3 shows an example of the last_used_passwords parameter configuration window and how parameters can be overwritten for a System Value, either all tenant databases or an individual tenant database value under the Select Database dropdown list.

Figure 12.3    Changing Password Policy Settings for last_used_passwords

The configuration window will list the Default and Active values for the setting. In addition, you can click the Restore Default button to quickly restore the default value for the setting. To change the configuration setting, enter the desired value in the provided field and click the OK button. To cancel changes before they’re saved, click the Cancel button. Password policy settings are implemented instantly within the SAP HANA system; no reboot is required for them to take effect.

SAP HANA Cockpit: Authentication Password Policy GUI

The SAP HANA cockpit also offers a dedicated GUI to manage the password policy. You can access the GUI by clicking the Password Policy link in the Authentication section of the System Overview page of the SAP HANA cockpit. Figure 12.4 shows an overview of the password policy management GUI in the SAP HANA cockpit. Notice that the same configuration settings listed in the previous section are available in this GUI as well.

To modify the password policy, click the Edit button found at the top right side of the window. For each setting, an editable field or radio button option will appear. Click the Save button located at the bottom to save the changes. Click Cancel to discard any unsaved changes.

Figure 12.4    Password Policy Configuration GUI in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The GUI also offers an additional Password Blacklist tab, located at the top, next to the Password Policy tab, as shown in Figure 12.4. This interface, shown in Figure 12.5, allows an administrator to define a list of specific words, phrases, or password combinations that won’t be accepted by the system for a given user.

Figure 12.5    Password Blacklist Configuration GUI

To add a blacklist item, click the Edit button on the top right side of the Password Blacklist tab. In the columns provided, click the Add Entry button to insert a new phrase into the list. If you want the system to look for the word within the provided password, select the checkbox beside the Contained in Password option. For example, if the blacklisted word is “welcome,” the password “welcome1234” wouldn’t be accepted because it contains the target word. If the Contained in Password option isn’t selected, the system will only prevent the exact word as listed in the first cell. Using the same example, the password “welcome1234” would be acceptable because it isn’t an exact match for “welcome.” If the word should be evaluated using the exact case of the entered text, select the Case-Sensitive checkbox. For example, if the Case-Sensitive option is selected, then “Welcome” would be accepted if the provided blacklisted word is “welcome.”

You can also execute the following SQL statement to view a list of configured blacklisted password words defined in the system:

SELECT * FROM "_SYS_SECURITY"."_SYS_PASSWORD_BLACKLIST"

SAP HANA Cockpit: User Group-Specific Password Policy

Starting with SAP HANA 2.0, you can also define user groups. Users groups are organizational units that help you group users into containers for delegated administration purposes and password policy purposes. User groups are not currently used for authorization purposes. With user groups, you can give specific administrators access to a select group of users. You can also define a unique password policy for each group.

Within the SAP HANA cockpit, you can access this password policy from the same tile and link we used to create and edit groups. Locate the User & Role Management tile and click the Manage User Groups link, which will launch the User Group management window. Within the management window, you’ll see a list of previously defined user groups. Click a group within the list to open the management options for the group. With the group management window open, click the Password Policy tab. You’ll then see a list of configured password policy options for the group. Click the Edit button to modify the password policy for the group.

Note that, if an individual password policy is not explicitly configured for a user group, the value will default to the value configured for the system or tenant database. You can also issue the following SQL statement to view the password policy for a given user at any time to see their effective password policy:

SELECT * FROM "SYS"."M_EFFECTIVE_PASSWORD_POLICY" WHERE USER_NAME = '<USER_NAME>';

SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench Security Manager

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface to manage security settings, including password policies.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager by updating the following two URLs to match the details of your environment:

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, expand the Security node on the left. Figure 12.6 shows the Security Console interface and the Password Policy tab.

Figure 12.6    Password Policy Configuration in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

Click the Security icon 1 shown in Figure 12.6. The Security Console tab 2 will open. This tab contains all the same options available in the SAP HANA cockpit, including a Password Blacklist area, located at the bottom of the Security Console tab.

SAP HANA also supports a few external or third-party authentication providers for SSO to the system. In the next section, we’ll review these external providers in more detail.

12.2    SAP HANA and LDAP Authentication

Starting with SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 03, LDAP-based users can now be provisioned within SAP HANA, and their LDAP-managed passwords can be used for authentication. When an SAP HANA user is set up for LDAP authentication, standard local password authentication is disabled. Thus, the user can only authenticate via one of the supported SSO providers or using their LDAP credentials. For example, if your Active Directory account is configured as an LDAP account in SAP HANA, you could access SAP HANA Studio using your Active Directory-managed password. You could not set up a locally managed SAP HANA password for that same account.

Before you can create LDAP users, SAP HANA must also be preconfigured with an LDAP provider, and SAP standard roles should be mapped to LDAP groups. Based on the configuration of the LDAP provider, LDAP users can be automatically created in SAP HANA. In addition, you can use the CREATE USER <USER_NAME> WITH IDENTITY FOR LDAP PROVIDER SQL statement to create an LDAP user manually, and the SAP HANA cockpit provides an option, when creating a user, for you to choose the authentication password mode (Local or LDAP). Note that user accounts can be changed from local to LDAP password authentication within the SAP HANA cockpit or with SQL by first running ALTER USER <USER_NAME> DISABLE PASSWORD and then ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE LDAP.

Again, before you can use LDAP authentication or authorization, you must first create an LDAP provider, which any administrator with the LDAP ADMIN system privilege can do via the SQL console.

Prior to configuring an LDAP provider, you must fulfill the following prerequisites:

  • The LDAP source must be LDAP v3 compliant.

  • You must have the system privilege LDAP ADMIN, which allows you to configure the LDAP provider.

  • You must create a certificate collection with purpose LDAP and import the certificate from the LDAP server into this collection. Without this certificate, SAP HANA and LDAP will not have secure communications.

  • You must verify that the [authentication] parameter with key authentication_methods in the global.ini configuration file has ldap included in the comma-separated list of providers.

  • You must identify LDAP groups that will be mapped to SAP HANA roles.

Again, you’ll create the LDAP provider using SQL. Listing 12.2 shows an example of how you would create an LDAP provider against an Active Directory LDAP. Assume that the Active Directory domain name is ecorp.local and that SSL is required for communication. We’re also assuming that the LDAP provider can automatically create LDAP-based users within the SAP HANA database.

CREATE LDAP PROVIDER ldap_ecorp
CREDENTIAL TYPE 'PASSWORD' USING 'user=CN=HDBLDAP,OU=Service Accounts,DC=ecorp,DC=local;password=N0tIt2018'
USER LOOKUP URL 'ldap://ecorp.local:389/CN=Users,DC=ecorp,DC=local??sub?(&(objectClass=user)(sAMAccountName=*))'
NESTED GROUP LOOKUP URL 'ldap:// ecorp.local:389/DC=ecorp,DC=local??sub?(member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=*)'
ATTRIBUTE DN 'distinguishedName'
ATTRIBUTE MEMBER_OF 'memberOf'
SSL ON
DEFAULT ON
ENABLE PROVIDER 
ENABLE USER CREATION FOR LDAP;

Listing 12.2    SQL User to Create an LDAP Provider within SAP HANA

To ensure that SSL is working, you’ll need to export the SSL certificate from the ecorp.local Active Directory domain controller and then import the certificate into the LDAP certificate collection.

As a domain admin from an Active Directory domain controller server, run the following command, in the command line, to generate the certificate text:

certutil -ca.cert c:\ecorp_ca_name.cer

Copy the certificate text that appears in the command line output window. You must use this text in the SQL command shown in Listing 12.3. (You should not open the .cer file.) Using that certificate text, run the CREATE CERTIFICATE FROM command, as shown in Listing 12.3.

CREATE CERTIFICATE FROM '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MfdsgFDGdfHgfhdD9gAVErJNkl7RYP0HKzANBgkqhkiG8hsdfE
MRUwEwYKCZImiZPyLGQBGRYFbG9jYWwxHTAbBgoJkiaJk/SDFSDFre4567ujfgdfd
...
PA78M4CX8fSrBI2lT433h4hjtG9fM8QKIgzLjVi3tFNaYkkZ4VzgF1MxvSRT9YRa
pG0RDSFsdgfadgfasrty==
-----END CERTIFICATE-----' 
COMMENT 'AD Certificate';

Listing 12.3    SQL Example Adding the Active Directory LDAP Certificate to SAP HANA

Next, you’ll create a certificate personal security environment (PSE) and set its purpose to LDAP in SAP HANA. In the SAP HANA database, you’ll use the PSE to organize and store SSL certificates. To create the required LDAP PSE, execute the following SQL statements:

CREATE PSE LDAP_PSE; 
SET PSE LDAP_PSE PURPOSE LDAP;

You’ll then assign the imported certificate to this PSE, which is a two-step process. First, find the certificate ID of the certificate you just imported. You can run the following example SQL to identify the system-generated ID. Look for the comment we added when importing the certificate to properly identify it:

SELECT * FROM CERTIFICATES; /*Get Certificate ID*/

With the ID identified, you’ll then run the following example SQL to assign the certificate to the PSE collection:

ALTER PSE LDAP_PSE ADD CERTIFICATE 378500; /*Use Certificate ID from above*/

If everything is set up properly, you can validate the LDAP provider and authentication for a specific user, for example, JONATHHAU99, using the following example SQL statements:

VALIDATE LDAP PROVIDER ldap_ecorp CHECK USER JONATHHAU99 PASSWORD "NeverG0ing2Get!t";

If the user does not already exist in SAP HANA, you can validate that the LDAP provider would automatically create a missing user, for example, JIMGTO88 using the following example SQL:

VALIDATE LDAP PROVIDER ldap_edcorp CHECK USER CREATION FOR LDAP USER JIMGOT88 ;

12.3    Supported Third-Party Authentication Providers

SAP HANA supports several well-established, third-party authentication mechanisms for the purposes of SSO. This support simplifies the process of authentication within SAP HANA from trusted third-party applications. However, unlike with LDAP authentication, users cannot directly authenticate with their third-party passwords when using SSO. With third-party authentication, users aren’t required to manually reenter their user name and password each time they access resources within the SAP HANA platform. Instead, the SAP HANA system will trust that the external system has already properly authenticated the user and will therefore securely trust requests for the user from the external system. SAP HANA supports third-party system access via the HTTP, HTTPS, ODBC, and JDBC protocols, which allow for access to both web-based applications and data hosted in the SAP HANA platform. In this section, we’ll discuss several third-party authentication mechanisms, namely, Kerberos, SAML, X.509, SAP logon tickets, and SAP assertion tickets, and JWT identity providers, starting with Kerberos authentication.

12.3.1    Kerberos Authentication

Kerberos is a network authentication protocol based on work done at MIT dating back to the early days of networked computing. This protocol is designed as a robust protocol to protect against many forms of unauthorized access. This protocol uses strong cryptography, which makes it difficult to compromise. Because MIT released publicly available implementations of the protocol, and due to its robustness, Kerberos has been integrated into many computing systems over the years. One of the key integrations of Kerberos is its inclusion in Microsoft’s popular Active Directory solution. As a result, in almost every business environment using Microsoft Windows, when you log on to your desktop, you’re likely using a form of Kerberos authentication.

Kerberos relies on the principles of public/private key cryptography to achieve its robust exchange of identity information and it relies on a central authority to manage credentials. This central system is known as a key distribution center (KDC). At a high level, supported client applications request tickets from the KDC and then send them to SAP HANA as a form of authentication. Figure 12.7 shows a high-level overview of the Kerberos ticket exchange process facilitating authentication via SSO. In this example, you can assume that the client is the SAP HANA Studio application running on a user’s desktop.

Figure 12.7    High-Level Kerberos Ticket Exchange among Client, KDC, and SAP HANA

You can assume that the client shown in Figure 12.7 has already authenticated with a master source that supports Kerberos authentication. When attempting to access SAP HANA resources, the client obtains an encrypted Kerberos ticket from the KDC. This ticket is then routed to the client, decrypted with client credentials, and sent to the SAP HANA system, along with other information, and used for authentication. The SAP HANA system accepts the ticket and locates an SAP HANA user with a matching Kerberos identity. All effective privileges assigned to this SAP HANA user account are then validated as the client interacts with the SAP HANA system.

In most implementations today, the KDC is provided by Microsoft Active Directory services. This reliance on an external central authority can make the configuration of an end-to-end Kerberos solution somewhat cumbersome. Kerberos was developed in the era of desktop software, so it works well in conjunction with desktop tools like SAP HANA Studio and protocols like ODBC and JDBC. However, configuring Kerberos for Java-based applications and web-based applications can be difficult.

You can also use Kerberos for web-based SSO through several additional standards that integrate Kerberos into web browsers. These standards, although first introduced by Microsoft Internet Explorer, were later adopted by most modern web browsers. The XS engine and its web-based applications can leverage Kerberos with the Simple and Protected GSSAPI Negotiation Mechanism (SPNEGO) available in most modern browsers. For example, a client can log on to a personal computer, then, when the client accesses a trusted web application, the browser will use the initial logon credentials, obtain a ticket, and send the credentials to the web application for authentication.

Additional Resources and SAP Knowledge Base Articles (KBA)

For more technical details on Kerberos, we recommend the following resources:

  • MIT’s Kerberos project page (http://web.mit.edu/kerberos/)

  • The Kerberos Consortium (http://www.kerberos.org/)

  • Microsoft’s Negotiate and SPNEGO protocols (https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms995329.aspx)

Information pertaining to the configuration of Kerberos within the SAP HANA platform can be found in the following resources:

  • SAP HANA Administration Guide (http://s-prs.co/V498208)

  • SAP Note 1837331: Detailed Instructions for Kerberos Configuration (https://launchpad.support.sap.com/#/notes/0001837331)

  • SAP Note 1813724: Automation Tools to Assist with Kerberos Configuration (https://launchpad.support.sap.com/#/notes/1813724/E)

  • SAP Note 2303807: Smart Data Access: SSO with Kerberos and Active Directory (https://launchpad.support.sap.com/#/notes/2303807/E)

You can configure Kerberos identities for a user via the SAP HANA user management options or via SQL commands. For example, to configure a Kerberos identity for a user in the SAP HANA cockpit, open the user management interface, select a user in the list, and select the Edit option for the given user. In the user management tab of the SAP HANA cockpit, click the Authentication Mode tab, as shown in Figure 12.8, to enable Kerberos SSO, select the Kerberos checkbox. Then, provide the external Kerberos identity in the External ID field. The format of this identity should match the user principal name (UPN) attribute of the external user Kerberos system user account. This attribute is typically in the user@domain.com format, in which the user portion is replaced with the external system’s user name and domain.com is replaced with the external system’s domain name.

You can also use SQL statements to add a Kerberos identity to a user and to enable Kerberos support for a given user account, as follows:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ADD IDENTITY 'user@domain.com' FOR KERBEROS;
ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE KERBEROS;

The <USER_NAME> variable should be replaced with the name of an existing user account in the SAP HANA system. The string value following the IDENTITY statement should match the UPN from the external system; that is, the 'user@domain.com' string value will contain a value specific to an individual user’s UPN attribute in the external system. You should now have a basic understanding of the how Kerberos is supported within the SAP HANA system. Next, let’s look at how SAML authentication can be leveraged in a similar fashion.

Figure 12.8    Configuring a Kerberos Identity for a User Account

12.3.2    SAML Authentication

SAML is an authentication standard that comes from an open-source standards body called OASIS. One of SAML’s key benefits is that transporting authentication and security data occurs via simple XML messages, which makes implementing SAML support in applications quite straightforward.

SAML is somewhat different from Kerberos in that SAML has a much more decentralized architecture. This style of authentication solution is often referred to as a federated identity system. The solution is described as “federated” because a loose coupling of multiple systems cooperate with each other by exchanging authentication and authorization data. Instead of a single centralized system that manages all identity information (as with Kerberos), SAML can support multiple identity providers that manage the authentication of users from various parties.

In the SAP portfolio of products, the use of SAML is one example of SSO between SAP BusinessObjects Business Intelligence (BI) and SAP HANA. Although Kerberos is supported for SSO as well, the SAML configuration is significantly easier to implement and maintain. When using SAML with SAP BusinessObjects BI and SAP HANA as an end-to-end authentication solution, SAP BusinessObjects BI acts as the identity provider for the interaction. As a result, you won’t need to configure anything beyond the SAP BusinessObjects BI and SAP HANA systems to get the solution working. In addition, because SAP BusinessObjects BI is the identity provider, any users that have successfully authenticated with SAP BusinessObjects BI can then access data in SAP HANA using their SAML identity. This arrangement offers a wide degree of flexibility. You could authenticate with the SAP BusinessObjects BI platform via Kerberos, LDAP, or SSO and then access data in the SAP HANA system using SAML. Figure 12.9 shows an overview of the SAML authentication process.

The client shown in Figure 12.9 represents a user that authenticates with the SAP BusinessObjects BI system using assigned credentials. The SAP BusinessObjects BI system, which is serving as the identity provider (IdP), manages and validates these credentials.

Figure 12.9    High-Level SAML Authentication Process

The SAP HANA system is acting as the service provider (SP). If a trust relationship is defined between the two systems, a SAML identity is sent to the SAP HANA system, and the authentication is accepted. The user in the SAP BusinessObjects BI system can query the SAP HANA system as an identified user based on the SAP HANA user’s SAML identity. All effective privileges assigned to this SAP HANA user account are then validated as queries are issued by the SAP BusinessObjects BI system, which includes filter conditions required by any granted analytic privileges.

SAML is also a supported SSO mechanism for XS engine web applications. SAP HANA supports multiple SAML providers, allowing a variety of systems to perform SSO authentication for web-based applications hosted in SAP HANA. For example, support for ODBC/JDBC connections can be used to interact with the SAP HANA relational database management system (RDBMS). In theory, any vendor application can use SAML SSO when authenticating with SAP HANA. Keep in mind that the vendor is responsible for providing the integration between its application and SAP HANA’s SAML provider configuration.

Additional SAML Resources and Configuration Guides

For more technical details on SAML, refer to the following resources:

  • Technical overview of SAML (http://s-prs.co/v498209)

  • Complete SAML specification (http://saml.xml.org/saml-specifications)

For help configuring SAML SSO between SAP BusinessObjects BI and SAP HANA, review the following guides:

  • SAP BusinessObjects BI Administration Guide, Section 18.1.3.14: Implementing SAML SSO from SAP BusinessObjects BI to SAP HANA (http://s-prs.co/v498210)

  • SAML SSO for BI Platform to HANA (http://s-prs.co/v498211)

SAML identities can be configured for a user via SAP HANA’s user management options or via SQL commands. For example, you can use the SAP HANA cockpit. In the SAP HANA cockpit user management window, select the SAML checkbox to enable SAML SSO. You must then provide the external SAML identity by clicking the add SAML Identity link below the SAML checkbox, as shown in Figure 12.10.

Figure 12.10    Configure SAML Identity for User Account

In the Identity Provider dropdown list, choose an existing SAML identity provider configured in the SAP HANA system. Toggle the Automatic Mapping by Provider off to specific the external identity. In the External Identity field, enter the name of the user in the external system. Note that this value is case sensitive.

You can also use SQL statements to add a SAML identity to a user and to enable SAML support for a given user account, for example, the following statement:

ALTER USER <USER NAME> ADD IDENTITY '<SAML IDENTITY STRING>' FOR SAML 
PROVIDER <SAML PROVIDER>;
ALTER USER <USER NAME> ENABLE SAML;

The <USER NAME> variable should be replaced with the name of an existing user account in the SAP HANA system. The '<SAML IDENTITY STRING>' variable should match the user name found in the external system. The <SAML PROVIDER> should match the name of a SAML provider configured in the SAP HANA system.

Recall that you can also configure a single SAP HANA account to support all users in an external system. For this step, you’ll need to use the IDENTITY ANY clause, for example, in the following statement:

ALTER USER <USER NAME> ADD IDENTITY ANY FOR SAML PROVIDER <SAML PROVIDER>;

You should now have a basic understanding of the how SAML is supported within the SAP HANA system. Now, let’s look at how X.509 authentication can be leveraged in a similar fashion.

12.3.3    X.509 Authentication

X.509 is the standard for the public key infrastructure (PKI) implemented to manage digital certificates for the purposes of verification, encryption, and authentication in some cases. SAP HANA supports the use of X.509 certificates for SSO access to XS engine applications.

Root certificates can be generated from a trusted certificate authority (CA) and imported into the XS engine trust store and the SAP Web Dispatcher trust store. When XS engine applications are deployed, you can use the SAP HANA XS application administration tool to configure X.509 SSO support for that specific web-based application.

SAP HANA users can be configured with a specific X.509 identity, which can be configured using SAP HANA user management options or with specific SQL commands that add external identities to user accounts. For example, the following SQL code will enable X.509 authentication for a user and add an X.509 identity to the same user account:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE X509;
ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ADD IDENTITY 'CN=MyUserName, O=ecorp, C=com' 
ISSUER 'CN=ecert_so, O=ecorp, C=com' FOR X509;

The <USER_NAME> variable should be replaced with the name of an existing user account in the SAP HANA system. The string value in single quotes, following the IDENTITY statement should match the string value specific to the generated certificate. For example, the string value CN=MyUserName will contain a value specific to an individual user.

To complete the process, a client certificate is generated, related to the SAP HANA user identity, and imported into a client’s web browser. When a user attempts to access an XS engine application, the browser will ask the client to select a certificate for authentication. If the correct certificate is selected, the SAP HANA system will trust the client’s certificate, locate the associated user account with the corresponding X.509 identity and allow the client to interact with the XS application. Because the certificate was mapped to an existing user account, all granted privileges will be available during the session.

Additional Configuration Information

For additional configuration details, refer to the “Maintaining Single Sign-On for SAP HANA XS Applications” section in the SAP HANA Administration Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498212.

12.3.4    SAP Logon Tickets

SAP logon tickets act as digital credentials for authenticating an SAP system user with supported external systems. In the case of SAP HANA, logon tickets can provide SSO from SAP applications to XS engine web-based applications. For example, a user could log on to a web-based application hosted on an SAP NetWeaver Application Server (SAP NetWeaver AS). Within that application is a proxy link to an XS engine-based web application. The SAP NetWeaver-based application is configured to generate a logon ticket and store this ticket in the user’s browser as a temporary session HTTP cookie. The XS engine application is configured to support logon tickets. When the proxy link is clicked, the SAP HANA system finds the cookie in the browser and uses it to authenticate with the XS engine application.

Before the SAP HANA system will trust the logon ticket, external SAP application server certificates must be imported into the SAP HANA trust store. Once this trust is established, each SAP HANA user must be configured to support this authentication mechanism. The assumption is that the user ID found in the cookie will match the ID of a user configured in the SAP HANA system. Unlike Kerberos and SAML, no options are available for explicitly defining the external identities of users with logon ticket authentication enabled.

Additional Configuration Information

For additional configuration details, refer to the “Configure SSO with SAP Logon Tickets for SAP HANA XS Applications” section in the SAP HANA Administration Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498213.

The SAP HANA Security Guide also provides a few additional details about the configuration process. Look for the “Single Sign-On Using SAP Logon and Assertion Tickets” section: http://s-prs.co/v498214.

Each SAP HANA user account must be configured to support logon tickets. You can enable support for a user within the user management options in the SAP HANA cockpit or with SQL commands.

To enable logon tickets for a user in the SAP HANA cockpit, open the user management window. In the user management window, select the SAP Logon Ticket checkbox located just below the Kerberos configuration area, as shown in Figure 12.11.

Figure 12.11    Enable Logon Ticket in the SAP HANA Cockpit

To perform the same operation using SQL, execute the following command in the SQL console, replacing the <USER_NAME> variable with an SAP HANA user:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE SAP LOGON TICKET;

12.3.5    SAP Assertion Tickets

SAP assertion tickets work like logon tickets, with a few exceptions. The main difference is that assertion tickets are transmitted in an HTTP header from one application server to the next. In the case of SAP HANA, SAP credentials are obtained from the HTTP header, not from a session cookie. These tickets are configured to work with only one specific target system and have a fixed lifetime of 2 minutes. Once used, an assertion ticket is deleted. Most experts would argue that assertion tickets are somewhat more secure than logon tickets because of these factors. Outside of these differences, the assertion ticket process is like the logon ticket process.

An SAP HANA user account must be configured to support assertion tickets. You can enable support for a user with the user management options in the SAP HANA cockpit or with SQL commands.

To enable assertion tickets for a user in the SAP HANA cockpit, open the user management window. In the user management window, select the SAP Assertion Ticket checkbox, as shown in Figure 12.12.

Figure 12.12    Enable Assertion Ticket in the SAP HANA Cockpit

To perform the same operation using SQL, execute the following command in the SQL console, replacing the <USER_NAME> variable with an SAP HANA user:

ALTER USER <USER_NAME> ENABLE SAP ASSERTION TICKET;

12.3.6    JWT Identity Providers

JSON Web Token (JWT), sometimes pronounced “jot,” is an open standard (RFC 7519) that outlines a means for communicating security information between two parties using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) objects. SAP HANA uses this standard for the purpose of third-party SSO and authentication for the SAP HANA smart data access feature between two SAP HANA systems. Much like SAML, you must import a shared certificate within a PSE configured for the purpose JWT authentication.

When configuring the SAP HANA smart data access source, the SAP HANA system is registered as a JWT provider in the SAP HANA cockpit or via SQL commands. For the JWT provider, you’ll use the JWT claims setting to configure how the user will be identified. In most cases, you’ll use the ’user’ value in the JSON file that is transmitted. Certificates are shared between the two SAP HANA databases to protect and trust the exchange of credentials.

Additional Information on the Configuration of JWT for Authentication and SSO

Because this setup is only supported for a specific use case, we won’t go into further details in this chapter. Review the SAP HANA Administration Guide for SAP HANA Platform, especially the “Managing Single-Sign On (SSO) with JSON Web Tokens” section available at http://s-prs.co/v498215.

12.4    Case Study: Adding SAML Identity User Accounts

When originally implementing SAP HANA, E-Corporation created several hundred user accounts before deciding to implement SAML authentication. Now, the company needs a script that will update existing user accounts and add the appropriate SAML identities. In Chapter 4, we discussed how E-Corporation imported user data from a file and used stored procedures to provision users. That procedure could create new users and add their SAML identities, but it couldn’t perform the same action on existing user accounts. To remedy this situation, E-Corporation has decided to create a new stored procedure that will add SAML identities to existing accounts. The procedure will only add SAML identities for users that are listed in the Security.Tables::adusers table that don’t already have SAML identities.

The company has the following additional requirements for the stored procedure and the process needed to update user accounts programmatically:

  • User accounts will only be updated with a SAML identity if they have a record in table Security.Tables::adusers. This table is populated with user attributes obtained from an external system.

  • The user account’s internal basic authentication password won’t be changed; users can continue to use internal basic authentication and SAML authentication for SSO.

  • The user account’s internal basis authentication password lifetime will comply with the configured password policy at E-Corporation.

To create the repository-based stored procedure in SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench editor, right-click the Security.Provisioning package and choose New • HDB Procedure.

The New Stored Procedure window will appear. In the File Name* field, enter “ADD_SAML_TO_EXISTING_USERS,” using uppercase letters. In the schema field, enter or choose Security_tables. Click Create to save the file and open the ADD_SAML_TO_EXISTING_USERS.hdbtable configuration file for editing. A blank template will appear and can be used as a guide when defining the procedure.

To define the ADD_SAML_TO_EXISTING_USERS repository-based stored procedure in SQL, use the syntax shown in Listing 12.4. Activate the design-time script by pressing (Ctrl)+(S).

PROCEDURE "security_tables"."Security.Provisioning::ADD_SAML_TO_EXISTING_USERS" ( ) 
  LANGUAGE SQLSCRIPT
  /* Procedure invoker must have privileges to create users */
  SQL SECURITY INVOKER
  AS
   BEGIN
/*Use a Cursor for future use. The following only 
loops one time based on each record from SQL statement */

 DECLARE CURSOR c_users_list FOR
/* Find Active Users in SAP HANA that have no SAML Identity. If the
User is listed in the security table, add SAML Identity */
/* We need to escape the single quote mark around 
SAMUSER and EMAILADDRESS with three single quote 
marks ''' a total of 4 are needed */

SELECT 
UT.AD_USER_NAME, 
upper(UT.USER_NAME) as HANAUSER, 
'''' || UT.AD_USER_NAME || '''' as SAMUSER
FROM  "security_tables"."Security.Tables::adusers" UT
WHERE upper(UT.USER_NAME) IN 
    (SELECT upper(USER_NAME) FROM "SYS"."USERS" WHERE USER_NAME NOT IN 
       (SELECT USER_NAME FROM "SYS"."SAML_USER_MAPPINGS") ) 
and UT.ACCOUNT_STATUS = 'A';

 FOR cur_row as c_users_list DO
    --- Add SAML identity to user
    EXEC 'ALTER USER ' || cur_row.HANAUSER || ' ADD IDENTITY ' 
        || cur_row.SAMUSER || ' FOR SAML PROVIDER TEST_SAML_PROVIDER';
    --- Enable SAML Authentication for the user account
    EXEC 'ALTER USER ' || cur_row.HANAUSER ||' ENABLE SAML';
   
 END FOR;
 
END;

Listing 12.4    Syntax for Stored Procedure to Create Users

The script uses a cursor to generate a list of users based on existing user accounts in the system with matching active records in table Security.Tables::adusers. The cursor query also validates that the users don’t already have SAML identities. After validation, the script loops through the user list, executing two ALTER USER statements: The first ALTER USER statement adds the SAML identity listed in table Security.Tables::adusers. The second ALTER USER statement enables the SAML identity for the user. The script can be executed in the SQL console as needed using the following SQL command:

call "security_tables"."Security.Provisioning::ADD_SAML_TO_EXISTING_USERS"();

12.5    Summary

Authorization through the granting of privileges allows the SAP HANA system to determine permissible actions for a given user. However, before the system determines authorizations, the user must authenticate with SAP HANA. SAP HANA provides a basic internal authentication mechanism that supports password authentication. SAP HANA also supports external authentication providers, such as Kerberos, SAML, and X.509 certificates. External providers can only be used for the purposes of SSO with the JDBC, ODBC, or HTTP protocols.

13    Certificate Management and Encryption

Protect the data transmitted to and from SAP HANA, as well as the data stored in SAP HANA, is vitally important. In this chapter, we’ll discuss SAP HANA’s offerings for stronger security: communication encryption and data-level encryption to prevent unauthorized access to the system and its data.

In addition to authorization and authentication, you’ll also need encryption to protect your SAP HANA systems. Encryption starts with the management of Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) certificates. You then must enable communication encryption between clients and the SAP HANA system. Finally, you must also encrypt the persistent storage volumes that contain a copy of the in-memory data. In this chapter, we’ll discuss these encryption stages. Using and enabling encryption is an excellent way to protect data within SAP HANA.

13.1    SSL Certificates

X.509 is the standard for the public key infrastructure (PKI) implemented to manage digital certificates for the purposes of verification, encryption, and in some cases authentication. SAP HANA supports the use of X.509 certificates for securing both internal and external communication protocols.

In general, we refer to communication protocol security as Transport Layer Security (TLS) or, historically, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). You’ll often hear both referred to as SSL protocols. The goal of SSL protocols within SAP HANA is to secure the communication channel between a client and the SAP HANA platform.
