In the last step, the transport administrator will access the target SAP HANA application lifecycle management instance and pull the delivery unit from the source to the target.

As a reminder, you can access SAP HANA application lifecycle management using a URL specific to each instance, as follows:

  • https://<host_name>:43<instance number>/sap/hana/xs/lm

  • https://w5-3db-hana01.e-corp.root.local:4300/sap/hana/xs/lm

Or, if SSL isn’t configured:

  • http://<host_name>:80<instance number>/sap/hana/xs/lm

  • http://w5-3db-hana01.e-corp.root.local:8000/sap/hana/xs/lm

On the SAP HANA application lifecycle management instance Home page, you’ll see a series of tiles. Just above the tiles is a menu bar, as shown in Figure 14.10. The third tab in that menu bar is Transport; click this tab to start the transport process.

Figure 14.10    SAP HANA Application Lifecycle Management Home Page

The transport management window has three main tabs or menu options just under the main menu bar. The System tab is selected by default, and the Transports and Logs tabs are available as well, as shown in Figure 14.11.

Figure 14.11    Transport Management Window and System Option

Before the transport process can begin, you must register a source system in the SAP HANA application lifecycle management instance of the target system. To register a new system, click the + Register button just below the submenu bar. The Register System window will appear, as shown in Figure 14.12.

Figure 14.12    Register System Window in SAP HANA Application Lifecycle Management

In this window, enter the Host of the source SAP HANA instance. Enter the TCP/IP port for the source SAP HANA instance’s XS engine in the XS Engine HTTP(S) Port field. The Comment field is optional. Click Next once you’ve entered the correct information. A new window will appear labeled Configure Destination. This window explains that you must configure the connection and authentication details specific to the source SAP HANA instance. To configure these details, click the Maintain Destination button to open a new window titled HTTP Destination Details.

In this window, specify the connection details for the source system. Click the Authentication Details menu option to open its configuration page. On the Authentication Details page, click the Edit button at the bottom right. Now, you can specify the authentication details for the source. The most common option is to select the Authentication type of Basic. You can then use the User and Password fields to specify the logon credentials for the source system. The source system service account used will need the sap.hana.xs.lm.roles::Transport role granted at a minimum. Once the credentials are entered, click the Save button located at the bottom right. Close the HTTP Destination Details window by clicking the X located in the top-right corner of the window. Click Finish on the Register System window. Your source system should now be registered in the transport system list.

The next step in the process is to define a transport route. To create the transport route, click the submenu item titled Transports, as shown in Figure 14.13.

Figure 14.13    Transport Management Window and Transport Option

To create a new transport route, click the + Create button. The Create Transport Route window will appear, as shown in Figure 14.14.

Figure 14.14    Create Transport Route Window

Enter the Name of the transport route and choose the Source System. The Source System dropdown list will only contain registered systems. The target system value is fixed and can’t be changed. In the Content section, select the Delivery Units radio button and then select one or more source system delivery units to transport. Click the Create button at the bottom right.

With the transport route defined, you can now start the transport process, as shown in Figure 14.15. To transport a delivery unit, select the transport route in the list 1. Once selected, start the transport process by clicking the Start Transport button 2.

Figure 14.15    Selecting Transport Package and Starting Transport Process

Once the Start Transport button is clicked, the Start the Transport window will appear to confirm the start action. Click the OK button to start the transport process. The window will disappear, and you’ll return to the transport route-listing page.

To view the status of the transport request, click the submenu item labeled Logs. You’ll see the current and historical status of transports initiated within the system. If any issues have arisen, the Status column will show a red triangle. If the transport is complete, the Status column will show a green square.

14.3.2    Exporting a Delivery Unit to a File

In addition to using SAP HANA application lifecycle management to export a delivery unit in Section 14.2.3, you can also use SAP HANA Studio. This functionality is not available in the SAP HANA cockpit, so we’ll explain how SAP HANA Studio can be used in this chapter. SAP HANA Studio provides an interface to export a delivery unit to a compressed file. This compressed file can be imported back into the SAP HANA repository later. Developers often use this export process to serve as a backup of their code. However, this functionality also can be used for lifecycle management, even though SAP HANA application lifecycle management is the preferred tool to manage transports between SAP HANA instances.

To start the process, switch to the administration console perspective within SAP HANA Studio. From the menu bar, choose File • Export. The Export window will appear. Within the Select an Export Wizard section, expand SAP HANA Content, and then choose Delivery Unit. Click Next to continue. The Select Source System window will appear. In the list of systems, select the system that will serve as the source of the delivery unit. Click Next to continue. The Export Through Delivery Unit window will appear with the subtitle Select Delivery Unit. This window is used to specify the delivery unit export options, as shown in Figure 14.16.

Figure 14.16    Export Options in SAP HANA Studio

In this window, use the Delivery Unit dropdown list to choose the delivery unit for export. The export tool will include all development artifacts associated with the packages listed in the section labeled List of Packages. However, you also have the option of exporting development artifacts based on their activation date. Use the Filter by time checkbox to enable the time-based filters. With the Filter by time checkbox selected, choose a Time Internal using the provided dropdown list. The dropdown list provides the following intervals: Last Week, Last Month, and Time Range. Choose Time Range to specify custom From and To dates.

When exporting the delivery unit file, you can choose to place the file on the server or download the file to SAP HANA Studio’s client system. Typically, you’ll export to the client system because most developers don’t have access to the SAP HANA server’s file system. Click Export to Client in the Export Location section. In the Location field, specify the local file path where the delivery unit file will be downloaded. The File Name field will be prepopulated with a file name based on the current time, system, and delivery unit name. You can change the name, but be sure to retain the file extension .tgz. Click Next to continue. A Summary page will appear with an overview of the export settings. Click Finish to start the export process. Once completed, a file will appear in the configured path. Once created, the file can be used as a backup or as an import source.

14.3.3    Importing a Delivery Unit from a File

In addition to using SAP HANA application lifecycle management to import a delivery unit in Section 14.2.3, you can also use SAP HANA Studio. This functionality is not available in the SAP HANA cockpit, so we’ll explain how SAP HANA Studio can be used in this chapter. SAP HANA Studio provides an interface to import a delivery unit file into a package repository. The tool will import all development artifacts found in the file and activate them within the repository. The file can be imported into an SAP HANA instance, assuming that the export source and import source share a similar SAP HANA software version.

To start the import process, switch to the administration console perspective in SAP HANA Studio. From the menu bar, choose File • Import. The Import window will appear. Within the Select an Import Wizard section, expand SAP HANA Content and then choose Delivery Unit. Click Next to continue. A new popup window will appear titled Target System. In the list of systems, select the system that will serve as the import target for the delivery unit file. Click Next to continue. The Import Through Delivery Unit window will appear, as shown in Figure 14.17.

Figure 14.17    Import Options in SAP HANA Studio

To configure the import options, start by choosing the import file location. Choose the Client location for files stored on the SAP HANA Studio client system. Click the Browse button to specify the path of the file. In the Actions section, choose from the following options: Select the Overwrite inactive versions checkbox to import the delivery unit content even if another version of the content already exists in the target. Select the Activate objects checkbox to have the import wizard activate the newly imported development artifacts. If this option isn’t selected, the objects will be imported without activation.

In the Activate Mode dropdown list, decide how the wizard should handle inconsistencies. The Activate and ignore the inconsistencies in affected objects mode will activate the objects directly found in the delivery unit file even if their activation causes existing development artifacts to become inconsistent. The Stop activation in case of inconsistencies in affected objects option will stop the activation process if any inconsistencies are detected during import. The default option is to Activate and ignore the inconsistencies in imported objects and in their affected objects. With this option selected, the import wizard will attempt to activate development artifacts found in the delivery unit file even if some of the artifacts and their affected objects fail to import.

The Object import simulation section contains a listing of the development artifacts that will be imported. In addition, you’ll see the anticipated activation status based on a review of the target repository. Note that objects might fail to import even if the simulation indicates that no errors will arise. Click Finish to import the objects.

To monitor the status of the import job, locate the Job Log tab, as shown in Figure 14.18, which will appear at the bottom of the window once the import process is started. Within the Job Log tab, the import job type name will be listed as Import (Delivery Unit). Use the Status column to determine the import status.

Figure 14.18    Job Log Tab in SAP HANA Studio

If errors arise, double-click the Job Status row to open the Job Details window, which will provide a detailed import status for each development artifact included in the delivery unit. Identified issues will need to be resolved, and the import process will need to be repeated once issues are resolved.

14.4    Additional Options in SAP HANA Application Lifecycle Management

In addition to the management of delivery units and the transportation of delivery units between systems, SAP HANA application lifecycle management offers a few other features that might benefit the lifecycle management of security-related artifacts. SAP HANA application lifecycle management provides the ability to use a change recording mechanism and also supports the Change and Transport System (CTS). Let’s take a closer look at each of these options.

14.4.1    Change Recording

Change recording is an option you can enable in the SAP HANA repository. When enabled, the initial activation of a development artifact will need to be assigned to a change list or change ID until the change list is released. The purpose of the change list is to track changes within a development artifact. Recall that artifacts are assigned to a package and that packages are assigned to a delivery unit. When change recording is enabled, delivery unit changes aren’t available for transport until they’re confirmed and released within the change management interface of SAP HANA application lifecycle management. Thus, you can’t transport a change until its individual revision is confirmed and the change list is released using the change management area of SAP HANA application lifecycle management.

When change recording is enabled, your organization will have a middle layer within the transport process. This middle layer requires that all changes be approved before they’re transported or even exported to a delivery unit file. Without change tracking, a delivery unit would be composed of the most recent changes each time the transport process executes or each time a delivery unit file exports from SAP HANA Studio. All objects within the delivery unit and package would need to be transported even if they weren’t ready. Change tracking allows the transport manager to reassign changes to different change lists. For example, let’s assume that a delivery unit contains five development artifacts. One of the five artifacts must be promoted to QA as soon as possible. However, the remaining four artifacts haven’t been validated. The transport manager can reassign the one artifact needed in QA to a new change list and then approve and release the change list for transport, thus allowing the transport manager to transport individual development artifacts within a package and delivery unit if needed.

14.4.2    Using the Change and Transport System

The Change and Transport System (CTS) is a utility that organizations often use to manage the lifecycle of a traditional SAP NetWeaver Application Server (SAP NetWeaver AS). CTS facilitates the promotion of development projects in the ABAP Workbench. Although independent applications, SAP HANA application lifecycle management offers integration with the CTS. When this integration is enabled, your organization can use the tools and processes available from the CTS to manage the promotion of native SAP HANA development artifacts between SAP HANA instances.

14.5    Summary

Managing the full lifecycle of a security model is vital for eliminating potential security vulnerabilities from your landscape. For an SAP HANA security model, the lifecycle management process involves the use of software tools, adherence to policies, and adherence to procedures. You’ll use tools such as SAP HANA application lifecycle management to ensure consistency within the model between environments. You’ll develop policies and procedures to properly test and audit your security design.

15    Auditing

Implementing a security model is just the beginning. You’ll also need to set up rules to record and track select changes made within the SAP HANA system. In this chapter, we’ll discuss SAP HANA’s internal auditing mechanism for recording and tracking changes by user name, client address, and other attributes.

Auditing allows organizations to configure rules that record important activities conducted within the SAP HANA system. For example, administrators can record any SQL statement issued containing the ALTER ROLE or GRANT ROLE syntax. These details are recorded to a log that can be reviewed as needed. In this chapter, we’ll discuss why you need auditing within SAP HANA. We’ll also discuss the steps required to enable auditing and define policies to record critical activities. Finally, we’ll walk you through a case study in which you’ll create auditing rules to track important changes within the SAP HANA landscape.

15.1    Why Do You Need Auditing?

From a technical standpoint, auditing on its own doesn’t protect the SAP HANA system from unauthorized access. However, auditing can, in many instances, determine the source of unauthorized access. In addition, auditing can serve as a deterrent to users who may want to fraudulently change the data or maliciously harm the system’s integrity. You need to implement auditing with SAP HANA for many reasons, such as the following:

  • Provide accountability
    When auditing is enabled, your organization will have accountability for the configuration, security, and object changes made within the SAP HANA system. This information can be used for a variety of purposes. Most importantly, auditing can provide your organization with insight into the events that lead to changes within the SAP HANA system. Organizations often must grant administrators significant access to the SAP HANA system. When auditing is enabled and set up properly, users understand that their actions are being recorded, making them accountable for any changes they implement.

  • Regulatory compliance
    Many organizations are subject to several regulatory compliance measures. These measures often require that systems like SAP HANA not only remain secure but also have specific auditing measures in place. Audit logs and audit rules are principal requirements for most regulations. Auditing doesn’t prevent a security breach, but it can help authorities identify the source of the breach.

  • Discourage incongruous actions
    When enabled, auditing discourages others from performing unauthorized or malicious actions within the system. The auditing mechanism records actions by user name and records information about the computer used to make the change, such as IP address, host name, and operating system user name. This information can help identify the true source of actions executed within the SAP HANA system.

  • Monitor suspicious activity
    When auditing is enabled, your organization could set up monitors that probe the audit log data for suspicious activities. For example, monitors can be developed to search for multiple sequential failed logon events. Multiple consecutive failed logons from a single source could indicate that someone is attempting to gain unauthorized access to the SAP HANA system. Monitoring the logs might be an organization’s only mechanism to stop a breach before sensitive data is stolen or the system is compromised.

  • Improve processes and procedures
    Audit log data can be reviewed to ensure that administrators are following proper procedures. For example, you can set up events to track instances in which privileges are assigned directly to a user account. If policy mandates that a user account should only be granted roles, not privileges, you can query the audit logs to make sure your administrators are following this rule.

  • Gauge system utilization and concurrency
    Audit log data can be queried to determine the frequency and concurrency of user actions. This data is helpful from a system sizing and maintenance standpoint. For example, you can use the audit log data to determine the number of concurrent users querying the system. You can also use this information to determine the best time for system maintenance.

  • Database forensics
    In the event of a security breach or fraud, audit log data can provide forensic information related to the source and scope of the breach. In the event of fraud, a properly configured audit system can identify the source and scope of changes that were made to the SAP HANA system.

  • Chronological audit trail
    When auditing is enabled and configured properly, your organization will have a way to review changes made by users chronologically. This level of information is critical to investigations of fraud and malicious activities. Without this level of detail, suspicious and fraudulent activities can be conducted without accountability.

15.2    Configuring Auditing

By default, SAP HANA auditing is not enabled, nor are systems configured to capture specific events within SAP HANA. To enable and configure auditing, SAP HANA offers several interfaces. The most commonly used interfaces are within the SAP HANA cockpit and the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager. However, you can also use SQL statements to configure audit policies. Let’s look at each of these three approaches in more detail.

15.2.1    Enable Auditing with the SAP HANA Cockpit

The SAP HANA cockpit provides a graphical user interface (GUI) where you can manage auditing is an SAP HANA database. To access the security manager, log on to your SAP HANA cockpit and connect to the desired database. Click the Auditing tile. Within this tile, click the Auditing header to access the Auditing interface.

In the Auditing interface, you’ll see several options and links. Figure 15.1 shows an overview of the auditing interface home screen. If auditing is enabled, you’ll see existing defined audit policies. In the following sections, we’ll look at each of these options and links in detail before moving on to a discussion of auditing levels.

If auditing is not already enabled for the system, you’ll see the Enable Auditing button on the right. Click this button to enable auditing. If auditing is already enabled and you wish to disable it, the button will labeled Disable Auditing. Again, click this button to disable auditing.

Notice the Audit Policies, Configuration, and Audit Trail tabs. The Audit Policies tab is the default link selected from the homepage of the interface. Under this tab, you’ll see a list of defined audit policies. The Configuration link interface will appear differently if you’re connected to a system database versus a tenant database in a multiple database container (MDC) configuration. MDC is the default for SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 01. When connected to a system database, the Configuration tab will show options for the Overall Audit Trail Target plus options to record different alert levels to different targets. Assuming we’re connected to a system database, let’s look at the audit trail target options in more detail.

Figure 15.1    Auditing Interface Home Screen in the SAP HANA Cockpit

15.2.2    Audit Log Targets and Options in the SAP HANA Cockpit

Audit targets refer to the location where SAP HANA will record audit policy events. SAP HANA provides a robust set of targets and options to record audit events. Let’s look at the available targets, namely the syslog, database table, CSV file, and kernel trace, in more detail. We’ll also discuss some available options for recording audit levels to one or more audit targets.

Syslog

Operating systems that run SAP HANA have a secure central location to which events can be written, called a syslog. This location can contain audit logs and other event data from software packages running on the Linux operating system (OS). When the Syslog (Default) option is chosen, configured audit event rules will record activity within the operating system syslog. Your organization should use this option when events need to be collected in the syslog, but you must also ensure that the syslog is configured properly and is operational. SAP HANA will discard events if events can’t be written to the OS-level syslog. The syslog could also be altered without the SAP HANA system knowing. For example, the log can be cleared by an operating system with access to the syslog files.

Database Table

Events can also be written to a table hosted within the SAP HANA instance. In most cases, using the internal Database Table option for SAP HANA audit logging is best. When this option is selected, audit events are recorded to the system table SYS.AUDIT_LOG. Because the data is written to a database table, SQL SELECT statements can be crafted to analyze the data. For example, you can use the following SQL statement to query the audit log table for actions executed by a specific user within SAP HANA:

SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_LOG WHERE USER_NAME = 'ADMIN_JHAUN';

This table only allows SELECT statements. For example, users cannot insert, update, or delete audit log records regardless of their privileges. To clear the audit log, a user must have the AUDIT OPERATOR system privilege and also issue a specific SQL command to delete entries within the audit log. The following example SQL command will clear the audit log of all records before the specified date:

ALTER SYSTEM CLEAR AUDIT LOG UNTIL '2016-01-01 23:59:59';

When this statement is executed, a mandatory system-generated event is recorded in the audit log, indicating the source and user account that issued the statement. This event is recorded after the log is truncated. This event must be recorded because it may be evidence that a particular user attempted to delete suspicious activity.

CSV File

Events can also be written temporarily to a CSV file. When this option is selected, the events are written to a file using the directory specified in the Directory Name field. This field is found just below the Audit Trail Target field. The specified path is local to the SAP HANA host operating system. This option should only be used temporarily for testing purposes because these CSV files are not secure. If a directory name isn’t specified, audit logs will be written to the default trace file path in SAP HANA. Users with access to the trace files will also have access to this audit log CSV file.

Kernel Trace

You can also specify that events are written to the SAP HANA database kernel trace. The kernel trace file is managed by the SAP HANA system and contains other trace information relevant to the SAP HANA database. This option should only be used at the direction of SAP Support.

Audit Level Trail Targets

When defining an audit rule, its audit level can be classified as Emergency, Critical, Alert, Warning, or Info. We’ll discuss these levels further in Section 15.3.1. However, events classified as Emergency, Critical, or Alert can be directed to one or more targets. To configure these alternative target locations, you’ll need to configure the options found in Configuration tab. Figure 15.2 shows these options, just below the Overall Audit Trail Target field for a connected system database.

For each listed alert level, you can define one or more targets using the provided checkboxes. If you choose not to define this section, alerts will be recorded based on the options configured for each audit policy or they will default to the Overall Audit Trail Target setting.

Figure 15.2    Audit Level Trail Targets Configured in Configuration Section

This option is particularly useful when you need to record important events to multiple target locations. For example, some organizations might want to record events to the audit table and the syslog because they use third-party software to monitor the Linux syslog. You can configure alert, emergency, and critical events for all three possible target locations. For example, you can configure emergency alerts to be written to the audit table, the syslog, and a CSV file on the operating system.

15.2.3    Viewing Audit Logs in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The Audit Trail tab will open an interface where you can view recorded audit policy events targeted the SAP HANA audit option Database Table. The interface list records events, as shown in Figure 15.3. This section will not list audit events recorded to CSV, syslog, nor the kernel trace.

Figure 15.3    Viewing Audit Events in the Audit Table Using the SAP HANA Cockpit

You can also use this interface to truncate or delete recorded audit events. As shown in the top right of Figure 15.3, you’ll see a link titled Delete Audit Events. When you click this link, the Delete Audit Events window will appear. To truncate the audit table, you have three options: Use the Older than option to delete events older than the number of days entered into the provided Days field. Use the Before option to delete audit events recorded before the date entered in the provided field. Use the All Entries option to delete all audit event history. Note that a user must be granted the AUDIT OPERATOR system privilege to perform this action.

Once you’ve specified the desired options, press the Delete button to delete the audit events. Use the Cancel button to discards your changes.

Now that we’ve reviewed the options and workflows necessary to enable auditing and to define audit targets within the SAP HANA cockpit, let’s briefly review how these options can be configured in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the SAP HANA extended application services, classic model engine (XS engine).

15.2.4    Enabling Auditing with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface to configure SAP HANA auditing.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. To use this tool, a user must have the sap.hana.xs.ide.roles::SecurityAdmin role at a minimum. The following two URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

  • http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

In the last example, replace <sap_hana_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, you’ll see a series of buttons located to the top-left of the GUI’s ribbon. The icon depicting a vertical key and server opens the security console; click this icon to open the Security Console tab on the right side. Click the Auditing tab to reveal audit configuration options. The options and interface are nearly identical to those found in SAP HANA Studio, with a few exceptions. Figure 15.4 shows an example of the security console with the auditing options visible.

To enable auditing, use the Auditing Status dropdown list and choose Enable. Specify the Audit Trail Target using the dropdown list. Based on our testing using SAP HANA 1.0 SPS 12 and SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, the Audit Level Trail Target settings aren’t working in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench; these settings will have to be maintained using the SAP HANA cockpit (Section 15.2.1).

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench has a few differences from the SAP HANA cockpit. First, the truncate database table audit trail icon (pink eraser) is in the icon bar just below the Audit Policy settings. Click the icon to open a popup window where you can specify the end date for the audit event truncation. Also, in this icon bar, note the table icon to the right of the log truncation button. When clicked, the table icon will open a new window that launches the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench catalog interface and its web-based SQL console. The console will be prepopulated with an SQL statement that queries the audit log table. Note that this option, though available, was not working in SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04 during our testing. In Section 15.3.1, we’ll also discuss how audit policies can be individually configured with a specific audit trail target. For example, you can specify that a particular audit policy should output information to a CSV file.

Figure 15.4    Managing Auditing Settings in the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

15.2.5    Enabling Auditing with SQL

In addition to using the GUIs, users with INIFILE ADMIN system privilege can also use ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION SQL scripts to configure the auditing mechanism within SAP HANA. Using a script is helpful if you need to ensure that all SAP HANA systems within your landscape use the same settings.

To enable auditing, you’ll need to update the setting for enabling the audit configuration (global_auditing_state) in the global.ini file. Execute the following SQL code to set the value to true:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'global_auditing_state') = 
'TRUE' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

To specify the audit trail type, you’ll need to update setting for specifying the audit trail type (default_audit_trail_type) in the global.ini file. The setting name has three options: CSTABLE, SYSLOGPROTOCOL, and CSVTEXTFILE. To use the system database table, execute the following SQL code:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'default_audit_trail_type') = 
'CSTABLE' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

To write events to the Linux syslog, use the SYSLOGPROTOCOL option, and to use a CSV file as the target, use the CSVTEXTFILE option.

When using the CSV file option, you should also specify a secure path where the CSV file will be stored. To specify the path, update the path setting (default_audit_trail_path) in the global.ini file. For example, you can execute the following SQL code to specify that the audit log CSV file use the path /usr/sap/HDB/HDB00/auditlog:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'default_audit_trail_path') = 
'/usr/sap/HDB/HDB00/auditlog' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

You can also use SQL to define custom audit log targets based on levels. You can choose from among alert, emergency, and critical audit levels. Three specific global.ini file settings are used for the auditing configuration: emergency_audit_trail_type, critical_audit_trail_type, and alert_audit_trail_type. For example, execute the three SQL statements shown in Listing 15.1 to specify custom audit targets for the alert, emergency, and critical audit levels.

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'emergency_audit_trail_type') = 'CSTABLE, SYSLOGPROTOCOL, CSVTEXTFILE' WITH RECONFIGURE ; 

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'critical_audit_trail_type') = 
'CSTABLE, SYSLOGPROTOCOL' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'alert_audit_trail_type') = 
'CSTABLE, SYSLOGPROTOCOL' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

Listing 15.1    SQL Statements for Configuring Custom Audit Targets

Simply enabling auditing isn’t sufficient. You must also define audit policies to track specific events within the SAP HANA system. In the next section, we’ll discuss how audit policies are configured.

15.3    Creating Audit Policies

As mentioned earlier, auditing is disabled by default within the SAP HANA system. In addition, no custom audit policies are included out of the box. Audit policies can be defined to track specific events based on specific conditions. Audit policies are defined by an audit administrator based on your organization’s requirements. In an ideal situation, your organization would record every event within its SAP HANA system. However, recording all events to an in-memory database is costly, both financially and architecturally. Therefore, you must configure specific audit policies to record only events that are critical to the security and stability of the system.

Even after auditing is enabled globally, most events won’t be recorded until specific audit policies are defined, although SAP HANA does have several mandatory audit policies that cover events specific to the audit mechanism itself. For example, if you disable auditing, change auditing settings, or truncate the audit logs, these events will be recorded in the default target location even if no policies are defined. A user must have the AUDIT ADMIN system privilege to define audit policies.

Most actions within the SAP HANA system can be audited. Audit policies are comprised of a combination of specific actions, an action status, and a user performing the action. The action status is based on one of three status options: successful, unsuccessful, or all.

Some actions can only be activated if they reference one or more user accounts. In addition, policies can also be enacted for all users except specified users. If an action doesn’t require a referenced user, the assumption is that the action applies to all users within the system. Furthermore, some actions also require a referenced catalog object. For example, you must reference a user and a catalog object when defining audit policies with data manipulation actions.

Before we review the makeup of an audit policy and the various tools used to define them, let’s look at the 16 different categories of actions that can be audited. In the following section, we’ve outlined these categories and provided a few examples of the specific actions they encompass.

15.3.1    Components of the Audit Policy

An audit policy is comprised of an audit action, audit action statuses, audit levels, target object(s), target user(s), and a trail target. In the following sections, we’ll look closer at each of these items.

Actions Available for Auditing

Twenty different categories of actions can be monitored within SAP HANA. Most of the actions within these categories directly correspond to the SQL statements executed to perform actions related to the category. Within each category, you’ll find a variety of actions that can be configured and selected. Most audit policies can only be defined using actions from the same action category. In addition, some actions within each category can range from broad to specific. To better understand the types of actions that can be audited, let’s review the twenty categories:

  1. All actions
    The all actions category includes a single audit action by the same name. This action must be mapped to specific users or excluded from specific users. When enabled, all actions within the system will be audited based on the configured audit action status and selected user. In general, you don’t want to enable this rule for many users because this rule can negatively influence the performance of the system. You should limit this category to events that don’t occur often. For example, this category can be used as a universal policy to capture all unsuccessful events for all users except the system accounts. In this case, the system will record any action by a user when he isn’t authorized to perform the action. A policy referencing all actions must be mapped to specific users or must be mapped to a list of excluded users. This category can’t be universally applied to all users in the system.

  2. Application auditing
    The application auditing category can be selected for auditing events and actions taking place in SAP HANA XSA applications. Application deployed in the SAP HANA XSA can be configured to record events to the SAP HANA XSA audit log service. This service records events in the SAP HANA database audit system.

  3. Authentication provider management
    The authentication provider category can be selected when you want to audit events and actions related to Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), or JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication providers. Any changes to these providers can be recorded as well as when these providers are created.

  4. Audit configuration
    The audit configuration category can be selected when you want to specifically record when an audit policy is disabled or enabled within a tenant database by a user with sufficient access.

  5. Backup deletion
    The backup deletion category includes only the BACKUP CATALOG DELETE action. This action is useful for monitoring users that delete backup catalog entries and files. Policies with this action do not have to be assigned to specific users.

  6. Certificate and PSE store
    The certificate and personal security environment (PSE) store category includes all ALTER, CREATE, and DROP SQL actions related to the management of the PSE or certificates within the SAP HANA system. Policies with this action do not have to be assigned to specific users.

  7. Client-side encryption
    The client-side encryption category records events when client-side encryption is created, altered, or dropped for a given table column. Client-side encryption is a feature where data within a column can be encrypted and subsequently only decrypted when a client has the proper key pair to view it.

  8. Data definition
    The data definition category includes almost all CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and RENAME SQL actions that can be performed against a catalog object. Catalog objects include tables, views, schemas, indexes, and triggers, among others. The actions listed in this category are specific to particular catalog objects. For example, you’ll find CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE PROCEDURE, and CREATE actions for most catalog objects in this category. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users.

  9. Data provisioning
    The data provisioning category includes ALTER, CREATE, DROP, and PROCESS REMOTE SUBSCRIPTION EXCEPTION commands related to external adapters, agents, and remote subscriptions. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users.

  10. Data query and manipulation
    The data query and manipulation category includes all SQL actions performed against a specific target catalog object. These actions are related to SQL commands such as DELETE, EXECUTE, INSERT, SELECT, and UPDATE. For example, you can record actions when a user issues a SELECT statement against a specific table or all objects in a schema. Basing the rules on a schema is beneficial for auditing all catalog objects within the schema. The actions selected are not specific to any particular catalog object type, but you must specify the target object and target user when defining the policy. To avoid any negative performance impacts, audit policies based on these rules should be limited.

  11. Volume encryption
    The data volume encryption category includes all SQL actions related to the ALTER command against application, data, and log encryption. This category also includes the ALTER command used to change the root key backup password. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users.

  12. Granting and revoking authorizations
    The granting and revoking authorizations category contains actions specific to the use of SQL commands such as GRANT and REVOKE. These commands are used to grant or revoke privileges to users or roles. The system will only capture instances in which a user is the grantee of the privilege. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

    Note that most organizations use repository-based roles within their security model. Actions in this category won’t capture granting and revoking repository-based roles. Organizations will need to set up policies that monitor the execution of the stored procedures within the _SYS_REPO schema. For example, a data and query manipulation action must be set up to monitor the execution of the _SYS_REPO.GRANT_ACTIVATED_ROLE stored procedure.

  13. License deletion
    The license deletion category contains one action, which can be used to audit instances in which the SAP HANA license key is removed from the system. For example, if a user executes the SQL statement UNSET SYSTEM LICENSE within the SQL console or uses the SAP HANA Studio GUI to delete the license key, this action will be recorded as an event. Policies with this action do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

  14. License installation
    The license installation category contains one action, which can be used to audit instances in which an SAP HANA system license key is added to the system. For example, if a user executes the SQL statement SET SYSTEM LICENSE within the SQL console or uses the SAP HANA Studio GUI to install a new license key, this action will be recorded as an event. Policies with this action do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

  15. Operations on multitenant database containers
    The operations on multitenant database containers category records activities within the system database related to tenant databases. Actions such as ALTER, CREATE, DROP, RENAME, START, and STOP can all be recorded.

  16. Repository content operations
    The repository content operations category contains actions specific to importing, exporting, and activating development artifacts within the SAP HANA repository. Policies using these actions must specify one or more user accounts to either include or exclude from the policy. It’s important to limit the scope of these actions because they might negatively affect the performance of the system.

  17. SAP HANA dynamic tiering
    The SAP HANA dynamic tiering category contains actions specific to the management of dynamic tiering. These policies are only necessary when dynamic tiering is installed and enabled within the SAP HANA cluster. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

  18. Session management and system configuration
    The session management and system configuration category contains actions related to session management, stopping services, and system configuration changes. In most cases, these actions should be included in any audit policy. For example, you’ll need to record any system configuration changes and any instances in which a user’s session is terminated. Note that configuration changes related to auditing do not require a policy defined with these actions. Audit changes are system-mandatory and always will be recorded. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

  19. Structured privileges management
    The structured privileges management category contains actions specific to the management of repository analytic privileges and catalog structured privileges. Structured privileges are catalog objects used to restrict access to information views and catalog views. When restricting an SAP HANA information view, these privileges are called analytic privileges, but they are still technically structured privileges.

    Note that the system account _SYS_REPO will be recorded in the audit logs as the action user when a repository analytic privilege is changed or created. To properly audit repository-based analytic privileges, you’ll also need to enable actions within the repository content operations category using a separate policy rule. Both actions will have the same timestamp, which can be used to correlate the two events. Policies with these actions do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

  20. User and role management
    The user and role management category contains actions specific to actions that alter, drop, or create a user account or standard role. For example, when a user is created, these events can be included in a policy to capture the action within the audit logs.

Note that these actions do not audit repository-based roles. Organizations will need to enable actions within the repository content operations category using a separate policy rule to monitor the creation of repository-based roles. Policies with this action do not have to be assigned to specific users or target objects.

Audited Action Status

In an ideal scenario, organizations would audit all actions within the SAP HANA system. Unfortunately, auditing all actions can affect the performance of the system negatively and can lead to a significant increase in memory consumption based on the growth of the audit log table. Therefore, audit rules must be defined based on necessity. Fortunately, you can specify several conditions when defining audit policies; one such condition is the audit action status.

When defining an audit policy, you can choose from one of three status options. When a user is authorized to perform an action, the status of the action will be successful. Audit policies can be defined to capture only successful actions, or you can define an audit policy based on instances in which a user was prevented from performing an action. In these instances, the status of the account would be labeled unsuccessful. You can use this status to capture only actions carried out by users that are not authorized to perform them. It’s important that you monitor unauthorized access because it’s often a leading indicator that someone is attempting to compromise the system or data. As a third option, you can also choose to audit both successful and unsuccessful audit status with the all audit status.

Audit Levels

When defining an audit policy, you can choose to assign our audit policies to one of the following audit levels: Emergency, Critical, Alert, Warning, or Info. As mentioned in Section 15.2.1, the first three levels are useful when Audit Level Trail Targets are implemented. Overall, they can also be used to classify the severity of the action that was audited. For example, you can establish a policy configured with an audit level of Emergency. Because this value is written to the audit log, the audit event can be easily identified.

Target Objects

When defining an audit policy that uses actions from the data query and manipulation and procedure execution categories, you must also choose a target object. Target objects are catalog objects within the SAP HANA system. If you choose a schema object, all objects within the schema will be subject to the audit rule. If you choose an individual table, view, index, sequence, or procedure, only changes to the selected object will trigger an audit policy. Within each individual audit policy, you can specify one or more target catalog objects.

Target User

When defining an audit policy, you have the option to specify one or more users. When a user is selected, the audit policy will only be triggered for the selected users. Some policies require that target users be specified before they are activated. However, all policies can be configured based one or more users. The policy also supports the use of rules by which all users are audited except those selected, which is helpful when you want to ignore activity created by system user accounts. Note that some policy actions support all users. If a user isn’t included or excluded from the policy, the policy assumes that it applies to that user.

Audit Trail Target

On a per audit policy basis, you can override the global audit target settings, which is helpful when you need to capture specific events to a particular target. For example, you can capture all SELECT statements issued to a schema and store them in a CSV file, which can be loaded to a database and analyzed for capacity planning or load analysis purposes.

15.3.2    Managing Policies with the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench

The SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, hosted within the XS engine, provides an interface to define audit policies.

You can access the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench via a supported Internet browser. To use this tool, a user must have the sap.hana.xs.ide.roles::SecurityAdmin role at a minimum. The following two URLs can be customized to match the details of your environment:

  • http://sap-hana.myhost.com:8000/sap/hana/ide/security

  • http://<sap_hana_host>:80<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

In the last example, replace <sap_hana_host> with the host name of the SAP HANA system in your environment and <instance_number> with the two-digit instance number corresponding to your SAP HANA system.

For secure access, the following examples should help you construct the correct URL:

  • https://<sap_hana_host>:43<instance_number>/sap/hana/ide/security

  • https://sap-hana.myhost.com:4300/sap/hana/ide/security

Once you have access to the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security manager, you’ll see a series of buttons located at the top left, in the ribbon. The vertical key and server icon opens the Security Console tab on the right. Click the Auditing tab to open the audit policy management interface.

At the bottom of the Auditing tab, you’ll see a section titled Audit Policies, as shown in Figure 15.5.

Figure 15.5    Interface to Define One or More Audit Policies

Under the Audit Policies label, you’ll see four icons. The plus icon (+) lets you define a new audit policy. The X icon deletes a selected audit policy. The pink eraser icon deletes audit events from the audit log. The final icon is a table with a green gear overlay. You can use this icon to open the SQL console where you can query the audit log table or execute SQL commands.

To define a new audit policy, click the plus icon (+). A new row will appear in the audit policy table. To begin the process, enter a unique name for the policy within the Policy column using the Enter Name cell. In the Policy Status column, click the down arrow within the cell and select Enable from the options. In the Audited Actions column, click the icon within the cell that contains two stacked boxes to open a new window, Edit Actions Audited by Policy. In this window, you can choose from some of the available audit actions by category. Select the actions that need to be audited; remember that the selected actions must be from the same category. When finished, click the OK button located at the bottom right.

Within the Audited Actions Status column, click the down arrow located to the right of the cell. Choose Successful, Unsuccessful, or All. Within the Audit Level column, click the down arrow located to the right of the cell. Choose Emergency, Critical, Alert, Warning, or Info.

In the Users column, click the two stacked boxes icon within the cell. The Select Users window will appear. Use the options in the window to search for one or more existing users. Once users are located, click the Add button located between the Matching Items list and Selected Items list to add the selected users to the right side of the window. Choose Include Selected Users in policy or Exclude Selected Users from policy above the Selected Items area. Click OK once you’ve selected users to include or exclude. Note that most actions don’t require that you select a user. When this field is left blank, the system assumes that the policy should be applied to all users. If the policy won’t activate without a user, you can assume that the policy action requires a referenced user.

If the audit policy uses actions from the data query and manipulation and procedure execution categories, you must also choose a target object. Within the Target Object cell, click the two stacked boxes icon. The Target Object window will appear. Within the search box, enter the name of the catalog object that will serve as the target for the audit policy. Click the OK button found in the bottom right once you’ve completed your selections.

If you want to define specific audit targets for the audit policy, use the cells in the Audit Trail Target column to define additional targets. Within the Audit Trail Target cell, click the two stacked boxes icon. The Select Targets window will appear. Select the checkbox for each audit target location. Click the OK button to continue.

Once the audit policy is defined, to save the audit policy settings, click the large disk icon on the main icon bar to save the changes or press (Ctrl)+(S).

In addition to defining audit policies this way, you can also use SQL commands, as we’ll discuss in the next section.

15.3.3    Managing Audit Policies with SQL

You can also use SQL statements to define SAP HANA audit policies. Using SQL isn’t as easy, but this scripting option can help you apply a consistent audit policy throughout your SAP HANA landscape. SQL script can be executed with the SQL console found in most management tools in SAP HANA. We’ve found that the GUI-based tools are at inconsistent times and don’t always support all audit policy options, but the SQL options support all possible audit configurations.

When creating an audit policy, use the generic SQL syntax shown in Listing 15.2.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY <POLICY NAME> 
AUDITING <STATUS> <ACTIONS>
ON <CATALOG OBJECTS>
FOR | EXCEP FOR <USER LIST>
LEVEL <LEVEL> 
TRAIL TYPE <TRAIL>;

Listing 15.2    SQL Template for Defining an Audit Policy

The <POLICY NAME> variable will be replaced with the name of the policy. The <STATUS> variable should be replaced with SUCCESSFUL, UNSUCCESSFUL, or ALL. The <ACTIONS> variable should be replaced with the syntax specific to the action being audited; for example, you can specify one or more actions, such as CREATE USER, ALTER USER, or ALTER ROLE.

Note

The syntax of all possible actions is quite extensive and can be found in the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide, in the “CREATE AUDIT POLICY Statement reference” section.

You can download the guide from http://s-prs.co/v498219.

The ON clause and the <CATALOG OBJECTS> variable are required for data manipulation actions. The <CATALOG OBJECTS> variable should be replaced with the fully qualified name of the catalog object.

The <USER LIST> variable can contain a comma-separated list of user accounts in the system. The FOR and EXCEPT FOR syntax is optional for most audit actions. The <LEVEL> variable can be replaced with EMERGENCY, ALERT, CRITICAL, WARNING, or INFO. The <TRAIL> variable can be replaced with TABLE, SYSLOG, or CSV.

To better understand the SQL syntax, let’s review a few complete SQL examples. To audit the management of standard roles, you can create an audit policy titled MANAGE ROLE with the following code:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE, DROP ROLE
LEVEL INFO;

To audit the management of user accounts, you can create an audit policy titled MANAGE USER with the following code:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER
LEVEL INFO;

To monitor instances in which the stored procedures in the _SYS_REPO schema are executed, you can create an audit policy using the SQL code shown in Listing 15.3.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL 
EXECUTE ON 
"_SYS_REPO"."*"
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.3    Creating a Policy Named GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS

To monitor all unsuccessful actions for all users except system account users, you can create a policy using the SQL code shown in Listing 15.4.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" 
AUDITING UNSUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
EXCEPT FOR 
_SYS_DI, _SYS_AFL, _SYS_XB, _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY, 
_SYS_TASK, _SYS_STATISTICS, _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER, 
_SYS_REPO, _SYS_ES, _SYS_EPM, _SYS_DI_TO, _SYS_DI_SU, 
_SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CATALOG, 
_SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG 
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.4    Creating a Policy Named ALL ACTIONS

When an audit policy is created using SQL, the audit policy disabled by default. To activate the policy, you’ll need to issue an ALTER AUDIT POLICY SQL statement. For example, you can issue the following SQL statement to enable an audit policy named ALL ACTIONS:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" ENABLE;

To disable an audit policy, you can issue the following SQL statement:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS" DISABLE;

To delete an audit policy, you must use a DROP AUDIT POLICY SQL statement. For example, you can delete the ALL ACTIONS policy as follows:

DROP AUDIT POLICY "ALL ACTIONS";
SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide

The complete syntax used to drop and alter audit policies can be found online in the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide. Look for the “ALTER AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control)” and “DROP AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control) sections.

The complete syntax used to create audit policies can be also be found in this guide. Look for the “CREATE AUDIT POLICY Statement (Access Control)” section.

Using SQL to define and manage audit policies is helpful for applying a consistent audit policy through the SAP HANA landscape. In the next section, we’ll briefly review how audit policies can be created in the SAP HANA cockpit.

15.3.4    Creating Policies with the SAP HANA Cockpit

The SAP HANA cockpit provides a GUI interface where you can manage auditing in an SAP HANA database. To access the security manager, log on to your SAP HANA cockpit and connect to the desired database. Click the Auditing tile. Within this tile, click the Auditing header to access the Auditing interface.

In the Auditing interface, look for the Audit Policies tab, as shown in Figure 15.6.

To define a new audit policy, click the Create Audit Policy link located above the list of defined audit policies. A new interface will appear with a two-step option that will eventually morph into a four-step process. In the first step, 1. Name, enter the name of the audit policy in the provided file, and a new button labeled Step 2 will appear. Click the Step 2 button to proceed to the next step.

Figure 15.6    Audit Policy Area in the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 2. Audited Actions and Action Status, will appear, as shown in Figure 15.7. On this page, you can configure the Audited Action Status and the specific audit action by category for the policy. Notice that you can search for a category or action using the Search box located over the listed audit events. Once an action is selected, the Step 3 button will appear. Click this button to proceed to the next step.

Figure 15.7    Configuring the Audit Action Status and Audit Policy Action within the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 3. Audited Users, will appear, as shown in Figure 15.8. Select an option for the under Select the users to be audited by the policy section. If you need to audit a specific user or several users, search for the user in the provided list and select the checkbox for each user to be audited. Click the Step 4 button below the list to proceed.

Figure 15.8    Configuring Audit Policy Target Users within the SAP HANA Cockpit

The next step, 4. Audit Trail, will appear, as shown in Figure 15.9. In this step, you’ll configure the Audit Level setting for the policy.

Figure 15.9    Configuring the Audit Policy Audit Trail in the SAP HANA Cockpit

For a system database, you can configure one or more audit trail targets. For a tenant database, you can only choose the default trail target configured for the database. Click the Step 5 button to continue.

The final step, 5. Policy Status, allows you to choose to Enable or Disable the policy when saving, as shown in Figure 15.10. Click the Review button to go to a summary screen and review each individual setting and then click the Save button at the bottom once you’re ready to activate the policy.

Figure 15.10    Configuring the Audit Policy Status in the SAP HANA Cockpit

Once saved, you should now see the policy listed in the audit interface of the SAP HANA cockpit. To edit the policy after creation, click on the policy name in the list to option the policy details. Click the Edit button on the top right of the overview screen. With edit mode enabled, you can change the Policy Status, Audited Action Status, and Audit Trail Target options. In the Audited Actions section, as shown in Figure 15.11, you can delete actions by clicking the X within a circle icon to the right of each action. You can add additional actions by clicking the Add Actions button located on the top right side.

Figure 15.11    Interface for Modifying an Existing Audit Policy in the SAP HANA Cockpit

You’ll follow a similar process when modifying Audited Objects and Users Included in Policy section. Once your changes are completed, click the save button at the bottom right of the window.

You should now have a strong understanding of the components that make up an audit policy. In addition, you should have a strong understanding of how policies are configured using the SAP HANA Web-Based Development Workbench security console, the SAP HANA cockpit, and SQL statements. In the next section, we’ll review various system views that contain audit-specific data.

15.4    Querying Audit Data

You can query three main system views that are related to audit data and the auditing configuration within SAP HANA. These views are useful for a variety of purposes. The three views are AUDIT_ACTIONS, AUDIT_LOG, and AUDIT_POLICIES and are all located in the SYS schema.

Note

For more information on each of these views, refer to the SAP HANA SQL and System View Reference Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498219.

  • AUDIT_ACTIONS
    The audit actions view provides access to a listing of all possible auditable actions within the SAP HANA system. This view provides a listing of audit actions and flags to indicate actions that require a user or catalog object reference. This view is useful when you need to see a listing of supported audit actions. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:

    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_ACTIONS;

  • AUDIT_LOG
    The audit log view provides access to all recorded actions based on enabled audit policies. When an audit policy is enabled, events are written to the hidden system table _SYS_AUDIT.CS_AUDIT_LOG_. The audit log view references this system table. Administrators can create a variety of audit-related queries referencing this system view, and the view contains several columns. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:

    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_LOG;

  • AUDIT_POLICIES
    The audit policies view provides a complete listing of all audit policies defined within the system. This view can be queried to determine the quantity and scope of audit policies defined within the SAP HANA system. Note that a single policy might have multiple records within the view; each record represents a unique configuration option. For example, if you reference multiple users in the policy, a record for each user will be represented in this view. To query the view, issue the following SQL statement:

    SELECT * FROM SYS.AUDIT_POLICIES;

The views listed in this section are useful when your organization needs to examine the data that is collected from auditing and the configuration of the auditing mechanism itself. In the next section, we’ll walk you through a case study that outlines the decision-making process E-Corporation used when defining its audit policies. We’ll also show you the SQL the company used to define its audit policies.

15.5    Case Study: Defining Audit Policies

E-Corporation recently enabled auditing within the SAP HANA landscape. Its internal audit group determined that capturing audit events for the purposes of regulatory compliance and best practices was necessary. E-Corporation contacted its SAP HANA security consultant and requested help reviewing and implementing proposed audit policies. Thus, E-Corporation listed its requirements followed by its consultant’s recommendations, which we’ll review in the following sections. The consultant will use SQL statements to define the exact policy recommended.

E-Corporation requires that the audit policy be configured to facilitate proactive event monitoring, audit reporting, authentication actions, unauthorized access, system change, security management, and super user events. Let’s look at each requirement in detail.

15.5.1    Proactive Event Monitoring

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that the SAP HANA audit system support external tools that can proactively mine the system’s audit logs. These tools will require Open Database Connectivity (ODBC) and Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) access to the audit log tables.

Solution

Audit policies should be configured to support events that can be proactively monitored. These events include, but are not limited to, failed logon events, unauthorized actions, excessive query access to the system, and other activities. In addition, events will need to be recorded to the internal SAP HANA database table to allow these events to be available via JDBC or ODBC connections and via SQL queries. Most monitoring tools support this type of access.

15.5.2    Audit Reporting

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all audit log data be accessible using the ODBC and JDBC protocols.

Solution

Audit events must be recorded to the internal SAP HANA database table, which will allow these events to be available via JDBC or ODBC connections and via SQL queries. Most reporting tools support this type of access.

15.5.3    Authentication Auditing

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all connection and disconnection attempts are recorded within the audit logs. However, E-Corporation doesn’t want to record authentication attempts made by internal system accounts.

Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy be created to record these activities to table AUDIT_LOG within SAP HANA. An audit policy titled USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT will be created to monitor all SUCCESSFUL connections and subsequent disconnection actions performed by standard users. Unsuccessful attempts won’t be recorded in this policy because they’ll be captured in a subsequent audit policy. The policy won’t record events for system-generated accounts.

The policy will be defined using the SQL code shown in Listing 15.5.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT" 
AUDITING SUCCESSFUL CONNECT, DISCONNECT SESSION 
EXCEPT FOR 
     _SYS_AFL,
     _SYS_DI,
     _SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG,
     _SYS_DI_SU,
     _SYS_DI_TO,
     _SYS_EPM,
     _SYS_ES,
     _SYS_REPO,
     _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER,
     _SYS_STATISTICS,
     _SYS_TASK,
     _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY,
     _SYS_XB,
     SYS_XS_SBSS 
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.5    SQL Code to Create Policy Named USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT

To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "USER CONNECT AND DISCONNECT" ENABLE;

15.5.4    Unauthorized Action Auditing

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all unsuccessful actions be recorded to the audit logs. Users with a high number of unsuccessful actions within a given day are to be questioned immediately. A high number of unsuccessful actions often indicates that someone is trying to compromise the system’s security using their own account or someone else’s account.

Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy named ALL FAILED ACTIONS be created to record this activity to table AUDIT_LOG within SAP HANA. The policy will be configured to record all UNSUCCESSFUL actions performed within the system.

The policy will be defined using the SQL code shown in Listing 15.6.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALL FAILED ACTIONS" 
AUDITING UNSUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
EXCEPT FOR 
_SYS_DI, _SYS_AFL, _SYS_XB, _SYS_WORKLOAD_REPLAY, 
_SYS_TASK, _SYS_STATISTICS, _SYS_SQL_ANALYZER, 
_SYS_REPO, _SYS_ES, _SYS_EPM, _SYS_DI_TO, _SYS_DI_SU, 
_SYS_DI_SEARCH_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CDS_CATALOG, _SYS_DI_CATALOG, 
_SYS_DI_BI_CATALOG 
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.6    SQL Code to Create Policy Named ALL FAILED ACTIONS

To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALL FAILED ACTIONS" ENABLE;

15.5.5    System Change Auditing

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all system configuration changes be recorded to the audit logs. These events should also be set up using the EMERGENCY level so that they’re easily identified within the audit logs. In addition, these events should be written to a CSV file stored in a secure directory in the operating system.

Solution

The security consultant recommends that an audit policy titled ALTER SYSTEM be created to record this activity to table AUDIT_LOG table and a CSV file within SAP HANA. The policy will be defined using the following SQL code:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ALTER SYSTEM" 
AUDITING ALL SYSTEM CONFIGURATION CHANGE 
LEVEL EMERGENCY
TRAIL TYPE CSV, TABLE;

Note that the SQL code uses a LEVEL of EMERGENCY and a TRAIL TYPE of both CSV and TABLE. To activate the policy, the following SQL statement must be executed:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ALTER SYSTEM" ENABLE;

Because the policy will record such events to a CSV file, the system needs to be configured with a new default audit trail CSV file path. A directory was created within the path /usr/sap/HB5/HDB00/auditlog/, which will store audit trail files containing system configuration changes. No other audit rules within the system will use the CSV file option. To configure the CSV file path within SAP HANA, the following SQL statement must be executed:

ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') 
   SET ('auditing configuration', 'default_audit_trail_path') = 
'/usr/sap/HB5/HDB00/auditlog/' WITH RECONFIGURE ;

15.5.6    Security Management Task Auditing

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all security-related activities be recorded to the audit log, including the management of users, roles, and repository roles, as well as granting and revoking of privileges and roles to other users.

Solution

The security consultant recommends that a series of audit policies be created to record this activity to table AUDIT_LOG within SAP HANA. The audit policies MANAGE ROLE, MANAGE USER, GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS, GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES, ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES, and ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS will be created.

The MANAGE ROLE policy will record all attempts to create, alter, or drop roles within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation’s standard policy is to create repository-based roles, and such roles would not be covered using this policy. However, this policy will identify security administrators that are not following policy. In addition, their actions related to standard roles will be recorded. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE, DROP ROLE
LEVEL INFO;

The MANAGE USER policy will record all attempts to create, alter, or drop users within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation allows security administrators to create users within the system. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" 
AUDITING ALL CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER
LEVEL INFO;

The GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS policy is designed to record the use of stored procedures within the _SYS_REPO schema. These procedures are used by security administrators and give them the ability to grant privileges to repository-based objects, including repository-based roles. These procedures should be closely monitored because repository object privileges are always granted by _SYS_REPO regardless of the user executing these procedures. To create the policy, the SQL code shown in Listing 15.7 must be executed.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL 
EXECUTE ON 
"_SYS_REPO"."*"
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.7    SQL Code to Create Policy Named GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS

The GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES policy will record all attempts to grant or revoke privileges within the SAP HANA system. E-Corporation’s standard policy is to create repository-based roles, and privileges within repository-based roles are granted or revoked by the system account _SYS_REPO. However, this policy will identify security administrators that are not following policy. In addition, their actions related to the granting and revoking of privileges will be recorded. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES" 
AUDITING ALL GRANT ANY, REVOKE ANY 
LEVEL INFO;

The ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES policy will record any attempts to create, alter, or drop structured privileges within the SAP HANA system. Because these privileges provide data-level security, auditing these privileges is important. Note that classic repository-based analytic privileges will be created, altered, and dropped by the system account _SYS_REPO. To create the policy, the SQL code shown in Listing 15.8 must be executed.

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES" 
AUDITING ALL 
ALTER STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE, 
CREATE STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE, 
DROP STRUCTURED PRIVILEGE 
LEVEL INFO;
CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL ACTIVATE REPOSITORY CONTENT 
LEVEL INFO;

Listing 15.8    Two SQL Statements to Create ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS and ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES Policies

The ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS policy is required to capture the true source of changes related to repository roles and other repository-based objects. When a repository object is activated, many auditing events will record that the _SYS_REPO user performed a series of actions. To properly correlate those actions to an actual user, you must ensure that all repository activations are also audited. In this way, you can know the identity of the user that initiated the actions carried out by the _SYS_REPO user. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" 
AUDITING ALL ACTIVATE REPOSITORY CONTENT 
LEVEL INFO;

Once created, the policies will need to be activated. To activate these policies, the SQL shown in Listing 15.9 must be executed.

ALTER AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE ROLE" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ANALYTIC PRIVILEGES" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE PRIVILEGES" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "MANAGE USER" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "GRANT OR REVOKE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;
ALTER AUDIT POLICY "ACTIVATE REPOSITORY OBJECTS" ENABLE;

Listing 15.9    Seven SQL Statements to Activate Seven Audit Policies

15.5.7    Super User Event Auditing

Requirements

E-Corporation requires that all users with elevated privileges have all their actions recorded. Super users at E-Corporation have user names prefixed with ADMIN_. Every month, the audit team will query the audit logs to make sure that super user activities fall within the acceptable usage requirements for their given responsibilities.

In addition to super users, E-Corporation requests that all actions performed using the SYSTEM user account be recorded. This account is typically disabled and only used when necessary.

Solution

The SUPER USER AUDIT policy is required to record the SUCCESSFUL actions of all super users set up within the SAP HANA system. UNSUCCESSFUL actions will be recorded by the ALL FAILED ACTIONS policy. To create the policy, the following SQL code must be executed:

CREATE AUDIT POLICY "SUPER USER AUDIT" 
AUDITING SUCCESSFUL ACTIONS 
FOR SYSTEM, ADMIN_JHAUN, ADMIN_PETER, ADMIN_BOB
LEVEL INFO;

Once the policy is created, the following SQL must be executed to activate the policy:

ALTER AUDIT POLICY " SUPER USER AUDIT " ENABLE;

The policies recommended by the SAP HANA security consultant will grant E-Corporation better insight into the critical actions that take place within its SAP HANA system, help E-Corporation remain compliant with many regulations, and help E-Corporation manage compliance with its own internal policies.

15.6    Summary

A critical component of any SAP HANA security model, auditing allows your organization keep users accountable to policies and procedures related to security and system changes. Auditing can help your organization proactively identify unauthorized access attempts. Finally, auditing can help your organization reconstruct events after a security breach has occurred.

Within an SAP HANA landscape, auditing should be enabled, and specific audit policies should be implemented to protect the security and stability of the system.

16    Security Tracing and Troubleshooting
