A list of installed applications will appear, as shown in Figure 18.2. The name of the application will appear in the first column, and the URL used to access the application will appear on the far-right column.

To access the xsa-cockpit application, locate it in the list of applications. Note the URL and port needed to access the application. As shown in Figure 18.2, we’ll use the following partially masked URL:

https://##hana-01:51030

Figure 18.2    Listing SAP HANA XSA Applications and URL with Port Information

Enter this URL into a supported browser. For this book, we’re using the Chrome browser to access the application. The web application will redirect you to the SAP HANA XSA login. Enter credentials with access to the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. Once loaded, you’ll land on the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen, as shown in Figure 18.3.

Figure 18.3    Homepage of the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

The interface is divided into two panes. On the left is an accordion menu with options for managing Organizations, Security, Tenant Databases, Host Management, User Management, and More. On the right side are additional options specific to each item selected within the accordion menu.

18.2.2    Managing SAP HANA XSA Users

To create and manage SAP HANA XSA users, click the User Management menu option, as shown in Figure 18.4. On the right, you’ll see a list of users that have already been configured in the SAP HANA XSA system. These users correspond to users in the tenant database or SYSTEMDB that operates SAP HANA XSA. However, only the user account and password apply within SAP HANA XSA security. SAP HANA database roles, granted to these same users, have no bearing on their access within the SAP HANA XSA platform. SAP HANA XSA uses a separate application role security mechanism to determine application-level authorizations. We call these SAP HANA XSA role collections.

To create a new user, click the New User button located just above the list of users, as shown in Figure 18.4. A new window will appear requesting the User Name, First Name, Last Name, E‐Mail, and Password. Enter the requested information for the new user and then click the Create button. Click the Migrate SAP HANA User button to import an existing user within the associated SAP HANA tenant or SYSTEMDB. The new or existing user will now be listed in the interface.

Figure 18.4    SAP HANA XSA Cockpit User Management Interface

Next to each user is a series of icons. Click the pencil icon to edit the existing user’s name and email address. Click the key icon to manage the user’s password. Click the trashcan icon to delete the user from SAP HANA XSA and the database.

18.2.3    Managing SAP HANA XSA Role Collections

To manage role collections, click the Security option within the accordion menu to reveal the Role Collections option. On the right side of the interface, you’ll see a listing of existing role collections, as shown in Figure 18.5.

Figure 18.5    SAP HANA XSA Role Collection Management Interface

Role collections are comprised of elements defined within the SAP HANA XSA application at design time using the xs-security.json file. This file is added to the application’s project via SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. Within this file, each application will have an application identifier or xsappname again defined in the xs-security.json file. Application roles are also defined in the xs-security.json file within the scopes section. The description of each scope item will be presented as a role when defining a role collection within the SAP HANA XSA cockpit.

Finally, scope items will be organized into role templates (role-template section) within the xs-security.json file. Again, these items will be presented to you when defining the role collection in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. However, note that the actual SAP HANA XSA application roles and role templates are defined by the developer and configured within the xs-security.json file that is part of the overall design-time SAP HANA XSA code and project.

More Information on Defining Roles within an SAP HANA XSA Application

For more information on defining roles and roles templates within your SAP HANA XSA application, refer to the SAP HANA Developer Guide for XS Advanced Model, available at http://s-prs.co/v498220.

The “Assign Functional Authorization Scopes for an XS Advanced Application” section provides more details on the structure of the xs-security.json file.

To define a role collection, click the New Role Collection button. The New Role Collection window will appear. Enter the name and a description for the role collection. Click Save and the role collection will now be present in the list.

To add SAP HANA XSA application roles to the role collection, locate the collection in the list and click its name. A new interface will appear where you can add SAP HANA XSA application roles. Click the Add Role button. The Add Role popup window will appear. Using the cascading Application Identifier, Role Template, and Role dropdown lists and locate an application role for the collection, as shown in Figure 18.6. Click the Save button once you’ve located the role.

Figure 18.6    Defining a Role Collection within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

You can delete the assigned application role from the list by clicking the trashcan icon located on the right of each assigned role. No general save button for the role collection is available when viewing the role list. Once you click save in Add Role popup window, as shown in Figure 18.6, the role is considered assigned to the role collection. To navigate back to the list of role collections, click the Home button at the top part of the interface on the right side. To delete a role collection, click the trashcan icon to its right. To edit a role collection, click the pencil icon to its right within the list, as shown in Figure 18.5.

To grant or revoke a role collection associated with a user, return to the User Management interface found within the accordion menu of the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen. Locate a user within the list. To the right of the user, within the list, click the user and padlock icon. The Assign Role Collections : <USER> window will appear, as shown in Figure 18.7. Click the Add button within the popup window and then use the search bar to filter the list. Select the checkbox to the left of each desired role collection. Click the OK button to assign the role collection to the user. You’ll return to the Assign Role Collections : <USER> popup window.

Figure 18.7    Granting or Revoking a Role Collection Associated with a User in the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

To delete an assigned role collection, locate it in the Assign Role Collections : <USER> popup window and click the trashcan icon to its right. Click the Save button to activate the assigned role collections for the given user.

18.2.4    Managing Organization and Space Access

Developers will need to be assigned access to an organization or a space within an organization allowing them to create a container and deploy design-time content within an HDI container. To create and manage organizations and spaces, click the Organizations menu option from the SAP HANA XSA cockpit Home screen, as shown in Figure 18.8. Locate an existing organization on the page. A separate tile will be created for each organization, with the title of each tile being the organization. Click the organization tile to drill into the configuration options and spaces associated with it.

Figure 18.8    Managing Organizations and Spaces in SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

When you click into the organization, the accordion menu changes on the right and includes new menu options for the organization. Click the Members menu option. A list of organization members will appear. To add a new member, click the Add Members button. When adding a member, you can grant one of two privileges. The first privilege is the organization manager, which grants full access to the organization and all spaces within the organization. Select the checkbox beside the Organization Manager role to grant it to the member. Grant the organization auditor role for members that only need read access to the organization and all spaces within the organization. Modify the assignments by using the pencil icon to the right of each listed member. You can also delete a member by clicking the trashcan icon to the right of each member.

To access the spaces within the selected organization, click the spaces button in the accordion menu to the right. Spaces within a selected organization will be displayed as tiles on the right side of the interface. Click the name of a space to drill down into the space options. Again, the accordion menu will change to show options specific to the management of spaces. Once again, click the Members menu item in the space-specific accordion menu. A list of existing members will appear on the right, as shown in Figure 18.9.

Figure 18.9    Managing Members within a Space Using the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit

Use this interface, shown in Figure 18.9, to add members and space-specific role assignments. Three space roles are available. A space manager will have the ability to change various options for a given space using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit or other available interfaces. The space developers role grants a member the ability to manage applications and services deployed to the space. For example, a developer needs this access to use this space within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to build a project or deploy it to its runtime HDI container. The space auditors role allows a member to view the configuration of the space without the ability to make changes. Developers cannot deploy runtime content with this role. Again, be sure you understand that SAP HANA XSA users will often need access to an organization or space within to deploy applications based on that space. Also, organization and space access is managed independently of application access granted with role collections.

You should now understand how users, organizations, spaces, and role collections are managed within the SAP HANA XSA platform using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. Note that SAP HANA XSA role collections and SAP HANA XSA application roles are decoupled from the SAP HANA database. Thus, developers cannot deploy applications that are runtime without to proper access to a space. Next, we’ll review another important tool that developers use in the SAP HANA XSA platform from a security standpoint, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

18.3    Working with SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, a web-based application hosted within the SAP HANA XSA platform, is used by developers to create applications for the SAP HANA XSA platform. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA can also be used by developers to create SAP HANA database catalog objects, SAP HANA calculation views, SAP HANA core data services (CDS) artifacts, and SAP HANA XSA-based repository roles. From a security perspective, you can use SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to manage roles deployed within a specific HDI container. As an SAP HANA and SAP HANA XSA security administrator, you must understand the role of this tool and the steps required to grant developers access to it. In the next section, we’ll provide an overview of the tool and the components that govern its security.

18.3.1    SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Overview

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA is deployed within the SAP HANA XSA platform. Before you can access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, you’ll need to verify a few items. First, when SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA 2.0 is installed to the SAP HANA XSA platform, the deployment does not create role collections in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. You must log on to the SAP HANA XSA cockpit and create two new role collections. You only need to do this once in most cases. For example, you can create the role collections shown in Table 18.1.

Role Collection Name

Application Identifier

Included Role/Role Template

ZXS_WEBIDE_ADMIN

webide!i1

WebIDE_Administrator

ZSX_WEBIDE_DEVELOPER

webide!i1

WebIDE_Developer

Table 18.1    Example Roles Collections to Create before Accessing SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

With the two role collections created, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA user must be granted at a minimum the ZSX_WEBIDE_DEVELOPER role collection example shown in Table 18.1. The application role WebIDE_Developer allows a user to access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and the SAP HANA database explorer. The WebIDE_Administrator role grants access to additional tools within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA such as the space enablement tool.

In addition to these custom role collections, a user might also need the following SAP HANA XSA privileges depending on their function:

  • At a minimum, the user needs the role collection XS_CONTROLLER_USER granted to work with spaces and organizations when building projects or deploying them to the runtime.

  • For a given space, they’ll need the space role space developers to build or deploy projects to the runtime.

If you have an SAP HANA XSA user and have the correct access to the space, organization, and SAP HANA XSA platform, you should be able to log on to the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. Before you can log on, you must identify the URL used to access the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. If you’re unsure of the URL, you can access the SAP HANA XSA command line and run the following commands to list each deployed application and its URL:

xs login
xs a

Once you have the URL, access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and provide your credentials. You’ll then land on the application’s homepage, as shown in Figure 18.10.

Figure 18.10    SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Homepage

The interface is divided into menu icon options on the left, a file menu bar on the top a workspace area containing your code, and then a working area on the right. As you open objects in the workspace, they will open in the working area on the right.

In this section, we won’t go into detail about how to use SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to develop content. That topic is beyond the scope of this book. The goal of this section is to make sure administrators understand how to set up security for SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and how users access the application.

More Information on Development within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

You can find more information on SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA within the SAP HANA Developer Guide for SAP HANA XSA, available at http://s-prs.co/v498221.

Look for the section titled “SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Reference.”

18.3.2    SAP HANA Database Explorer in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA also provides the SAP HANA database explorer where you can connect to an SAP HANA database or HDI container schema to look for and work with catalog objects at runtime. From SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA homepage, locate the file menu bar and select Tools • Database Explorer to access the SAP HANA database explorer.

Within this interface, you can add connections by clicking the large plus sign (+) in the pane just below the file menu bar. You can connect to the following Database Types: SAP HANA database, SAP HANA database (Multitenant), HDI Container, or a specific Application Managed Service Instance. Select the HDI Container option to connect to the HDI container schema. In the HDI Schema list, locate the service instance name for your HDI container. The service instance name starts with your current logon user name and ends with your container name flowed by -hdi_db. To connect to classic SAP HANA database objects, select either SAP HANA database or SAP HANA database (Multitenant) and fill in the connection information for the database.

Once you’ve established a connection to the database, you can access the SQL console where you can execute SQL statements. In addition to the standard SQL console, you can also choose the Open SQL Console (Admin) option, which launches the console as a system user with API access to the HDI container schemas and procedures. Note that you can only launch this console if you’re using an HDI container service-based connection. You can use this admin console to grant users access to runtime HDI container objects.

For each connection, you’ll be provided with a graphical list of various catalog object types. For example, if you’re searching for a table, click the table icon and then use the search bar in the pane below to locate a table by name. Once you locate an object in the list, double-click the object to reveal its metadata, or right-click the object to launch a popup window containing options for interacting with the selected object. You should now have a basic understanding of the SAP HANA database explorer within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

More Information on the SAP HANA Database Explorer

For more information on the SAP HANA database explorer, refer to the SAP HANA Database Explorer Guide, available at http://s-prs.co/v498222.

In the next section, we’ll go into more detail about HDI containers from a security perspective, and we’ll also revisit the SAP HANA database explorer using an example use case. We’ll also further explore SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA as we’ll discuss how HDI container roles are created.

18.4    HDI Containers and Security

With the SAP HANA XSA framework, SAP HANA development occurs within a service layer called the SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI). Like the SAP HANA XS or _SYS_REPO model, HDI containers have a design-time concept and a runtime concept, but as you’ll see, HDI has several differences. When creating an HDI container, SAP HANA will separate out a design-time container and a runtime container. The design-time container will host metadata and code representing database artifacts and applications. The design-time container is not part of the runtime SAP HANA database but is always attached to its corresponding runtime container. The runtime container represents deployed objects that have been activated in the SAP HANA database within a specified SAP HANA XSA space. A runtime container is part of the SAP HANA database, and when built, several corresponding database objects will be created.

From a security perspective, each HDI container is isolated from other containers and even from other SAP HANA database catalog objects out of the box. In general, a container only has access to runtime objects within that same container. HDI container-based roles, like repository roles in SAP HANA XS, can be created within the container and granted to developers and users. At design time, no known security exists: Design-time workspace security is decoupled from the SAP HANA database. A developer has access to all development artifacts within the design-time container assuming the code was shared with them from outside of SAP HANA. If they import that same content into their SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace and have been granted access to the corresponding SAP HANA XSA managed organization or space, they can potentially modify security at runtime.

This arrangement alone poses the most pressing security concern when using HDI containers to manage HDI-based repository roles. In theory, a developer could escalate their own privileges or the privileges of other users by modifying the makeup of an HDI container-based role. In addition, a developer could modify analytic privileges that govern access to data. In our opinion, a developer should not have the ability to elevate their own privileges inside or outside a container. With the SAP HANA XS repository, you could use package organization and package privileges to prevent developers from elevating their own privileges at design time. With the SAP HANA XSA development environment, you would have to set up and manage a complex landscape of independent HDI containers to decouple security objects from development objects. This decoupling is complex because HDI containers are not aware of each other, nor do they have access to each other’s content without a significant amount of repetitive administration.

To this end, we recommend that administrators continue to manage their SAP HANA security model using the SAP HANA XS repository-based roles and continue developing SAP HANA calculation views, database objects, and other items in SAP HANA XS until SAP addresses these security concerns. This recommendation is limited to the use of SAP HANA as a business intelligence solution or where the security of data is crucial. If you’re simply managing applications like OData services or GUIs, the current security capabilities of SAP HANA XSA are probably sufficient.

Now, let’s take a closer look at the architecture of the HDI container.

18.4.1    Security Architecture of the HDI Container

At runtime, an HDI container is comprised of a series of database schemas. The name of the schemas is directly based on the name of the project you define in the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace. For example, if you create the project shown in Figure 18.11, with the name MyProj, any corresponding runtime objects will be stored in a schema named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1.

Figure 18.11    Example SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA Project Structure

A corresponding database user named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 will also be created, and that user will be the owner of any runtime object deployed to the database. Note that all users created by this process are restricted users that have no critical privileges, nor can they be used to access the database. These users also have no known password. In some cases, the user accounts are also deactivated. SAP HANA XSA includes a Node.js application that will broker the creation of objects from their design-time scripts in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to their runtime equivalents within the database. In addition to the creation of the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 user, other user accounts and schemas are also created for the storage of metadata and to host other deployment APIs. Using the same example, you’ll find the following users and schemas in an SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04 system:

  • One user and schema named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI. This user and schema contain APIs as stored procedures and metadata tables. For example, you can use a stored procedure in this schema to grant standard users access to the HDI schema MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1.

  • The object owner user and schema named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO. This user is an important user from a security standpoint, which we’ll explain in more detail shortly.

  • Multiple users using the naming pattern MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1_<GUID>_DT. What roles these users play is unclear, but from a security standpoint, they can use EXECUTE on some critical API stored procedures in the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI schema.

  • Multiple users using the naming pattern MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1_<GUID>_RT. What roles these users play is unclear, but from a security standpoint, they can use EXECUTE on some critical API stored procedures in the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI schema.

From a complete list of granted privileges, users, schemas, and other database objects associated with our example HDI container named MYPROJ, you can run the example SQL statements shown in Listing 18.1 to see details concerning the deployment.

SELECT * FROM SYS.SCHEMAS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.TABLES WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.VIEWS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.PROCEDURES WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.OWNERSHIP WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.USERS WHERE USER_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.ROLES WHERE ROLE_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_ROLES WHERE ROLE_NAME like '%MYPROJ%';
SELECT * FROM SYS.SYNONYMS WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%'; 
SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_PRIVILEGES 
WHERE  SCHEMA_NAME like 'MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#%';

Listing 18.1    Example SQL to See What Is Created in the SAP HANA Database to Support an HDI Container

In addition to these users, two roles are also created. The first is the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::access_role, and the second is the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::external_privileges_role. MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::access_role is granted limited object privileges on the schema MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 and is also granted privileges defined in .hdbgrants scripts for the application user or within the application_user value array. The role MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::external_privileges_role has no defined privileges by default.

The user account that ends in “#OO” or MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO using our working example is the first account we’ll examine. “OO” is short for “object owner,” and we’ll use the term #OO at times in this chapter when referring to this user. By default, this user has limited access to the database but has the CREATE ANY, CREATE VIRTUAL PACKAGE, and SELECT METADATA object privilege on the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 schema. On its own schema, this user is only granted the CREATE TEMPORY TABLE object privilege. This user is also granted the roles _SYS_DI_OO_DEFAULTS and the PUBLIC role. The _SYS_DI_OO_DEFAULTS role provides “API”-like access to stored procedures and access to metadata views for manipulating the runtime objects in an HDI container. This role is also granted to all #OO users by default. Any privileges this role has been granted would apply to all #OO users in the database. However, we do not recommend leveraging this role in your security model design.

Out of the box, the #OO user will have access to objects in the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 schema because it is the creator or “object owner” of all objects in that schema. In SAP HANA, if you create a catalog object, you have full privileges access to it. When an HDI container requires access at runtime to non-HDI container catalog objects (i.e., classic runtime objects in the database) or other runtime objects deployed by another HDI container, the #OO user must also have access to those catalog objects. For example, if you’ve deployed SAP S/4HANA on the SAP HANA database and SAP S/4HANA created the schema SAPABAP1, you would need to log on to SAP HANA as SAPABAP1 and run the following statement for the HDI container MyProj to access tables in that schema at runtime:

GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO WITH GRANT OPTION;

A second process exists that SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developers can use to grant the #OO user access to external objects using standard database role, .hdbgrants files, user-defined services, and .hdbsynonym files within your projects. We’ll explain this process in more detail in Section 18.4.3.

The second user of interest is the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI user, or #DI user for short. This user is the owner of a schema that contains tables, views, and stored procedures that are important to the mechanics of the HDI container at runtime. As mentioned earlier, you cannot log on as this user. Therefore, you would technically need another database user that has EXECUTE access to this schema, or the procedures within the schema, before you can grant external access outside of the HDI container. This process is quite complicated and requires executing a series of stored procedures in a variety of schemas and as different users to effectively give a non-HDI user the ability to grant access to the HDI user schema instead of creating SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developer artifacts. Luckily, with SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, the SAP HANA database explorer provides an option for a user to open the SQL console as the “admin” or as _SYS_DI or as other technical system-generated users with EXECUTE access on the procedures.

Users with EXECUTE Access to the #DI Schema Procedures

Note that we could not determine the exact user that is impersonated when launching the SQL console as an admin within the SAP HANA database explorer. By querying the SAP HANA metadata views, we could see that the system account _SYS_DI is the owner of the procedures within the #DI schema. We can also see that other system-generated users also have the access. For example, the following SQL will list the user account with EXECUTE access on the procedure for the HDI container named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1:

SELECT * FROM SYS.GRANTED_PRIVILEGES 
WHERE  SCHEMA_NAME like 'MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#%' 
and OBJECT_NAME like 'GRANT_CONTAINER_%'

You can also query the ownership view to see the owner of the procedures. The following SQL will list the owners of the procedures for the HDI container named MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1:

SELECT * FROM SYS.OWNERSHIP 
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME like '%MYPROJ%'
and OBJECT_NAME like 'GRANT_CONTAINER_%';

Opening the SQL console as the “admin” is a shortcut explained in Sections Section 18.3.2 and Section 18.4.3. Another option, which we’ll discuss later in Section 18.4.2, is to create HDI container roles and then grant them to users. However, you’ll still need to use the SAP HANA database explorer’s SQL console run as an admin to grant the role to other users. Therefore, technically, you have two additional options to achieve the same result. However, these “easier” options give SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developers security access and the ability to escalate their own privileges at runtime. This access is a major security concern because you cannot selectively prevent the editing of objects at design time like you could in the SAP HANA XS _SYS_REPO platform.

In the next section, we’ll review HDI container roles and how they you can use them to provide access to catalog objects, schemas, calculation views, and other items within an HDI container.

18.4.2    HDI Container Roles

Effectively, you’ll use HDI container roles as the basis for granting database users access to runtime objects within an HDI container’s schema. Once an HDI container role is created, you can then use a special SQL console, found in the SAP HANA database explorer, to execute special stored procedures that can grant HDI container roles to users. Within this section, we’ll provide an overview of HDI container roles, describe the steps for granting HDI container roles using the SAP HANA database explorer, and finally describe the steps required to authorize a standard database user EXECUTE access to the store procedures in the HDI container’s #DI schema.

Defining HDI Container Roles

HDI container roles are like legacy the SAP HANA XS repository roles we discussed in Chapter 6; however HDI container roles can only provide security access to objects within the container by default. For the HDI role to reference external catalog objects, the #OO user must have the same access to the external catalog object including the WITH GRANT OPTION. In most cases, HDI container roles are created by developers within their project. As such, HDI container roles are not a feasible alternative to the SAP HANA XS repository-based roles that you could use to manage an entire database system’s security model. This limitation is the case for two major reasons:

  • First, no design-time security exists to prevent developers from manipulating HDI container roles when they have access to the design-time content and the ability to deploy it to container at runtime. Without this protection, developers could elevate their access to HDI content, external objects, and data within the SAP HANA database, thus bypassing standard security-based segregations. In this case, we’re specifically referring to tables, analytic privileges, and calculation views typically used in an SAP HANA-based business intelligence solution.

  • Second, the HDI container database #OO user, by default, has no access to objects outside of the container. This user would need access similar to what the _SYS_REPO user had if you were to create system-wide HDI container roles to manage the entire database’s security model. This approach would in turn give anyone with the corresponding HDI container design-time access the ability escalate their own privileges if even a single HDI container role was granted to the developer’s user account. In addition, granting HDI container roles to standard SAP HANA users is difficult, as is setting up cross-HDI container access exclusively for a security team. A complex SQL statement is required to grant HDI container roles, and complex scripts are required to grant cross-container access. This model would not be compliant with the segregation of duties and would not be secure, nor would this solution be scalable as a system-wide security model.

This process would also not be a one-time activity since, as each additional HDI container is created, access to runtime objects within that container would need to be granted to the legacy containers containing HDI roles used to govern the SAP HANA security model. The tedious nature of this arrangement also makes this solution unscalable.

Hopefully, SAP HANA will one day devise a solution where a system-managed HDI container is deployed within every SAP HANA database. A container that would have access to all new HDI containers and any classic runtime database objects in a way that is both secure from a design-time perspective and scalable from a management perspective. In the SAP HANA XS model, the _SYS_REPO service account was deployed with a high level of database access and had access to grant access to all design-time objects it owned. You could also easily grant _SYS_REPO access to runtime objects that were not created at design time. Furthermore, this grant activity only needs to be executed one time for each newly created runtime schema.

With that said, in this section, we’ll explain the makeup of HDI container roles and show you how they can be granted to users. An understanding of this process is necessary even if not recommended for supporting a system-wide security model. Some organizations have already began developing content within SAP HANA XSA, where establishing security for HDI containers is important.

HDI container roles are design-time scripts, using a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)-compliant syntax, that when built or activated, create runtime roles in the SAP HANA database. The privileges specified within the script must be possessed by the HDI #OO user, and the privileges must include the WITH GRANT OPTION. For catalog objects created in the HDI container, the #OO user will be the owner and therefore will have the necessary privileges.

For objects outside the container, #OO users will need to be granted permission, will need references to external schemas, and will need synonyms to reference external catalog objects. The synonym is required so that the .hdbrole can find the external object in the database. Based on testing, the .hdbrole only looks for catalog objects in the HDI container schema. Synonyms allow you to alias external objects in a way that the .hdbrole builder can find them. You can easily define a .hdbsynonym file to create the needed synonyms, and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA has a GUI to help you create synonyms.

For external schemas, you’ll also need a schema reference, which can be configured in a .hdbconfig file. No GUI exists for this file, and we’ll share the JSON syntax for this file in Listing 18.5. Let’s start by looking at the syntax for the .hdbrole file. Listing 18.2 shows a basic .hdbrole file with no privileges being granted.

{ 
  "role":{ 
                "name":"MyProj.db.roles::EMPTYROLE" 
          }
 }

Listing 18.2    A Basic .hdbrole File with No Privileges Being Granted

The format starts with opening and closing curly brackets, as in {<some text>}. At the next value level, you’ll define a JSON value titled “role”: { <some text> }. Within that value pair level, you’ll define the “name”:”<namespace + role name>”,{<privilege text>} value. The namespace follows the project’s folder structure. For example, if you create this role in the MyProj project and store the role in the folder path MyProj • db • src • roles, the namespace would be MyProj.db.roles:: followed by the name of the role.

The remaining structure varies based on the privilege type. To further describe the syntax, let’s specify some requirements and then provide an example .hdbrole script. For example, let’s say you need to create a role granting SELECT access on the HDI table MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS, the external table in the SYSTEM schema CUSTOMERS, the entire SYSTEM schema, and the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 schema. You would define the role using the code shown in Listing 18.3.

{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM",
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ]
    }
   }

Listing 18.3    Example .hdbrole

In addition to the .hdbrole file, you’ll also need to define .hdbsynonym and .hdbroleconfig files for the externally referenced catalog table objects and schemas. Listing 18.4 shows the syntax of the required SYSTEM.hdbsynonym file. This file is required because “MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS” is actually a synonym pointing to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMERS table.

{
  "MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS": {
    "target": {
      "object": "CUSTOMERS",
      "schema": "SYSTEM"
    }
  }
}

Listing 18.4    Required SYSTEM.hdbsynonym File for External Catalog Object References

The synonym is created in the HDI schema MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 and is required when objects within an HDI container must reference objects outside the HDI container. Again, the #OO user must have access to this object, or the project will fail to build.

In addition, you’ll need to create a .hdbroleconfig file that describes a reference to the external schema SYSTEM. Listing 18.5 shows an example of the file that is required. This JSON file requires that you map the HDI container role, by name, to an external schema reference or alias. You’ll then use the reference name "REF_SYSTEM" within the definition of your .hdbrole file.

{ 
  "MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
    }
  } 
}

Listing 18.5    Required ROLEREF.hdbroleconfig File for External Schema References

Now that we’ve reviewed the example file, let’s look at some other syntax values that you can use. An .hdbrole file can reference existing roles in the HDI container within the "global_roles" value array. The following code is an example of the value string used to reference existing roles:

"global_roles":[ 
    "HDI_ROLE_1", 
    "HDI_ROLE_2" 
]

System privileges can be configured using the "system_privileges" value array. In the following example, we are referencing two system privileges:

"system_privileges":[  
   "BACKUP ADMIN",
   "USER ADMIN"
 ]

Analytics privileges or structured privileges can be referenced using the "schema_analytic_privileges" value array. The syntax required depends on the referenced object. If you’re referencing an analytic privilege that is within your HDI container, you would use the following syntax:

"schema_analytic_privileges":[
{
"privileges": ["MyProj.db.aps::AP_CUSTOMER"]
}

In this case, you’ll only need the namespace or package folder structure and the name of the analytic privilege entered into the "privileges" value string. If you’re referring to an external structured privilege that has a schema, you would use the syntax shown in Listing 18.6.

"schema_analytic_privileges":[
   {
     "schema_reference":"APSchemaRef1",
     "privileges": ["AP1", "AP2"] }
 ]

Listing 18.6    Privilege Value String

As with external schemas, the schema reference must be defined in the supporting .hdbroleconfig file.

Additional Information on the Syntax of the .hdbrole File

For additional information on the complete syntax of the .hdbrole file, refer to the “SAP HDI Artifact Types and Build Plugins Reference” section in the SAP HANA Development Infrastructure Reference Guide for SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, available at http://s-prs.co/v498223.

Recall from Chapter 6 that repository-based roles in the SAP HANA XS platform could not be directly granted to a grantee using GRANT or REVOKE statements. You had to execute a stored procedure and provide input parameters to grant repository roles. This limitation is because only the owner _SYS_REPO can grant the role as no other user has the WITH GRANT OPTION. However, most of the GUI interfaces would automatically execute the procedures when you selected repository roles within the GUI workflow. HDI roles have a similar reequipment. Only system-managed technical users can grant HDI container roles out of the box. With the SAP HANA XS repository roles, you simply need to grant EXECUTE on the _SYS_REPO schema to security administrators, allowing them to perform the action. That process was easy to execute because the SYSTEM account had these privileges including the WITH GRANT OPTION. You could also include them in repository roles without much effort.

Within the HDI platform, only the _SYS_DI user and a few other technical users have these privileges directly by default. Therefore, you only have two options for granting these privileges:

  • You can use the SAP HANA database explorer based on a service connection of the HDI container. Within that connection, you can right-click and select Open SQL Console (Admin), which will open the SQL console that impersonates a user that has EXECUTE access to the procedures.

  • You can leverage the stored procedure in the _SYS_DI schema called GRANT_CONTAINER_API_PRIVILEGES_WITH_GRANT_OPTION. By default, the SYSTEM account has EXECUTE privileges on this procedure. However, running this procedure is not straightforward since you must run a series of other SQL statements in the correct sequence to use this procedure properly.

Let’s look at each of these options in more detail starting with the first option.

Granting HDI Roles with the SAP HANA Database Explorer

To grant an HDI role using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, you must first access the SAP HANA database explorer. In Section 18.3, we provided details for accessing the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA application. Once logged into the application, you’ll notice three icons on the vertical bar on the left side, as shown in Figure 18.12. The icon that appears as a set of stacked cubes or boxes is the icon used to launch the SAP HANA database explorer view. You can also use the file menu option Tools • Database Explorer to launch the SAP HANA database explorer interface.

Figure 18.12    SAP HANA Database Explorer in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

Before you can launch the Open SQL Console (Admin) option, you’ll need to create the correct type of connection to the database. To create the connection, locate the large plus sign (+) above the pane that contains the existing database connections shown in Figure 18.12. If this is the first time you’re accessing the SAP HANA database explorer, you won’t have an existing connection. Once you click the plus sign (+), the Add Database window will appear. Choose the Database Type of HDI container. Search for your current container. In our environment, the correct container was prefixed with the current logon user’s name followed by a serial code, and then our project name was suffixed with hdi_db, as shown in Figure 18.13.

Figure 18.13    Adding a Database from an HDI Container Connection

This connection will show you all the catalog objects in the HDI’s database schema. To access the SQL console as an admin, right-click the connection’s top node and choose Open SQL Console (Admin), as shown in Figure 18.14.

The SQL console will open on the right, where you can execute a series of SQL statements that will grant HDI container roles to a specified user. The SQL that must be executed is somewhat complex. You must run five different statements to grant the role. In addition, you’ll need the technical name of the HDI container.

Figure 18.14    Accessing the SQL Console as an HDI Container Administrator

If you need the technical name of the HDI container, you can run a SQL statement to view the name, but you’ll need to use a different SQL console. The Admin user does not have the correct access to show the technical container name, so you’ll need to run the SQL statement in a SQL console connected with a user with SELECT access on the _SYS_DI schema. For example, the SYSTEM user has this access by default. The following statement will show you the technical name of the HDI container:

SELECT * FROM "_SYS_DI".M_ALL_CONTAINERS WHERE CONTAINER_NAME like 'MYPROJ%';

After getting the technical name, make sure you’re in the SQL console connected as the HDI container admin before proceeding with the next steps. The first statement you’ll need to run sets the default schema used for your temporary tables:

SET SCHEMA "MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI";

The second statement will create a local temporary column table in the schema. You’ll use this temporary table to store role grant information used as an input parameter in the stored procedure:

CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #ROLES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_SCHEMA_ROLES;

The third statement will insert the role name information and target user into the temporary table named #ROLES. To grant the role MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS (input parameter 1) to the user SYSTEM (input parameter 3), you’ll need to adjust the following statement to match your use case:

INSERT INTO #ROLES ( ROLE_NAME, PRINCIPAL_SCHEMA_NAME, PRINCIPAL_NAME ) 
VALUES ( 'MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS', '', 'SYSTEM' );

The fourth statement will call the stored procedure in the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI schema. When crafting this statement, make sure you update the schema name to match the name of the #DI schema supporting your HDI container:

CALL MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_SCHEMA_ROLES(#ROLES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);

The output of this procedure will include multiple tabs of results. Look at the Results 1 tab to see a verbose message about the actions that were executed and to validate that the role was granted properly to the user.

Finally, you’ll drop the temporary table because it is no longer needed, as follows:

DROP TABLE #ROLES;

After running each of these statements correctly, your target user will be granted the HDI container role. Now let’s look at the second option in more detail.

Granting HDI Roles with a Database User

As a second option, you can also use a standard SAP HANA database user to grant the statements outlined above and effectively grant an HDI container role to a database user. However, the standard user must first be set up with the same privileges that the HDI container admin possesses. Fortunately, the _SYS_DI schema provides a procedure that you can use to grant the correct privileges to another user.

By default, only the SYSTEM account has the access necessary to execute the procedures in the _SYS_DI schema. Therefore, you’ll need to start by connecting to the SQL console as the SYSTEM user.

The first statement you’ll need to execute will set the default schema used in the example. Run the following SQL statement:

SET SCHEMA SYSTEM;

Next, you’ll temporarily move your HDI container to the _SYS_DI container group. This step is required because the procedure in the _SYS_DI container is hard-coded to reference this group and will not work on HDI containers in other groups. When we’re done, you’ll move the HDI container back to its original group. Before you move the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 HDI container, you’ll need to query the database to capture its current container group with the following statement:

SELECT * FROM "_SYS_DI".M_ALL_CONTAINERS WHERE CONTAINER_NAME like 'MYPROJ%';

Look for the value in the CONTAINER_GROUP_NAME column. In our example, our column was named CG_SYS_XS_HANA_BROKER_2. Again, we’ll move this container back to this group when we’re done granting the privileges.

Now, you can execute the SQL to temporarily move the HDI container into the required container group _SYS_DI with the following statement:

CALL _SYS_DI.MOVE_CONTAINER_TO_GROUP('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', '_SYS_DI', _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);

Next, you’ll create a local temporary table in the SYSTEM schema named #PRIVILEGES with the following statement:

CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #PRIVILEGES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_API_PRIVILEGES;

Next, you’ll insert all the API privileges into the temporary table. This array is required as an input for the stored procedure. In the following script, replace the target user name JHAUN with your target user account name:

INSERT INTO #PRIVILEGES (PRINCIPAL_NAME, PRIVILEGE_NAME, OBJECT_NAME) SELECT 'JHAUN', PRIVILEGE_NAME, OBJECT_NAME FROM _SYS_DI.T_DEFAULT_CONTAINER_ADMIN_PRIVILEGES;

Next, execute the stored procedure in the _SYS_DI schema that grants the array of privileges in the #PRIVILEGES temporary table. The name of the procedure is GRANT_CONTAINER_API_PRIVILEGES_WITH_GRANT_OPTION, which will grant all the API privileges to the user and include the WITH GRANT OPTION so that the user can selectively grant the same privileges to other users in the future. In your script, you’ll need to update the value for the first parameter to match the technical name of your HDI container, as follows:

CALL _SYS_DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_API_PRIVILEGES_WITH_GRANT_OPTION('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', #PRIVILEGES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);

The results of this procedure include multiple output tabs. Review the first tab, which will contain a verbose information about each grant action.

Next, you’ll need to drop the temporary table #PRIVILEGES. Run the following SQL:

DROP TABLE #PRIVILEGES;

Finally, you’ll need to return our HDI container back to its original HDI container group. This step is critical and can’t be skipped.

CALL _SYS_DI.MOVE_CONTAINER_TO_GROUP('MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1', 'CG_SYS_XS_HANA_BROKER_2', _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);

At this point, you can now log on to the SQL console as the target user and run the following statements. These examples are the same statements used in the previous section. Therefore, we’ll assume that you already understand each step and won’t go into detail about each step. Run the statements shown in Listing 18.7, adjusting the syntax for your specific environment.

SET SCHEMA "MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI";
CREATE LOCAL TEMPORARY COLUMN TABLE #ROLES LIKE _SYS_DI.TT_SCHEMA_ROLES;
INSERT INTO #ROLES ( ROLE_NAME, PRINCIPAL_SCHEMA_NAME, PRINCIPAL_NAME ) 
VALUES ( 'MyProj.db.roles::TABLE_READ_ONLY_ACCESS', '', 'SYSTEM' );
CALL MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#DI.GRANT_CONTAINER_SCHEMA_ROLES(#ROLES, _SYS_DI.T_NO_PARAMETERS, ?, ?, ?);
DROP TABLE #ROLES;

Listing 18.7    SQL Statements That Must Be Executed to Grant an HDI Container Role to a Database User

You should now have a basic understanding of the structure of the .hdbrole and the two dependent objects .hdbsynonym and .hdbroleconfig that are required when referencing external catalog objects. You should also understand the process for granting an HDI container role to a database user and also the process for creating an HDI container admin user. In the next section, we’ll provide you more details on .hdbsynonym files, which are also required when you develop calculation views against external tables. We’ll also show you the synonym GUI available in the latest version of SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA.

18.4.3    Granting the HDI Container Access to External Objects

When working within an HDI container using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, two security considerations must be addressed: First, developers might need access to runtime catalog objects that are outside of the HDI container as well as access to objects in other HDI containers. By default, developers will only have access to catalog objects within the HDI container or project workspace.

If you’re building a business intelligence solution, your tables and schemas will likely be in a non-repository-based schemas or a schema owned by a standard user account. Therefore, your HDI container will probably need access to external objects or other HDI containers. Second, when you deploy HDI container content referencing external objects, the #OO user will require access to those external objects at runtime. SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA provides mechanisms that address both situations, but neither mechanism can be completed exclusively within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA by developers. Therefore, you’ll need to explore each option and its requirements in detail. Let’s look first at the security considerations for external catalog objects, and then we’ll look at the considerations for other HDI containers.

Developer Access to External Catalog Objects at Design Time

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA uses user-provided services and services instances to proxy access to external catalog objects or HDI containers. This service is part of the SAP HANA XSA architecture and can be created in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA or within the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. You can also use the SAP HANA XSA cockpit to manage the service after it is created. A service is effectively a snippet of code that provides a Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) access bridge to the SAP HANA database. The snippet of code is in JSON format, as shown in the example in Figure 18.15.

Figure 18.15    Example Definition of a User-Provided Service within the SAP HANA XSA Cockpit GUI

Once defined and associated with your HDI container di-builder, you can configure your project to use this service. However, SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA also has a workflow to help you create the service, and we’ll walk you through this process in this section.

Before you build a service, let’s first discuss the security that the service user will require. The service bridge provides two features. First, at design time, the service can be selected when searching for external catalog objects. For example, when creating synonyms or SAP HANA calculation views, you might need to search for an external object using this service. Second, if you use .hdbgrants files to grant privileges to the #OO user, this service bridge will grant the permissions to the #OO user. Therefore, when using .hdbgrants, the service user must have the required privileges for both scenarios including the WITH GRANT OPTION. This service user will also become a permanent component of the project once referenced in .hdbgrants project files. The security team must carefully design the service account user on the SAP HANA database and ensure that the account only possesses the privileges necessary to support the application.

Now, let’s look at the process of creating a user-provided service using SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA GUI. Before starting this step, make sure your project has an assigned space and di-builder. Within your SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA project, right-click the db folder and choose New • SAP HANA Service Connection, as shown in Figure 18.16.

Figure 18.16    Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection

The Add External SAP HANA Service window will appear. Enter the details for the SAP HANA database, as shown in Figure 18.17, including the connection information and the credentials of a user in the local database.

Figure 18.17    Defining the Service Connection

Click OK to continue. The service will now be available to help you search for external objects outside the HDI container. For example, when creating a synonym, you can connect to the service and search for objects within the GUI. Again, from a security standpoint, only objects that the service has SELECT access on will be displayed. A developer doesn’t have to create this service if you are concerned about the developer having the credentials of the service user. A security admin and SAP HANA XSA admin can define the service using the SAP HANA XSA cockpit. The developer can then update the mta.yaml file and reference the service. For example, you can use the mta.yaml GUI editor to create or change the service value at any time.

Figure 18.18 shows an example of editing this value using the mta.yml GUI. You’ll find the mta.yaml file within the workspace of your project. By default, opening the file will launch the GUI editor. Select the Resources option and then choose the cross-container-servcie-1 to reveal the service-name attribute. Change the value to match the value of the user-defined service. Note that changing this value might impact any existing .hdbgrants files within the project because .hdbgrants files reference services for granting access to the #OO user at runtime.

Figure 18.18    Changing the Service-Name Associated with Our MTA Project within the mta.yaml File

Developer Access to Additional HDI Containers

We’ll use a similar process to provide design-time access to another HDI container. When defining the SAP HANA service connection, choose the option HDI Container and then select an existing HDI container. The list will only show HDI containers that are fully built and deployed to the database and have a service instance in SAP HANA XSA. A new service will be defined in the mta.yaml file that will also be selectable when defining calculation views and synonyms in the GUI. Note that you’ll need to grant the local project #OO user access to the remote container before you can build referencing objects. In the next section, we’ll explain how you can use the .hdbgrants file and HDI roles to grant the necessary access.

#OO Service User Access to Objects at Runtime

Before you can fully deploy or build content files in a project, the #OO user of the container must have access to the remote content it references. Remote content includes classic SAP HANA database objects as well as other HDI containers. You can create this access in three ways. Let’s look at each option available for a given scenario:

  • When access to external objects in the classic SAP HANA database is required, the security team can directly grant privileges. In short, they can grant the #OO user access to the external catalog objects using the SQL console or SAP HANA cockpit. This step can be completed independent of the developer and SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA artifacts. This option is the more secure option because the developer won’t need access to a user-provided service that can grant privileges.

  • Security admins can create standard roles within the database that can then be granted to the #OO user, using .hdbgrants files defined by the developers. In this case, the user-provided service will require the ability to grant these roles to the #OO user. The service user is the user that grants these roles to the #OO accounts based on the information in the .hdbgrants file. This approach can be less secure because a crafty developer could grant the #OO user access to an object and then update an HDI roles in that container, which is assigned to their account, to elevate their own privileges.

  • When developers require access to a remote HDI container, they can again use .hdbgrants files to provide the local #OO user access to remote HDI container objects. In this case, the remote HDI container will need two HDI roles created within their HDI container by a developer as well. With this scenario, developers can build the solution without any involvement from the SAP HANA database security team.

To better understand each of these options, let’s walk through an example setup scenario for each option. Let’s start with a detailed view of the first option where the SAP HANA database security team grants the privileges to the #OO user directly.

Directly Granting Privileges to the #OO User

When directly granting privileges to the #OO user, the SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA developer does not need to create .hdbgrant files within their project but will still need a service for design-time access to database objects outside of the HDI container. They will also need to communicate a list of external objects that they that their HDI container will access. Let’s start by explaining the process and requirements necessary to set up a service user.

In this scenario, the developer will use the service to view and read metadata from objects outside of the HDI container. The service account will need SELECT access to views and tables in the external schema as well as EXECUTE access to table valued functions and stored procedures. Let’s assume that the external schema is named SAPABAP1 and that the developers need to query all tables, views, and tabled valued functions in this schema. To achieve this setup, the administrator will execute the SQL shown in Listing 18.8.

CREATE USER SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 PASSWORD "<some password>" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE;
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1;
GRANT SELECT, EXECUTE ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;

Listing 18.8    Four Example SQL Statements Creating a Service Account and Roles for Design-Time Access to Catalog Objects outside the HDI Container

As shown in Listing 18.8, the first statement will create a service account user named SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 that the developer or SAP HANA XSA admin can utilize when creating the user-provided service. You’ll then create a standard role and then grant that role the privileges necessary to access the SAPABAP1 schema. Finally, we’ll grant the role SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE to the user account.

Next, you’ll need to grant the same privileges to the #OO user allowing the HDI content to access the same tables at runtime. The SQL shown in Listing 18.9 can be utilized to set up the necessary security.

CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE WITH GRANT OPTION;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO;

Listing 18.9    Three Example SQL Statements Granting the #OO User Access to a Catalog Schema at Run-time

As shown in Listing 18.9, you’ll start by creating a role that will be granted to the HDI container MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO or object owner user. You’ll then grant SELECT access to the role and include the WITH GRANT OPTION. The WITH GRANT OPTION is required as the #OO user is delegating access to the remote schema. Finally, you’ll grant the SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE to the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO user.

Again, with this option, the developer does not need to use .hdbgrants files within their project, nor does the service user require the ability to grant these same privileges to other users. The service account, used by the user-provided service, has limited access to the database.

Using .hdbgrants to Provide Access to External Catalog Objects

A second option, similar to the first option, is to leverage the .hdbgrants files within a project. However, one key difference is that the user-provided service must have the ability to grant two specific roles to the #OO user. In this scenario, the service user will require elevated privileges. Let’s start by examining the SQL that the SAP HANA security team will execute to create the service user, roles, and permissions.

First, you’ll need to create a service user SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 like we did in the previous section’s example. Execute the following SQL to create the service account user:

CREATE USER SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 PASSWORD "<some password>" NO FORCE_FIRST_PASSWORD_CHANGE;

Next, you’ll need to create two roles like you did in the previous section’s example. Execute the following SQL to create the two roles:

CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
CREATE ROLE SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE;

Next, you’ll need to grant access to the two roles. The first role would be used by the application layer user in the .hdbgrants file. The second role will be used for the object owner in the .hdbgrants file. The object owner will require the WITH GRANT OPTION. Execute the following SQL to grant permissions to the two roles:

GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA SAPABAP1 TO SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE WITH GRANT OPTION;

Finally, you’ll need to grant both roles to the SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 user account including the WITH ADMIN OPTION. The .hdbgrants file will use the service user to grant these roles to the #OO user. Therefore, the service account now needs elevated access to accomplish this. This arrangement is a major difference from the first option, where a security team member grants directly to the #OO user. When using .hdbgrants files, the service user does this task and therefore needs the required privileges. Execute the following SQL to grant the two roles to the service account, including the WITH ADMIN OPTION:

GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 WITH ADMIN OPTION;
GRANT SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE TO SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 WITH ADMIN OPTION;

Now, let’s walk through the process the developer would follow in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA to create the user-provided service, synonyms, and .hdbgrants files. Let’s start by accessing SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and opening the existing project MyProj for this example. Start by creating the user-provided service needed to access the SAPABAP1 schema at design time and to grant the created roles at runtime to the #OO user.

Right-click the folder db within the project and choose SAP HANA Service Connection, as shown in Figure 18.19.

Figure 18.19    Creating a New User-Provided Service within Our Project

Using the service account credentials created by the SAP HANA security team in our example, create a service named SAPABAP1, as shown in Figure 18.20. We recommend using the target schema name for the service to help other developers identify the right service.

Figure 18.20    Defining the User-Provided Service

To further demonstrate the example, let’s assume that the developer is creating a calculation view based on the table /SDF/SQLCUST in the SAPBAP1 schema. Assume that the developer is adding a new table to a project node within the calculation view. The Find Data Source window will appear, as shown in Figure 18.21. In this window, choose the External Services and then SAPABAP1 as the service name. Search for the table /SDF/SQLCUST. Select the table in the list and then click the Create Synonym button.

Figure 18.21    Using the External Service to Find the External Table and then Create a Synonym

SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA provides options to help developers easily create synonyms and .hdbgrant files. All a developer needs to know are the names of the two roles provided by the SAP HANA security team. On the next screen, shown in Figure 18.22, enter the desired Synonym Name in the provided field. The synonym is required to link the local HDI container to the external table.

In the section below the synonym list, choose the generate .hdbgrants file option and then enter the role “SVC_FOR_HDI_#OO_SAPABAP1_ROLE” in the Object Owner Role field. Then, enter “SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1_ROLE” in the Application User Role field. Note that you only need to choose these options the first time you use the service. Click Finish, and the development infrastructure builder will partially deploy to validate that the service user has the necessary access. In most cases, errors at this stage result from the service account not having the necessary privileges to grant items to the #OO user.

Figure 18.22    Defining the Synonym and Creating the .hdbgrants File in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA

Now, let’s look at the two files that were generated by the workflow. The first is the SAPABAP1.hdbgrants file, as shown in Figure 18.23. The syntax of the file links directly to the user-provided service name SAPBAP1 in the first value, which tells the builder to use that service connection and those credentials when granting privileges to the #OO user.

The next two values object_owner and application_user, define the roles that will be granted and their intended targets. The role entered into the object_owner value will be granted to the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO user, and the application_user value will be granted to the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::access_role role. This role is granted to system-managed user accounts tied to the HDI container only but can provide runtime access to developers in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. Therefore, this role should only have limited privileges to view, excluding the WITH GRANT OTION. When this file is built in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA, the specified roles will be granted by the service user SVC_FOR_HDI_PRJ_SAPABAP1 to the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1#OO and the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1::access_role role.

Figure 18.23    The SAPABAP1.hdbgrants File

The next file is the SAPABAP1.hdbsynonym file, as shown in Figure 18.24. This file defines synonyms for the HDI container that reference external catalog objects. Again, all development artifacts within the HDI container assume that objects in the HDI container schema. Therefore, you’ll need to use synonyms to link to external objects.

Figure 18.24    The SAPABAP1.hdbsynonym File

When this file is built, a runtime synonym will be created in the MYPROJ_HDI_DB_1 schema.

In summary, this option requires SAP HANA security team members and developers work jointly in finalizing the solution. The security team will create the service account users and roles. Then, developers will set up the .hdbgrants file referencing these roles. While developers can also create the service, SAP HANA XSA admins can create the service in the SAP HANA XSA cockpit, which prevents the developers from obtaining service account credentials.

More Information on Using .hdbgrants Files

The SAP HANA Developer Guide for XS Advanced Model includes a section called “Using Synonyms to Access External Schemas and Objects in XS Advanced.” The guide walks you through the complete example using an external classic schema or schema not maintained by the HDI container. The following link references this document and section: http://s-prs.co/v498224.

The “Syntax Options in the hdbgrants File” section provides more details on the various options available in the .hdbgrants file and is available at http://s-prs.co/v498225.

In the next section, we’ll review the processes used to manage security between HDI containers.

Using .hdbgrants to Provide Access between HDI Containers

Establishing access between two containers can be accomplished by developers without little intervention by the security team. This process assumes that developers have access to the spaces or organizations where the HDI containers are stored. While convenient, this arrangement also violates most segregation of duties standards. Despite this lack of control, organizations often find creating multiple containers and then granting access between the containers necessary. To help you understand this process, let’s establish the names of two containers within an example SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA workspace. The name of the first HDI container will be MyProj, an example we’ve already used many times throughout this chapter. The name of the second example HDI container will be EXAMPLE. We’ll refer to MyProj as the primary HDI container and EXAMPLE as the target HDI container.

To begin the setup process, you’ll need to create two HDI container roles in the primary container MyProj. These roles should be set up exclusively to manage the universal connection between containers. The following list includes runtime names of the two roles that will be created in the MyProj project:

  • MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS

  • MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#

In addition to the two roles, you’ll also need to create an .hdbroleconfig file that will map these two roles to a schema alias or schema reference. This step is required because you’ll grant external schema access to the target HDI container. Effectively, you’ll use the MyProj schema as a proxy to the external schema in the .hdbroleconfig file.

Within the project, you’ve created the folder structure db • src • roles and will be placing the role scripts in that folder. The design-time name of the first role will be MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS.hdbrole. Its runtime name will be MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS, and the role will be configured with JSON syntax shown in Listing 18.10.

{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM",
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ],
 "schema_analytic_privileges":[
   {
     "privileges": ["MyProj.db.aps::AP_CUSTOMER"]
    }
          ]
    }
   }

Listing 18.10    The MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS.hdbrole Script

The script shown in Listing 18.10 will grant the following:

  • SELECT to the HDI table "MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS"

  • SELECT to the HDI synonym "MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS" which actually points to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMER table.

  • SELECT to the schema reference REF_SYSTEM which actually points to the SYSTEM schema.

  • SELECT to the HDI container schema MYPRJ_HDI_DB_1

  • The HDI container analytic privilege MyProj.db.aps::AP_CUSTOMER

Note that, in the script found shown in Listing 18.10, anything granted in the "schema_privileges" value array that does not include a "reference" value is assumed to be a grant on the HDI container schema MYPRJ_HDI_DB_1.

The second role will similar to the first but will require the "privileges_with_grant_option" in the script for each privilege. This option will allow the grantee to also grant the same privilege to others. Recall that this ability is a requirement when granting privileges to the container’s #OO user. In addition, you must end the runtime name of the role with a #, which signifies that the roles contain the "privileges_with_grant_option" and the HDI infrastructure will only allow this privilege to be granted to the #OO user of a target container via an .hdbgrants file.

The design-time name of the second role will be MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS.hdbrole. Its runtime name will be MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#, and the role will be configured with JSON syntax shown in Listing 18.11.

{ 
  "role":{ 
    "name":"MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#", 
      "object_privileges":[ 
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
      } ,
      { 
       "name":"MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", 
       "type":"TABLE", 
       "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
      }
    ],
      
      "schema_privileges":[  
{  
    "reference":"REF_SYSTEM_2",
    "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
},
{  
    "privileges_with_grant_option":[ "SELECT" ]
}
  ]
    }
   }

Listing 18.11    MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS.hdbrole Script

The script shown in Listing 18.11 will grant the following access:

  • SELECT to the HDI table "MyProj.db::CUSTOMERS" including the WITH GRANT OPTION

  • SELECT to the HDI synonym "MyProj.db::CS_CUSTOMERS", which actually points to the SYSTEM.CUSTOMER table including the WITH GRANT OPTION.

  • SELECT to the schema reference REF_SYSTEM including the WITH GRANT OPTION which points to the SYSTEM schema.

  • SELECT to the HDI container schema MYPRJ_HDI_DB_1 including the WITH GRANT OPTION

Before you can build roles within your project, you’ll create the MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_ROLREF.hdbroleconfig file to provide link to the SYSTEM schema referenced in the Listing 18.10 and Listing 18.11 files. The file must contain the JSON statement shown in Listing 18.12.

{ 
 "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
        }
  },
   "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#":{ 
    "REF_SYSTEM_2":{ 
      "schema":"SYSTEM" 
        }
  }
 }

Listing 18.12    MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_ROLREF.hdbroleconfig File

Within your project, you can now build the three files that will deploy these roles at runtime. These roles will need to be active at runtime so that the EXAMPLE container can access them.

To complete the process, you’ll now need to access the target EXAMPLE project in SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA. In this project, we’ll create two items. First, you’ll need to create an SAP HANA service connection to the primary HDI container MyProj. Second, you’ll need to create the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file that will reference the two HDI roles you created in the prior steps.

Let’s start by creating the service connection to the primary HDI container MyProj. Access SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and expand the EXAMPLE project node to reveal the db folder. Right-click the db folder and choose the option New • SAP HANA Service Connection. Choose the HDI container option and then select the service in the list that references the MyProj container. The name of the service will start with the name of the user that activated it, followed by a serialized number and letter string and then end with -MyProj-hdb_db, as shown in Figure 18.25.

Figure 18.25    Choosing the MyProj Service When Creating an SAP HANA Service Connection

Click OK to add this service to your mta.yaml file. Note the name of the service because you’ll need to reference this name when defining your .hdbgrants file.

Next, you’ll need to define the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file. This file will grant the primary container MyProj roles to various HDI container systems users. This step is required to so that runtime content within the target EXAMPLE container can access runtime content within the MyProj container. Within the db • src folder, create the file MYPROJ.hdbgrants. The file should contain the JSON text shown in Listing 18.13.

{
  "XSA_ADMIN-x6o70e6hj4yiatlu-MyProj-hdi_db" : {
   "object_owner" : { 
      "schema_roles" : [
       "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#"
      ]
    },
    "application_user" : {
      "schema_roles" : [
        "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Listing 18.13    The MYPROJ.hdbgrants File in the EXAMPLE Project

Within the script, you’ll start by referencing the service name "XSA_ADMIN-x6o70e6hj4yiatlu-MyProj-hdi_db" : { . This name is specific to the name you set up in the mta.yaml project or when creating the SAP HANA service connection. You’ll then assign the two roles to the different service account users. The role "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_OO_ACCESS#" is the role with the highest level of access and must be granted to the #OO user within the "object_owner" JSON value array. The "application_user" JSON value array will be mapped to the "MyProj.db.roles::MYPROJ_EXT_HDI_APP_ACCESS" role.

Once the MYPROJ.hdbgrants is built and deployed to runtime, you can now reference MyProj runtime objects within the EXAMPLE project. Keep in mind that you’ll first also need to create synonyms in the EXAMPLE project that reference objects in the MyProj container. However, the GUI will walk you thought this process any time you browse for objects from the HDI container service connection. Again, the service connection allows developers to search for objects native to the primary HDI container MyProj at design time. In addition, the service connection allows the MYPROJ.hdbgrants file to grant its roles to the EXAMPLE_HDI_DB_1#OO user at runtime.

18.5    Summary

You should now have a basic understanding of the difference scenarios and options that security teams need to understand when supporting security in the SAP HANA XSA environment. The SAP HANA XSA cockpit is used to configure SAP HANA XSA users, access to organizations, and access to spaces. Many other options are available, including the management of the service connections key to providing security within SAP Web IDE for SAP HANA and with HDI containers.
